A.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
A.q: Which set of features characterizes a benign tumor?
opts: Autonomous growth, clonal origin, parenchyma and stroma, a single genetic alteration, no stimulus needed
Those describe any neoplasm, benign or malignant; a benign tumor specifically is well circumscribed, compresses surrounding tissue, and does not metastasize.
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses, abnormal differentiation, and invasion
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses and abnormal differentiation mark the malignant end; a benign tumor is usually well differentiated.
Circumscribed, compresses, often encapsulated, well differentiated, no metastasis, slow
Correct — each has a malignant counterpart: a ragged border, infiltration and invasion, various degrees of differentiation, possible metastasis, and rapid growth.
Ragged border, infiltrates surrounding tissue, no capsule, variably differentiated, may metastasize, grows rapidly
That is the malignant profile; a benign tumor is instead well circumscribed, often has a fibrous capsule, and does not metastasize.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which tinea subtype affects the nails?
opts: Tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis
Correct. Corporis is trunk and limbs, pedis foot, cruris groin, capitis head, facialis face, manuum hand, barbae beard.
Tinea capitis, also called onychomycosis
Tinea capitis affects the head; onychomycosis is the other name for tinea unguium, the dermatophyte infection of the nails.
Tinea manuum, affecting the nails of the hand
Tinea manuum affects the hand, not the nails specifically; the nail infection is tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis.
Tinea barbae, affecting nails and beard
Tinea barbae affects the beard area, not the nails; the nail infection is tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which mechanism explains the ototoxicity of gentamicin and tobramycin?
opts: They cross-link DNA in the stria vascularis, disturbing endolymph ion homeostasis
DNA cross-linking in the stria vascularis is the mechanism of the platinum agents, cisplatin and carboplatin, which cause bilateral permanent sensorineural loss.
Reactive oxygen species destroy outer hair cells from the base, so high pitches go first
Correct. Aminoglycosides induce reactive oxygen species that selectively destroy outer hair cells, starting at the cochlear base, so high-pitch hearing is lost first.
They alter the stria vascularis potential reversibly
That is the loop diuretic effect, and reversibility is what separates it from the aminoglycosides.
They inhibit the prestin motor protein in outer hair cells
Inhibiting prestin in outer hair cells is the salicylate mechanism, and its hallmark is tinnitus rather than permanent threshold loss.

A.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
A.q: What is the hallmark of dry, atrophic macular degeneration?
opts: Cotton-wool spots in the nerve fiber layer
Cotton-wool spots mark nerve fiber layer ischemia in diabetic retinopathy; the hallmark of dry macular degeneration is drusen.
Drusen — discrete yellow extracellular debris beneath the pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane
Correct — drusen are discrete yellow extracellular deposits of lipofuscin and apolipoproteins beneath the pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane, the hallmark of the dry form.
Choroidal neovascularization breaching upward into the subretinal space
Choroidal neovascularization breaching into the subretinal space is the wet form; the dry form's hallmark is drusen beneath the pigment epithelium.
Neovascularization on the optic disc
New vessels on the optic disc belong to proliferative diabetic retinopathy; dry macular degeneration's hallmark is drusen beneath the pigment epithelium.

A.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
A.q: Which statement correctly identifies the carcinogens produced by the combustion of tobacco?
opts: Aromatic amines, causing bladder and lung cancer; among the most powerful carcinogens known
Aromatic amines are classically emphasized in occupational bladder cancer; the tobacco combustion products are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
Nitrosamines, causing gastric and esophageal cancer
The key tobacco combustion products are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which cause bladder and lung cancer rather than gastric cancer.
Aflatoxins, causing hepatocellular carcinoma
Aflatoxin is not a tobacco combustion product; burning tobacco yields polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, among the most powerful carcinogens known.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, causing bladder and lung cancer
Correct — among the most powerful carcinogens known, and tobacco smoke contains numerous others besides.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: The term PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocyte) refers to which cells?
opts: All granulocytes
Correct. Polymorphonuclear leukocyte, abbreviated PMN, is used to refer to all granulocytes rather than to neutrophils alone.
Neutrophils only
Neutrophils are only one of the three granulocytes; PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocyte) covers neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils.
All mononuclear leucocytes
Mononuclear leucocyte is the alternative name for the agranulocytes, the opposite grouping.
Plasma cells and memory B cells
Plasma cells and memory B cells are mononuclear cells, not granulocytes; PMN (polymorphonuclear leukocyte) refers to all granulocytes.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Which pairing of removal mechanism and result of failed removal is correct for the meshwork of fibrinous inflammation?
opts: Complement fragment C3b; failure results in ulceration
C3b is an opsonin that binds foreign material; the fibrin meshwork can only be removed by fibrolytic enzymes, and failed removal results in scar tissue.
Macrophage digestion; failure results in gangrene
The fibrin meshwork can only be removed by fibrolytic enzymes, and failure results in scar tissue; gangrene is a severe form of necrosis instead.
Phagocytosis by neutrophils; failure produces pus
Pus defines the suppurative pattern; the fibrin meshwork is removed only by fibrolytic enzymes, and failure of that removal leads to scar tissue.
Fibrolytic enzymes; failure results in scar tissue formation
Correct. The meshwork can only be removed by fibrolytic enzymes, and failure of this results in scar tissue formation.

A.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
A.q: Which statement describes familial adenomatosis polyposis syndrome?
opts: Hundreds to thousands of premalignant polyps young, then colon cancer by fifty
Correct — five hundred to two thousand five hundred adenomatous polyps in the teens and twenties. The responsible gene is adenomatous polyposis coli.
Patients develop a single premalignant polyp in childhood, and colon cancer by age thirty
Patients develop 500 to 2,500 premalignant adenomatous polyps in their teens and twenties, and colon cancer by age 50.
Patients develop multiple neurofibromas at puberty, and sarcoma by age forty
Nervous system tumors follow neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2; this syndrome instead produces hundreds to thousands of colon polyps.
Patients develop skin cancer in sun-exposed areas from early childhood
Skin cancer in sun-exposed areas is xeroderma pigmentosum, an inherited inability to repair mutations caused by ultraviolet B radiation.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: What is a biomaterial?
opts: Anything not human that is put into a human
Correct. A biomaterial is anything not human put into a human, and it becomes coated with immunoglobulin G and C3b once implanted.
Any material that has been sterilized before implantation
Sterility is a separate property; a sterile implant still counts as a biomaterial and still provokes an inflammatory response.
Any tissue harvested from the patient's own body
The patient's own tissue is human; a biomaterial is anything not human that is put into a human, such as an implanted device.
Any protein produced during the inflammatory response
Mediators and opsonins are proteins of the response; a biomaterial is anything not human placed into a human, which those opsonins coat.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What can a myopic patient see well?
opts: Objects up close
Correct — myopia is nearsightedness, so near vision is the preserved one.
Objects far away
Distance vision is what fails in myopia, because the long globe focuses in front of the retina; near vision is the preserved one.
Neither near nor far without correction
Near vision is preserved in myopia; only distance focus fails, because the elongated globe places the focal point in front of the retina.
Only objects at the extreme periphery
Myopia is a refractive error of a long globe, not a field defect; it preserves near vision while distance vision blurs.

A.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
A.q: A temporal lobe lesion affecting part of the optic radiation produces which defect?
opts: Contralateral inferior quadrantanopsia instead
Inferior quadrantanopsia is not the temporal result; damage to the temporal optic radiation removes the contralateral superior quadrant, pie in the sky.
Bitemporal hemianopsia
Bitemporal hemianopsia comes from a central chiasmal lesion such as pituitary adenoma, not from the temporal optic radiation.
Monocular blindness
Monocular blindness needs an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm; a temporal lobe lesion of the optic radiation gives superior quadrantanopsia.
Contralateral superior quadrantanopsia, or pie in the sky
Correct — a temporal lobe lesion, surgery or middle cerebral artery stroke at the temporal optic radiation causes contralateral superior quadrantanopsia, pie in the sky.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: What are the two phases of allergic contact dermatitis?
opts: Irritation, then hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum
Irritant contact dermatitis needs no prior exposure, and hyperkeratosis is not a phase; allergic contact dermatitis runs through sensitization then elicitation.
Radial growth, then vertical growth
Radial then vertical growth are the growth phases of melanoma; allergic contact dermatitis proceeds through sensitization and then elicitation.

Sensitization, in which Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells to create specialized memory; and elicitation, in which re-exposure to the same hapten promotes T cell migration and cutaneous inflammation
Correct. Langerhans cells train T cells against a hapten, and re-exposure triggers T cell migration and inflammation, a delayed reaction at 48 to 72 hours.
Sensitization by mast cell degranulation, followed by elicitation through the release of histamine into the surrounding dermal tissue on every subsequent exposure to that same allergen thereafter
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine is the urticaria pathway; allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed, T cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: What is the sequence by which Eustachian tube dysfunction creates negative middle ear pressure?
opts: The tympanic membrane becomes stiff and pulls the ossicles inward
The drum is not the starting point. Failure of the tube to open lets the mucosa absorb oxygen and nitrogen, creating negative middle ear pressure.
The tube fails to open, so the mucosa absorbs the gases
Correct. The middle ear is an air-filled space; if it is not re-ventilated, the mucosa absorbs the gases and the pressure falls. That negative pressure is the start of the otitis media sequence.
Mucus production increases faster than the tube can drain it
The initiating step is not mucus overproduction. The tube fails to open, so oxygen and nitrogen are absorbed into the mucosa and middle ear pressure falls.
Bacterial infection erodes the tube lining and opens it permanently
The problem is not a tube held open. Negative pressure arises because the tube fails to open periodically, letting the mucosa absorb oxygen and nitrogen.

A.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
A.q: Which set of causes belongs to sensorineural rather than conductive loss?
opts: Eustachian tube dysfunction, middle ear effusion and stapes fixation
All three are conductive: effusion loads the drum with mass, and stapes fixation stiffens the chain. None involves the cochlea or the nerve.
Presbycusis, ototoxic drugs, noise trauma and acoustic neuroma
Correct. All four damage the cochlea or the nerve. Note acoustic neuroma sits here because cranial nerve VIII is part of the sensorineural pathway even though the tumor is outside the cochlea.
Cerumen impaction, otosclerosis, otitis media and tympanic membrane perforation
All four are conductive — they obstruct, load, stiffen or interrupt the sound-conducting apparatus.
Cholesteatoma, exostoses, foreign body and ossicular necrosis
All four are conductive: foreign bodies and exostoses obstruct the canal, cholesteatoma adds mass loading, and ossicular necrosis breaks the ossicular chain.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which protein deficiency contributes to atopic dermatitis?
opts: Insufficient elastin, reflecting loss of recoil
Elastin degradation is part of atrophy; the protein deficiency in atopic dermatitis is filaggrin, compromising the epidermal barrier.
Insufficient keratohyalin, reflecting loss of the granular layer
Loss of the granular layer is a feature of psoriasis; atopic dermatitis involves insufficient filaggrin from a compromised epidermal barrier.
Insufficient filaggrin, reflecting a compromised epidermal barrier
Correct. Insufficient filaggrin, due to a compromised epidermal barrier, combines with an overactive immune system and genetic, environmental and psychogenic factors.
Insufficient collagen, reflecting fibroblast failure
Collagen loss belongs to atrophy and ulceration; atopic dermatitis involves insufficient filaggrin and a compromised epidermal barrier.

A.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
A.q: Which dermal cell mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation?
opts: The fibroblast
Fibroblasts produce the collagen that gives the dermis tensile strength; the mast cell is the dermal cell behind immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation.
The melanocyte
Melanocytes are pigment cells of the epidermal basal layer; the mast cell is the dermal cell that mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation.
The keratinocyte
Keratinocytes make up about 90 percent of the epidermis and produce keratin; mast cells mediate immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation in the dermis.
The mast cell
Correct, and its degranulation is the mechanism behind both the wheal and urticaria.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Trauma versus a bee sting illustrates which distinction within acute inflammation?
opts: Inflammation that resolves completely versus inflammation that becomes chronic
Chronicity comes from persistent infection, toxic agents or autoimmunity; trauma versus bee sting contrasts purely physical damage with immune activation.
Serous versus fibrinous exudate
Serous and fibrinous are exudate patterns, a separate axis; trauma versus bee sting contrasts physical damage with immune activation.
Endogenous versus exogenous toxic agents
Endogenous versus exogenous describes toxic agents in chronic inflammation, such as atherosclerosis and silica; trauma versus bee sting is acute.
Damage that is purely physical versus damage that involves activation of an immune response
Correct. In acute inflammation, damage may be purely physical, as in trauma, or may involve activation of an immune response, as in a bee sting.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: Which mediator is distinguished from histamine and serotonin by also producing pain?
opts: Immunoglobulin G
Immunoglobulin G is an opsonin recognized through Fc receptors; bradykinin is the mediator that also causes pain.
Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen forms the thick meshwork of the fibrinous pattern; the mediator that adds pain is bradykinin.
Bradykinin
Correct. All three raise permeability, but only bradykinin also causes pain, along with a possible increase in leukocyte chemotaxis.
Complement component C3b
C3b is an opsonin that binds foreign material for recognition; bradykinin is the mediator that also causes pain.

A.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
A.q: What defines a secondary skin lesion?
opts: Any lesion that is palpable rather than flat
Palpability separates papules and nodules from flat macules within the primary group; a secondary lesion is a modified primary lesion.
Any lesion that arises from malignant rather than from benign underlying disease processes
Malignancy plays no part in the definition; a secondary lesion is a primary lesion modified by infection, trauma or other factors.
A modification or change of a primary lesion caused by infection, trauma or other factors
Correct, which is why a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble what it came from.
Any lesion appearing on a second body site after the first
Location is not the criterion; a secondary lesion is a primary lesion that has been modified or changed by infection, trauma or other factors.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
A.q: Is metastatic spread random?
opts: No — but only because lymphatic drainage is anatomically fixed
Metastatic spread is nonrandom because of venous blood flow, tumor and endothelial receptors, and genetic fitness, not lymphatic anatomy.
No — it is determined by blood flow, receptors, and genetically determined fitness
Correct — metastatic spread is not random but set by venous blood flow, tumor and endothelial receptors, and genetic fitness.
Yes — circulating cells lodge in whichever capillary bed they reach first
Spread is not random; venous flow, specific receptors on tumor and endothelial cells, and genetic fitness determine it.
Yes for hematogenous spread, no for lymphatic spread
The nonrandom pattern applies to metastatic spread generally, set by venous flow, receptors, and genetic fitness.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: What do B lymphocytes do?
opts: Cell-mediated killing of virus-infected cells through T cell receptors
Killing virus-infected cells is the role of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells; B lymphocytes make antibodies against antigens.
Returning immune function to its normal operation after infection, and preventing autoimmunity
Restoring normal immune function and preventing autoimmunity is the regulatory (suppressor) T cell's role, not the B lymphocyte's.
Releasing histamine to increase vascular permeability
Among the leukocytes, histamine comes from basophils; B lymphocytes make antibodies and act as antigen-presenting cells.
Making antibodies against antigens, acting as antigen-presenting cells, and developing into memory B cells
Correct. B lymphocytes make antibodies, act as antigen-presenting cells and become memory B cells; they drive the humoral immune response.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which two ototoxic effects are reversible or symptom-limited rather than permanent?
opts: Noise trauma and presbycusis
Both are irreversible — noise causes stereocilia degeneration and hair cell apoptosis.
Furosemide on the strial potential; salicylate on prestin
Correct. The loop diuretic effect on the strial potential is reversible, and the salicylate effect on the outer hair cell motor protein produces tinnitus. Neither destroys the cells outright.
Gentamicin and tobramycin damage
Gentamicin and tobramycin generate reactive oxygen species that destroy outer hair cells from the cochlear base, a destructive rather than reversible effect.
Cisplatin and carboplatin damage
Cisplatin and carboplatin cross-link DNA in stria vascularis cells and cause bilateral permanent sensorineural loss.

A.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
A.q: Which statement correctly describes the inherited defect in xeroderma pigmentosum?
opts: Defective apoptosis genes, so damaged cells cannot self destruct; increased risk of lymphoma
Xeroderma pigmentosum is a defect of repair genes, not apoptosis genes, and it raises skin cancer risk rather than lymphoma risk.
Defective protooncogenes, so growth signaling is lost; increased risk of aplasia
Xeroderma pigmentosum involves defective repair genes; protooncogenes cause cancer when mutated into oncogenes, not when lost.
Defective repair genes, so ultraviolet B damage cannot be repaired
Correct — the consequence is an increased risk of skin cancer in sun-exposed areas. It is a repair-gene disease rather than a tumor suppressor one.
Defective tumor suppressor genes, so cell growth cannot be inhibited; increased risk of nervous system tumors
Growth-inhibiting tumor suppressors such as NF-1 and NF-2 underlie nervous system tumors; xeroderma pigmentosum is a repair-gene defect.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: In the organ of Corti, what physically opens the tip-link channels on the hair cells?
opts: Shearing of the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane

Correct. Basilar membrane displacement bends the stereocilia against the rigid tectorial membrane, and that mechanical deflection is what opens the channels. Everything upstream exists to produce that shear.
Stapes vibration transmitted directly to the hair cells
The stapes vibrates the oval window and starts pressure waves in the scala vestibuli. Those displace endolymph and the basilar membrane, and only the resulting shear opens the channels.
Direct pressure of endolymph on the hair cell body
Endolymph displacement moves the membrane, but the channel opens because the cilia are bent against a rigid structure, not from fluid pressure on the cell.
Glutamate binding to the hair cell
Glutamate is released BY the hair cell onto cranial nerve VIII fibers after depolarization. It is the output, not the trigger.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: Which pairing of infection type and predominant reaction describes the eosinophil?
opts: Bacterial infection; predominating in suppurative inflammation
Bacterial defense and pus formation belong to neutrophils; eosinophils primarily deal with parasitic infections.
Parasitic infection; predominating in allergic reactions such as asthma, hay fever and hives
Correct. Eosinophils primarily deal with parasitic infections and are the predominant inflammatory cells in allergic reactions such as asthma.
Viral infection; predominating in cell-mediated immunity
Virus-infected cells are handled by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells; eosinophils primarily deal with parasitic infections.
Fungal infection; predominating in chronic granulomatous inflammatory processes
Neutrophils, not eosinophils, defend against fungal as well as bacterial infection; eosinophils primarily deal with parasites.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
A.q: Which three structures make up the uvea?
opts: The choroid, the retina and the sclera
The retina is the neurosensory inner tunic and the sclera the fibrous outer; the uvea is the choroid, ciliary body and iris.
The ciliary body, the lens and the zonules
The lens and zonules are not uveal tissue; the uvea, the vascular middle tunic, is the choroid, ciliary body and iris.
The iris, the cornea and the conjunctiva
The cornea belongs to the fibrous outer tunic and the conjunctiva is a mucosal lining; the uvea is the choroid, ciliary body and iris.
The choroid, the ciliary body and the iris
Correct — the choroid, ciliary body and iris form the uvea, the vascular middle tunic, with the highly vascularized choroid nourishing the retina.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Eczematous dermatitis results from which type of inflammatory reaction?
opts: Neutrophil-driven suppurative inflammation
Purulent, leukocyte-rich material fills a pustule; eczema results from T cell-mediated inflammatory reactions rather than suppurative inflammation.
Complement-mediated vessel destruction
Vessel destruction is not the mechanism of eczema; eczematous dermatitis results from T cell-mediated inflammation plus a filaggrin-deficient barrier.
T cell-mediated
Correct. Eczematous dermatitis typically results from T cell-mediated inflammatory reactions, with insufficient filaggrin compromising the epidermal barrier.
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation alone
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine produces the wheals of urticaria; eczema is a T cell-mediated inflammatory reaction.

A.io: f — Compare and contrast the different types of malignant tumors according to origin
A.q: What is a carcinoma showing squamous cell differentiation called?
opts: A papilloma
A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor with finger-like projections; a carcinoma with squamous cell differentiation is a squamous cell carcinoma.
A sarcoma
A sarcoma arises from mesenchymal, supportive tissue, so it cannot be a carcinoma with squamous differentiation.
Squamous cell carcinoma
Correct — a carcinoma with squamous cell differentiation is a squamous cell carcinoma; one with glandular growth is an adenocarcinoma.
An adenocarcinoma
Adenocarcinoma is the carcinoma with a glandular growth pattern, not squamous cell differentiation.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What are the two pathophysiological causes of strabismus?
opts: Lens opacification and loss of the red reflex
Lens opacification with loss of the red reflex is cataract; strabismus, a mechanical misalignment, comes from muscle imbalance or cranial nerve palsy.
Extraocular muscle imbalance and cranial nerve palsy of the third, fourth or sixth nerves
Correct — strabismus is mechanical: an extraocular muscle imbalance or a palsy of the third, fourth or sixth cranial nerve misaligns the visual axes.
Retinal detachment and vitreous hemorrhage
Retinal detachment and vitreous hemorrhage affect the image, not alignment; strabismus comes from extraocular muscle imbalance or cranial nerve palsy.
Raised intraocular pressure with progressive optic disc cupping and field loss
Raised pressure with disc cupping and field loss is glaucoma; strabismus arises from extraocular muscle imbalance or palsy of the third, fourth or sixth nerve.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What is amblyopia?
opts: Ocular misalignment arising from extraocular muscle imbalance or nerve palsy
Misalignment from muscle imbalance or nerve palsy is strabismus, a mechanical problem; amblyopia is the visual deficit that uncorrected strabismus can cause.
Progressive optic neuropathy from raised pressure
Progressive optic neuropathy from raised pressure is glaucoma; amblyopia is reduced best-corrected acuity from abnormal developmental visual processing.
Opacification of the crystalline lens
Opacification of the crystalline lens is cataract; amblyopia is reduced best-corrected acuity from abnormal visual processing in childhood.
Reduced best-corrected visual acuity from abnormal visual processing during the critical developmental period
Correct — amblyopia is a visual deficit rather than a mechanical one: best-corrected acuity stays reduced because visual processing developed abnormally during the critical pediatric period.

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: What drives the change from non-proliferative to proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
opts: Rising intraocular pressure forces new vessels to form
Intraocular pressure is not the driver; severe ischemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, which produces the fragile new vessels.
Accumulation of lipofuscin and apolipoprotein beneath the pigment epithelium
Lipofuscin and apolipoprotein deposits are drusen in dry macular degeneration; proliferative change is driven by ischemia and vascular endothelial growth factor.
Bacterial collagenase digestion of the retinal surface
Bacterial collagenases melt tissue in corneal ulceration; proliferative retinopathy arises when severe ischemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor.
Severe ischemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, producing neovascularization
Correct — chronic hyperglycemia occludes capillaries, severe ischemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, and fragile new vessels grow on the disc and retina.

A.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
A.q: Which statement correctly defines cancer and gives the origin of its name?
opts: A neoplasm that has metastasized; from the Greek for wandering, because cells migrate
Metastasis is a portion of a cancer that has migrated to other sites; cancer itself is any malignant neoplasm, named from the Latin for crab.
A precancerous lesion; from the Latin for disorder, because architecture is lost
Loss of architectural orientation describes dysplasia, a precancerous change; cancer is a malignant neoplasm, named from the Latin for crab.
A malignant neoplasm; from the Latin for crab
Correct — so named because it adheres to any tissue it seizes upon and reaches out with claws, invading surrounding tissue.
Any neoplasm at all; from the Latin for growth, because the mass enlarges without a stimulus
Cancer is specifically the malignant subset, and the derivation is the crab.

A.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
A.q: Where do impulses travel after leaving the optic nerve?
opts: To the temporal cortex
The temporal lobe carries part of the optic radiation but is not the destination; impulses end in the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe.
To the frontal eye fields
The frontal eye fields are not the destination; impulses travel from the optic nerve to the occipital cortex, the primary visual cortex.
To the superior colliculus alone
The superior colliculus is not on this route; the optic tract relays through the lateral geniculate nucleus and optic radiations to the occipital cortex.
To the occipital cortex
Correct — the signal runs from the optic nerve through the chiasm and optic tract to the lateral geniculate nucleus, then via the optic radiations to the occipital cortex.

A.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
A.q: What drives dizziness or lightheadedness, as distinct from vertigo?
opts: Cerebral hypoperfusion or metabolic imbalance
Correct. Dizziness is a non-vestibular sensation of impending faint or unsteadiness, driven by cerebral hypoperfusion, orthostatic hypotension or metabolic imbalance.
Asymmetrical input between the two vestibular apparatus
Asymmetrical vestibular input is the mechanism of vertigo itself, which is the thing dizziness has to be distinguished FROM.
Dislodged otoconia in the semicircular canals
Dislodged otoconia cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a vestibular cause of true vertigo rather than of lightheadedness.
Endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is Meniere disease, which is vestibular — so it produces vertigo rather than the presyncopal sensation of dizziness.

A.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
A.q: Why are there three semicircular canals rather than one?
opts: Each detects a different speed of rotation
The three canals are distinguished by the plane they occupy, not by the speed of rotation they detect.
Two detect rotation and one detects gravity
Gravity and linear acceleration are the otolith organs' job.
Redundancy in case one is damaged
Redundancy is not the explanation. Three canals exist because rotation happens in three planes.
They sit in three planes, so rotation in any direction is detected
Correct. Sagittal, coronal and transverse between them cover all rotational movement.

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: What is the conjunctival fornix?
opts: The dense fibrous plate giving the eyelid its shape
The dense fibrous plate giving the lid its rigid shape is the tarsus; the fornix is the flexible conjunctival cul-de-sac permitting globe rotation.
The sphincteric muscle responsible for blinking
The sphincteric blinking muscle is orbicularis oculi; the fornix is the flexible conjunctival cul-de-sac that permits free rotation of the globe.
The circular junction where the conjunctiva meets the edge of the cornea
The junction of conjunctiva and cornea is the limbus, where bulbar conjunctiva ends; the fornix is the flexible cul-de-sac permitting globe rotation.
A flexible junctional cul-de-sac that permits free rotation of the globe
Correct — the fornix is the flexible junctional cul-de-sac where palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva meet, and its slack permits free rotation of the globe.

A.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
A.q: What is a papilloma?
opts: A tumor with finger-like or warty projections from an epithelial surface
Correct — the projections are visible microscopically or macroscopically.
A tumor forming a glandular pattern or arising from a gland
A glandular pattern or gland of origin defines an adenoma; a papilloma instead has finger-like or warty projections.
A malignant tumor arising from supportive, mesenchymal tissue
A malignant tumor of supportive, mesenchymal tissue is a sarcoma; a papilloma is a benign tumor of an epithelial surface.
A malignant epithelial tumor showing squamous cell differentiation
Malignant epithelium with squamous differentiation is squamous cell carcinoma; a papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor.

A.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
A.q: Which sequence correctly orders the cellular events of acute inflammation after stasis?
opts: Transmigration, adhesion, aggregation, phagocytosis, chemotaxis
Adhesion must come before transmigration and chemotaxis is not last; the order after stasis is adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation, then phagocytosis.
Aggregation, chemotaxis, transmigration, adhesion, phagocytosis
Aggregation cannot come first; the order after stasis is adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation, then phagocytosis.
Leukocyte adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation, phagocytosis
Correct. Adhesion to the endothelium precedes movement across it, then directed migration, gathering at the site, and finally ingestion.
Chemotaxis, phagocytosis, adhesion, transmigration, aggregation
Chemotaxis cannot precede the adhesion and transmigration that place the leukocyte in the tissue.

A.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
A.q: What are mesenchymal tumors derived from?
opts: Neural tissue: peripheral nerves, nerve sheaths and the central nervous system
Mesenchymal does not mean neural; mesenchymal tumors derive from supportive tissue such as connective tissue, cartilage, and bone.
Supportive tissue: connective tissue, adipose tissue, cartilage, smooth and striated muscle, and bone
Correct — the same origin gives sarcomas when the tumor is malignant.
Epithelial surfaces: skin, gastrointestinal lining, respiratory lining and glandular ducts
That is epithelial origin, which gives adenomas and papillomas when benign.
Hematopoietic tissue: bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen and thymus
Hematopoietic tissue is not the mesenchymal category; mesenchymal tumors derive from supportive tissue such as bone and muscle.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Which histological findings go with chronic inflammation?
opts: White blood cells (lymphocytes and macrophages), proliferation of blood vessels, fibrosis and tissue necrosis
Correct. Chronic inflammation is associated histologically with lymphocytes and macrophages, new blood vessels, fibrosis and tissue necrosis.
Neutrophil predominance with an absence of vascular proliferation
Neutrophils are the leukocyte of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is accompanied by proliferation of blood vessels.
Eosinophil infiltration with mucus hypersecretion
Eosinophils dominate allergic reactions and mucus hypersecretion is the catarrhal pattern; chronic inflammation shows lymphocytes, macrophages, new vessels and fibrosis.
Serous exudate with low protein content, no cellular infiltrate, and no proliferation of blood vessels
That describes the serous pattern, which occurs early or with mild inflammation; chronic inflammation shows proliferation of blood vessels, fibrosis and necrosis.

A.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
A.q: Which demographic and inheritance profile fits otosclerosis?
opts: Young-to-middle-aged females, accelerated by pregnancy; 50% autosomal dominant
Correct. Otosclerosis is most common in young-to-middle-aged females and is accelerated by pregnancy; 50 percent of cases are autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.
Commonest in young females but entirely sporadic
The demographic is right, but it is not sporadic: 50 percent of cases are autosomal dominant, with variable penetrance.
Commonest in older males, with no hereditary component
Both halves are wrong: the peak is younger and female, and half of cases are autosomal dominant.
Commonest in children, autosomal recessive
Neither half matches: otosclerosis peaks in young to middle-aged women, and half of cases are autosomal dominant rather than recessive.

A.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
A.q: Which nodal findings require immediate assessment to exclude lymphoma?
opts: Persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults
Correct. Reactive nodes are usually tender and follow a regional infection. Rubbery, matted, persistent and supraclavicular in an older patient is the combination that changes the level of concern.
Any palpable cervical node at all
Palpable nodes are common and usually reactive. Persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults are what require assessment for lymphoma.
Tender mobile nodes during a viral upper respiratory infection
Tender nodes during a viral upper respiratory infection are reactive enlargement responding to regional infection, usually benign.
Bilateral small nodes in a child with otitis media
Nodes responding to otitis media are reactive enlargement from a regional head and neck infection, usually benign.

A.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
A.q: Which genes promote repair of damaged deoxyribonucleic acid?
opts: BRCA-1 and BRCA-2
Correct — a minority of breast cancer patients carry an inherited mutation in one of them.
NF-1 and NF-2
NF-1 and NF-2 (neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2) are tumor suppressor genes, which inhibit cell growth rather than repair damaged deoxyribonucleic acid.
Retinoblastoma and adenomatous polyposis coli
Retinoblastoma and adenomatous polyposis coli are tumor suppressor genes that inhibit cell growth; the repair genes are BRCA-1 and BRCA-2.
p16 and p53
p16 is a tumor suppressor linked to malignant melanoma, and p53 is needed to promote self destruction of mutated cells; neither is a repair gene.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 30

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: Which glands are involved in an external as opposed to an internal hordeolum?
opts: Both involve the tarsal plate itself rather than any gland
The tarsal plate houses the meibomian glands but is not itself infected; a hordeolum is a focal abscess of a Zeis, Moll or meibomian gland.
External involves the glands of Zeis or Moll; internal involves a meibomian gland
Correct — an external hordeolum is an acute abscess of the Zeis or Moll glands at the lash follicles, and an internal one involves a meibomian gland in the tarsal plate.
External involves a meibomian gland; internal involves the glands of Zeis or Moll
The assignment is reversed: the superficial glands of Zeis and Moll give the external form, and the deeper meibomian glands the internal one.
Both involve the lacrimal gland
Lacrimal gland inflammation is dacryoadenitis; a hordeolum infects the Zeis or Moll glands externally or a meibomian gland internally.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: In chronic inflammation, what roles do lymphocytes and plasma cells versus macrophages play?
opts: Both populations act solely to proliferate blood vessels
Vascular proliferation accompanies chronic inflammation but is not the role of either cell type; they mediate antibody production and antigen delivery.
Lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate antibody production; macrophages process and deliver antigen to immunocompetent cells
Correct. Antibody production belongs to lymphocytes and plasma cells, antigen processing and delivery to macrophages.
Lymphocytes release histamine; macrophages release serotonin
Among the leukocytes, histamine comes from basophils; lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate antibody production, macrophages deliver antigen.
Lymphocytes phagocytose the cellular debris at the site, while macrophages produce and secrete the antibody
This reverses the roles: lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate antibody production, and macrophages process and deliver antigen to immunocompetent cells.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: A patient reacts to a nickel earring 48 to 72 hours after wearing it. Which mechanism does the delay reflect?
opts: An immediate immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation occurring upon the very first contact with the metal
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation produces wheals, not a 48 to 72 hour delay; nickel allergy is a delayed T cell-mediated reaction.
Direct chemical injury requiring no prior exposure
Direct chemical injury without prior exposure is irritant contact dermatitis; a 48 to 72 hour delay reflects T cell migration after sensitization.
Viral proliferation within basal keratinocytes
Viral proliferation in basal cells is how human papillomavirus causes warts; the 48 to 72 hour delay reflects T cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
Delayed hypersensitivity requiring T cell migration after re-exposure to a hapten previously presented by Langerhans cells
Correct. The delay is the time the cellular response takes, which is what distinguishes it from an immediate mast cell reaction.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: What is the suspected mechanism of koilonychia?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue producing an opaque nail
Connective tissue overgrowth with an opaque nail is Terry's nails; koilonychia reflects impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia.
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots is leukonychia; koilonychia is a weakened, concave nail linked to deficiency anemia.
Impaired keratin synthesis associated with deficiency anemia, weakening the nail plate into raised ridges that are thin and concave
Correct. Koilonychia is thought to reflect impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia, leaving a weakened, thin, concave nail; the exact pathophysiology is unknown.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal transverse grooves across the surface of the nail plate itself
A halt of keratin production with transverse grooves is Beau's lines; koilonychia is a thin, concave nail from impaired keratin synthesis.

A.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
A.q: What does anaplasia mean?
opts: Disordered growth of epithelium with retained architecture
That is closer to dysplasia, and dysplasia does lose architectural orientation.
Lack of differentiation
Correct — the extreme of the grading scale, with no resemblance to the normal cell.
Close resemblance to the comparable normal cell
Close resemblance to the comparable normal cell is well differentiated, the opposite end of the scale from anaplasia.
Failure of a primordial tissue to develop into a mature organ
That is aplasia, which is a non-neoplastic developmental abnormality.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 12

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: Which condition can cause amblyopia?
opts: Raised intraocular pressure
Raised intraocular pressure compresses retinal ganglion cell axons in glaucoma; amblyopia follows uncorrected strabismus, severe refractive error or visual deprivation.
Posterior vitreous detachment
Posterior vitreous detachment is a risk factor for retinal detachment; amblyopia can follow severe myopia, hyperopia or astigmatism, or visual deprivation.
Drusen beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
Drusen beneath the retinal pigment epithelium are the hallmark of dry macular degeneration; amblyopia can follow deprivation such as congenital cataract or ptosis.
Uncorrected strabismus
Correct — uncorrected strabismus is a cause of amblyopia, the loss of best-corrected acuity from abnormal visual processing in the critical pediatric period.

A.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
A.q: Which statement correctly describes Epstein Barr virus in carcinogenesis?
opts: B cell lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma; it infects B lymphocytes
Correct — it immortalizes them, which is the key step, and it also infects epithelial cells of the oropharynx.
Hepatocellular carcinoma; it infects hepatocytes and causes chronic injury with regeneration
Chronic liver injury with regeneration leading to hepatocellular carcinoma describes hepatitis B and hepatitis C.
Cervical carcinoma; it infects cervical epithelium and integrates its genome
Integrating into cervical epithelium and causing cervical cancer describes human papillomavirus, not Epstein Barr virus.
Gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma; it colonizes the stomach
Colonizing the stomach and causing gastric cancers describes Helicobacter pylori, a Gram-negative bacterium, not a virus.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 33

A.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
A.q: What is the primary etiology of TRACTIONAL retinal detachment?
opts: Choroidal melanoma
Choroidal melanoma causes exudative detachment, with fluid collecting without a tear; tractional detachment follows proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Correct — the neovascular membranes of proliferative disease are the classic traction source.
Severe malignant hypertension
Malignant hypertension is an exudative cause, breaking down the blood-retinal barrier; traction comes from the membranes of proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Posterior vitreous detachment
Posterior vitreous detachment is a risk factor for rhegmatogenous detachment through a retinal break; traction arises from proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

A.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
A.q: Which description of an epidermal inclusion cyst is accurate?
opts: A sebaceous gland, and it contains only squalene
An epidermal inclusion cyst does not arise from a sebaceous gland; it arises from a hair follicle and is filled with keratin.
A blood vessel, and it contains clotted blood
Clotted blood is not its content; an epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin.
A hair follicle, and it contains keratin
Correct. An epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin, enclosed in a capsule within the dermis or subcutaneous layer.
A sweat gland, and it contains sodium and chloride
Eccrine sweat carries sodium and chloride, but an epidermal inclusion cyst arises from a hair follicle and contains keratin.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which description fits vocal cord polyps, as distinct from nodules?
opts: Unilateral fibrous calluses from chronic yelling
This mixes the two lesions. Calluses from chronic trauma are nodules and they are bilateral; polyps are unilateral and follow a single event.
Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma
Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma are NODULES. Polyps differ on every count — unilateral, soft, and from one event.
Bilateral soft lesions at the anterior commissure from reflux
Neither matches: polyps are unilateral on the middle third and follow acute strain, not bilateral at the commissure from reflux.
Unilateral, soft and pedunculated on the middle third, after one severe strain
Correct. One event rather than chronic repetition, and the healing response is inflammatory rather than a callus. Site and laterality both differ from nodules.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: Why can an implanted medical device provoke an inflammatory response even when it is sterile?
opts: Because implantation always causes bacterial contamination of surrounding tissue
The response occurs even when the device is sterile, because immune cells recognize its immunoglobulin G and C3b coating.
Because sterilization leaves residual endotoxin behind, and that endotoxin then acts as a chemotactic agent
Endotoxin plays no part; a sterile device provokes inflammation because it becomes coated with immunoglobulin G and C3b.
Because the material becomes coated with immunoglobulin G and C3b, and immune cells recognize that coating and attach to it
Correct. Opsonization of the biomaterial is what makes it a target regardless of sterility.
Because the device physically obstructs lymphatic drainage
Lymphatic obstruction is not the mechanism; the device is coated with immunoglobulin G and C3b, which immune cells recognize.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which mechanism drives psoriasis?
opts: Melanocytes proliferate at the dermal-epidermal junction
Melanocyte proliferation at the dermal-epidermal junction is the origin of melanoma; psoriasis is driven by active T cells infiltrating the epidermis.
Active T cells infiltrating the epidermis stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and excessive cytokine production, particularly tumor necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma and interleukin-12
Correct. Active T cells infiltrate the epidermis, stimulating keratinocyte proliferation and excess cytokines, so skin cells multiply up to ten times faster.
Mast cells release histamine which drives keratinocyte proliferation
Mast cell histamine release produces the wheals of urticaria; in psoriasis, active T cells stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and excess cytokine production.
Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells, producing a delayed hypersensitivity reaction 48 to 72 hours after each exposure to the allergen in question every single time
Langerhans cells presenting haptens to T cells is allergic contact dermatitis; psoriasis is driven by active T cells and cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor alpha.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which molecular pathway drives nasal polyp formation?
opts: Interleukins 4, 5 and 13, with eosinophil influx
Correct. Chronic type 2 allergic responses release interleukins 4, 5 and 13 and draw eosinophils into the tissue, forming benign edematous masses from the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
Interleukin 17, with mast cell influx
Interleukin 17 and mast cell influx are not the polyp pathway. Polyps are type 2 inflammation driven by interleukins 4, 5 and 13 with eosinophils.
Interleukins 1, 6 and tumor necrosis factor, with neutrophil influx
Neutrophil-driven cytokines do not form polyps. Polyps come from type 2 inflammation: interleukins 4, 5 and 13 with tissue eosinophil influx.
Interferon gamma, with lymphocyte influx
Interferon gamma with lymphocytes is not the polyp pathway, which is type 2 inflammation with interleukins 4, 5 and 13 and eosinophils.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which description fits inferior turbinate hypertrophy?
opts: Bacterial infection of the turbinate bone; osteomyelitis
Turbinates do not enlarge from bone infection. The triggers are allergic rhinitis, vasomotor instability and rebound hyperemia from topical decongestants.
Cartilage displacement off the midline; a congenital deformity
Cartilage displaced off the midline is a deviated septum, which divides the nasal cavity into asymmetric flow channels.
Venous engorgement, edema or bony hypertrophy; decongestant rebound
Correct. The inferior turbinates enlarge from venous sinusoid engorgement, mucosal edema or bony hypertrophy; rebound hyperemia from topical decongestants is rhinitis medicamentosa.
Eosinophilic polyp formation; an allergic reaction
Eosinophilic masses are nasal polyps from type 2 inflammation. Turbinate enlargement comes from engorgement, edema or bony hypertrophy.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: How do petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses differ?
opts: By size — petechiae 1 to 2 millimeters or less, purpura 3 to 10 millimeters, ecchymoses greater than 10 millimeters — with similar underlying pathology
Correct. All three are bleeding into the dermis with similar underlying pathology, separated by size, from pinpoint petechiae to ecchymoses over 10 millimeters.
By mechanism — petechiae from capillary rupture, purpura from vessel dilatation, and ecchymoses from melanin deposition in the dermis rather than blood
The mechanism does not change between them: all three are non-blanchable deposits of blood in the dermis, and ecchymoses contain blood, not melanin.
By depth — petechiae epidermal, purpura dermal, ecchymoses subcutaneous
All three are deposits of blood in the dermis, not at different depths; they are separated by size, from pinpoint petechiae to ecchymoses over 10 millimeters.
By blanchability — petechiae blanch, purpura and ecchymoses do not
None of the three blanches: petechiae and purpura are non-blanchable deposits of blood in the dermis, and the distinction between them is size.

A.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
A.q: Which statement correctly describes epidermal cell turnover?
opts: Every 6 to 12 months, and considerably more rapid in older patients
Turnover takes 30 to 60 days, not 6 to 12 months, and it is more rapid in younger patients rather than older ones.
Turnover ceases after adolescence
The epidermis keeps turning over, every 30 to 60 days, as cells rise from the basement membrane zone and eventually shed.
Every 30 to 60 days, and turnover is more rapid in younger patients
Correct. Epidermal cells turn over every 30 to 60 days, rising from the basement membrane zone to shed, and turnover is faster in younger patients.
Every 24 to 48 hours, with no age dependence
Every 24 to 48 hours is far too fast; epidermal turnover takes 30 to 60 days and is more rapid in younger patients.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Pseudomembranous inflammation consists of a superficial necrotic layer made up of which components?
opts: Granulation tissue, proliferating fibroblasts and newly formed capillary networks throughout
Proliferating blood vessels and connective tissue accompany chronic inflammation; the pseudomembrane is fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris.
Fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris, forming a membrane-like covering over the affected mucosa
Correct. Pseudomembranous inflammation is a superficial necrotic layer of fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris forming a membrane-like covering over mucosa.
Pus alone, without a fibrin component
Pus without any membrane describes the suppurative pattern; the pseudomembrane is a necrotic layer of fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris.
Mucus, plasma and erythrocytes
Mucus hypersecretion defines the catarrhal pattern; the pseudomembrane is a necrotic layer of fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris.

B.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
B.q: What proportion of severe blindness from macular degeneration does the wet form account for?
opts: About fifty per cent
Half understates it; the rapidly progressive wet form accounts for about ninety percent of severe blindness from macular degeneration.
About twenty-five per cent
A quarter is far too low; the wet form accounts for about ninety percent of severe blindness, while the dry form progresses slowly.
About ten per cent
Ten percent inverts the figure: the rapidly progressive wet form accounts for about ninety percent of severe blindness from macular degeneration.
About ninety per cent
Correct — the wet form progresses rapidly, because leaking new vessels cause rapid central vision loss, so it accounts for about ninety percent of severe blindness.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Which statement describes the timing of acute inflammation?
opts: Over minutes to hours only, beginning after a full 24 hours have elapsed since the injury
Acute inflammation lasts seconds to days, wider than minutes to hours, and begins within seconds rather than after a delay.
Over seconds, minutes, hours or days, beginning within seconds of tissue injury
Correct. Acute inflammation begins immediately — within seconds — following injury of tissues.
Over days to months, beginning once macrophages arrive
That timescale belongs to chronic inflammation, which is characterized by macrophages and lymphocytes; acute inflammation begins within seconds.
Over weeks, beginning after antibody production starts
Antibody-mediated reactions belong to chronic inflammation; acute inflammation begins within seconds of tissue injury.

B.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
B.q: What protects the outer third of the ear canal?
opts: Ciliated epithelium sweeping debris outward
The ear canal is not protected by cilia. Its outer third is protected by cerumen from ceruminous glands and by hair follicles.
A keratin plug at the isthmus
There is no keratin plug at the isthmus. What sits in the outer third is cerumen and hair.
Cerumen from ceruminous glands, and hair follicles
Correct. Ceruminous glands produce protective cerumen, and the outer third of the canal also has protective hair follicles.
Mucus from goblet cells
Mucus is not the canal's protection. Ceruminous glands produce protective cerumen, and the outer third of the canal also carries protective hair follicles.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Which cell types characterize chronic inflammation?
opts: Basophils and mast cells only
Basophils drive allergic and antigen responses through histamine; chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophages, monocytes and lymphocytes.
Fibroblasts in the absence of leukocytes
Connective tissue proliferation accompanies chronic inflammation but does not replace the leukocyte infiltrate.
Neutrophils and eosinophils predominantly, without mononuclear infiltrate
Neutrophils dominate the acute response and eosinophils allergy and parasites; chronic inflammation shows macrophages, monocytes, lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Macrophages, monocytes and mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells
Correct. Chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophages, monocytes and mononuclear cells, with proliferation of blood vessels and connective tissue.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: How do eccrine and apocrine sweat glands differ in secretion and function?
opts: Eccrine secrete keratin and apocrine secrete melanin
Neither gland secretes keratin or melanin; eccrine glands secrete water and electrolytes, and apocrine glands secrete protein and fatty lipids.

Eccrine open onto the skin surface and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling by evaporation; apocrine sit mainly in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids, functioning as scent glands
Correct. Body odor comes from bacterial degradation of apocrine sweat, not from the sweat itself, and eccrine sweat cools the body by evaporation.
Eccrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids; apocrine glands open onto the surface of the skin and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling the body
This swaps the two glands: eccrine glands open onto the skin surface for evaporative cooling, and apocrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas.
Both secrete sebum, differing only in the body regions they occupy
Neither sweat gland secretes sebum; eccrine glands secrete water and electrolytes, apocrine glands protein and fatty lipids, and sebaceous glands make sebum.

B.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
B.q: Which virus is the typical cause of viral conjunctivitis?
opts: Herpes simplex virus
Herpes simplex type 1 causes epithelial keratitis with a dendritic corneal ulcer; the typical viral cause of conjunctivitis is adenovirus.
Varicella zoster virus
Varicella zoster causes herpes zoster ophthalmicus in the first trigeminal division; the typical viral cause of conjunctivitis is adenovirus.
Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus is not the typical cause; conjunctivitis is viral from adenovirus, or bacterial, allergic or toxic, with hyperemia but no deep pain.
Adenovirus
Correct — adenovirus is the viral cause of conjunctivitis, which can also be bacterial, allergic or toxic, and shows hyperemia without severe deep pain.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: What defines telangiectasia at the tissue level?
opts: Capillary rupture with blood deposited into the dermis
Capillary rupture depositing blood in the dermis produces petechiae and purpura; telangiectasia is permanent vessel dilatation with no inflammatory infiltrate.
Dense inflammatory infiltration around dilated vessels
Inflammatory infiltration is absent in telangiectasia by definition; the vessels are permanently dilated and thinned, not inflamed.
Proliferation of new vessels driven by release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the surrounding dermis over a prolonged period
Vascular endothelial growth factor release with increased capillary density is nail clubbing; telangiectasia is permanent dilatation of superficial dermal vessels.
Permanent dilatation and thinning of the endothelium of capillaries, venules and arterioles in the superficial dermis, with NO inflammatory cell infiltration
Correct. The absence of inflammatory infiltrate is the discriminating feature.

B.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: In the sequence of events of acute inflammation, which vascular event comes FIRST?
opts: Increased vascular permeability
Increased vascular permeability is third, after vasoconstriction and then vasodilation; vasoconstriction is the first event.
Hemoconcentration and stasis
Hemoconcentration and stasis come fourth, after increased permeability; the sequence of events opens with vasoconstriction.
Vasoconstriction
Correct. The sequence opens with vasoconstriction, followed by vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, then hemoconcentration and stasis.
Vasodilation
Vasodilation is second, following the initial vasoconstriction.

B.io: l — Describe the tumor, nodes, metastases (TNM) staging system
B.q: What important caveat attaches to TNM (tumor, nodes, metastases) definitions?
opts: They replace histological grading, which is no longer used
Staging measures the extent of spread, while histological grading measures differentiation; neither replaces the other.
They are cancer-specific; for some cancers depth of invasion matters more than size
Correct — which is why a staging table applies to one named cancer rather than all.
They are identical across every cancer, which is what makes the system universal
The definitions are cancer-specific, not identical across cancers.
They apply only to epithelial malignancies and not to sarcomas
TNM definitions are cancer-specific rather than limited to epithelial tumors; for some cancers depth of invasion outweighs size.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 42

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
B.q: Which three interneuron types modulate the retinal signal before it reaches the ganglion cells?
opts: Horizontal, amacrine and Purkinje cells
Purkinje cells belong to the cerebellum, not the retina; the modulating retinal interneurons are bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells.
Rod, cone and ganglion cells
Rods and cones are the input and ganglion cells the output; bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells are the interneurons between them.
Bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Correct — bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells modulate the photoreceptor signal and route it to the ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.
Bipolar, Müller and astrocyte cells
Müller cells and astrocytes are not the modulating interneurons; bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells shape signals before the ganglion cells.

B.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
B.q: Which cancer patients may carry an inherited mutation of BRCA-1 or BRCA-2?
opts: The majority of breast cancer patients
Only a minority of breast cancer patients carry an inherited BRCA-1 or BRCA-2 mutation, not the majority.
All patients with familial adenomatous polyposis
Familial adenomatous polyposis follows an inherited alteration of the adenomatous polyposis coli tumor suppressor gene.
All patients with xeroderma pigmentosum
Xeroderma pigmentosum follows inherited defective repair genes that cannot fix ultraviolet B damage; BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 relate to breast cancer.
A minority of breast cancer patients
Correct — a minority of breast cancer patients have an inherited mutation of these deoxyribonucleic acid repair genes.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 40

B.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: Which statement correctly describes hypertrophy?
opts: An increase in the number of cells; especially important in labile tissues such as epithelium and bone marrow
An increase in cell number is hyperplasia; hypertrophy enlarges individual cells and matters most in skeletal and cardiac muscle.
Replacement of one mature cell type by another; especially important at epithelial junctions
Replacing one cell type with another is metaplasia; hypertrophy keeps the same cell type and enlarges each cell.
Autonomous proliferation of a clone of cells; especially important in glandular tissue
Autonomous proliferation of a clone of cells is a neoplasm; hypertrophy is enlargement of individual cells, not the addition of more cells.
Enlargement of the individual cells; especially important in permanent tissues such as skeletal and cardiac muscle
Correct — it may also occur in other tissues as part of adaptive growth.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 3

B.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
B.q: Which description of a fissure is accurate?
opts: A linear ulcer forming a crack in the epidermis, from loss of elasticity or flexibility, severe dryness and mechanical tension, with hyperkeratosis thickening the stratum corneum
Correct. A fissure is a linear ulcer cracking the epidermis where lost elasticity, severe dryness and mechanical tension act on a thickened stratum corneum.
A superficial loss of the epidermis that spares the dermal-epidermal junction and everything beneath it, so no collagen is ever destroyed in the process of healing
Superficial epidermal loss sparing the dermal-epidermal junction is an erosion; a fissure is a linear, crack-shaped ulcer in the epidermis.
A thickened plaque produced by chronic rubbing
A thickened plaque from chronic rubbing is lichenification; a fissure is a linear crack in the epidermis from dryness, lost elasticity and mechanical tension.
A dilated superficial vessel without inflammatory infiltrate
A dilated superficial vessel without infiltrate is telangiectasia; a fissure is a linear ulcer that cracks the epidermis under mechanical tension.

B.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
B.q: What is the classic symptom tetrad of Meniere disease?
opts: Continuous vertigo lasting days, unilateral tinnitus, unilateral loss, and nystagmus
That is labyrinthitis, whose vertigo lasts days and improves over weeks, against the hours-long episodes of Meniere disease.
Vertigo lasting under a minute on head movement, with no hearing loss
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
High-frequency hearing loss with tinnitus and no vertigo
High-frequency loss without vertigo fits presbycusis. Meniere disease pairs hours-long episodic vertigo with LOW-frequency tinnitus, low-tone loss and aural fullness.
Episodic vertigo for hours, low-frequency tinnitus, low-tone loss, aural fullness
Correct. All four, and the LOW-frequency emphasis is what distinguishes the hearing loss from presbycusis or noise damage, which take the high frequencies first.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Which pairing of endogenous and exogenous toxic agents in chronic inflammation is correct?
opts: Endogenous — atherosclerosis; exogenous — particulates such as silica
Correct. Atherosclerosis is the endogenous example and particulates such as silica the exogenous one.
Endogenous — bacterial infection; exogenous — viral infection
Bacteria and viruses both fall under persistent infection, a separate cause of chronic inflammation from toxic agents.
Endogenous — silica; exogenous — atherosclerosis
These are transposed: atherosclerosis is the endogenous toxic agent, and particulates such as silica are the exogenous one.
Endogenous — rheumatoid arthritis; exogenous — lupus
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are examples of autoimmunity, a separate cause of chronic inflammation from toxic agents.

B.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
B.q: Which description fits conductive hearing loss?
opts: Defective sound transmission, in the external or middle ear
Correct. The apparatus that carries sound inward has failed; the cochlea and nerve are intact. That anatomical split is what the tuning fork tests are detecting.
Central processing failure in the auditory cortex
Central auditory pathways are grouped with sensorineural loss, alongside the cochlea and cranial nerve VIII. Conductive loss sits in the external or middle ear.
Destruction of hair cells or auditory nerve fibers, in the inner ear
That is sensorineural loss, sited in the cochlea or cranial nerve VIII. Conductive loss is defective sound wave transmission to the oval window from the external or middle ear.
Failure of glutamate release at cranial nerve VIII
Glutamate release onto cranial nerve VIII is a step beyond the conducting apparatus, so its failure is sensorineural. The conductive defect lies in the external or middle ear.

B.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: Recognition and attachment during phagocytosis are enhanced by the presence of what?
opts: Serum factors known as opsonins
Correct. Opsonins such as immunoglobulin G and complement fragment C3b enhance recognition and attachment during phagocytosis.
Histamine released from basophils
Histamine acts on the vessels, causing dilation and increased permeability; recognition and attachment are enhanced by opsonins.
Fibrinogen deposited by the coagulation system
The coagulation system traps material in a fibrous network; recognition and attachment are enhanced by opsonins such as immunoglobulin G and C3b.
Bradykinin generated from plasma proteins
Bradykinin increases capillary permeability, causes pain and may increase chemotaxis; recognition and attachment are enhanced by opsonins.

B.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: From how many cells is the proliferating population of a neoplasm derived?
opts: One cell, which underwent a genetic alteration
Correct — the entire proliferating population derives from one cell that underwent a genetic alteration, so the neoplasm is clonal.
Many cells, each of which underwent an independent genetic alteration
The whole proliferating population derives from a single genetically altered cell, not from many independent ones.
Two cells, one parenchymal and one stromal
Parenchyma and stroma are the components of the mass, not two origins.
A variable number, depending on the tissue in which it arises
The number does not vary with tissue; every neoplasm's proliferating population derives from one genetically altered cell.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Which receptors carry the sensations of touch and pressure?
opts: Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles
Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles are not skin receptors; touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.
Langerhans cells and melanocytes
Langerhans cells are immune sentinels and melanocytes make pigment; touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.
Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells
Correct. Meissner's serve fine discriminative touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian respond to deep pressure and vibration, and Merkel cells serve light touch.
Ruffini endings, Krause bulbs and free nerve endings only
Free nerve endings sense touch, pain and temperature, but touch and pressure are carried by Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Which mechanism underlies basal cell carcinoma?
opts: Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction
Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction is melanoma; basal cell carcinoma arises from mutated basal keratinocytes via Hedgehog signaling.
The Hedgehog signaling pathway, following ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes in the epidermis
Correct. Ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes overactivates Hedgehog signaling and drives tumor growth in this slow-growing, rarely metastasizing cancer.
The tp53 tumor suppressor pathway, acting in the differentiated keratinocytes of the epidermis
The tp53 tumor suppressor gene mutation belongs to squamous cell carcinoma; basal cell carcinoma overactivates the Hedgehog signaling pathway in basal keratinocytes.
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, in immature keratinocytes
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 is proposed for benign seborrheic keratosis; basal cell carcinoma overactivates Hedgehog signaling.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Why are nasal polyps classed as non-neoplastic?
opts: No new tissue is grown; existing mucosa becomes edematous
Correct. Nasal polyps are benign edematous masses of the mucous membranes of the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells, not new neoplastic tissue.
They arise from cartilage rather than epithelium
They arise from the mucous membranes of the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
They regress without treatment in every case
Regression is not what the term means. Polyps are non-neoplastic because no new tissue grows: they are benign edematous masses of existing mucous membrane.
They are malignant but slow growing
Polyps are benign and not neoplastic at all, so describing them as slow-growing malignancy is wrong twice over.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Why does psoriatic skin become dry?
opts: The stratum corneum is lost entirely
The stratum corneum is not lost; psoriasis loses the stratum granulosum, and its dryness comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.
Sebaceous glands overproduce sebum, which dries the surface
Sebum does not dry the skin and is not the psoriasis mechanism; psoriatic dryness, or xeroderma, comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.
Epidermal cells fail to secrete lipids, producing xeroderma
Correct. In psoriasis, epidermal cells do not secrete lipids, and that failure of secretion produces xeroderma, or dry skin.
Eccrine sweat glands are destroyed by inflammation
Sweat gland destruction plays no part in psoriasis; the dryness, or xeroderma, comes from epidermal cells failing to secrete lipids.

B.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
B.q: Which description fits the cones of the retina?
opts: About 120 million, concentrated in the peripheral retina rather than the fovea
About 120 million photoreceptors in the peripheral retina are the rods, for dim light and night vision; cones number about 6 million.
About 6 million, spread evenly across the whole retina
Cones number about 6 million but are not spread evenly; they are concentrated in the fovea centralis within the macula.
About 60 million, concentrated at the optic disc
The optic disc is the blind spot, with no rods or cones; cones number about 6 million and are concentrated in the fovea centralis.
About 6 million, concentrated in the fovea centralis within the macula
Correct — about 6 million cones, serving color vision and sharp acuity, are concentrated in the fovea centralis within the macula.

B.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: Which leukocyte is characteristic of the exudate of acute inflammation?
opts: The eosinophil
Eosinophils are tied to allergic reactions and parasitic infections; the leukocyte of the acute exudate is the neutrophil.
The lymphocyte
Lymphocytes, with macrophages and plasma cells, characterize chronic inflammation; the acute exudate carries neutrophils.
The neutrophil
Correct. Acute inflammation involves exudation of fluid, plasma, proteins and leukocytes, and the leukocyte of that exudate is the neutrophil.
The plasma cell
Plasma cells belong to chronic inflammation, where they mediate antibody production; the acute exudate carries neutrophils.

B.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
B.q: Which statement correctly describes Helicobacter pylori?
opts: A fungus that colonizes the gastric mucosa in immunosuppressed patients
Helicobacter pylori is not a fungus; it is a Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach and causes chronic gastritis.
A Gram-negative bacterium causing chronic gastritis
Correct — it colonizes the stomach and may lead to atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia. It is the one bacterium among the microbial causes of cancer.
A Gram-positive bacterium that colonizes the stomach, causing acute ulceration and perforation
It is Gram-negative, and it causes chronic gastritis rather than acute ulceration and perforation.
A virus that integrates its genome into gastric epithelial cells
Helicobacter pylori is not a virus; it is a Gram-negative bacterium that colonizes the stomach and causes chronic gastritis.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 35
