B.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
B.q: Which structures detect linear acceleration and gravitational position?
opts: The organ of Corti
The organ of Corti transduces sound into neural signals. It is the hearing apparatus and plays no part in equilibrium.
The three semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect ROTATIONAL acceleration through cupula deflection. Linear and gravitational sensing belongs to the otoliths.
The otolith organs
Correct. They handle static and linear balance, while the semicircular canals handle rotation. The two systems together give the brain a complete picture of head position and movement.
The cupula and ampulla
Those are the sensing apparatus inside the semicircular canals, so again rotational.

B.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
B.q: Why does cerumen impaction cause conductive rather than sensorineural loss?
opts: It blocks the canal, so sound never reaches the conducting chain
Correct. The cochlea is untouched, and the defect is purely one of delivery.
It damages the outer hair cells
Wax sits in the canal and never reaches the cochlea, so the hair cells are untouched by it.
It stiffens the stapes footplate
Stiffening of the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a separate conductive mechanism entirely.
It loads the tympanic membrane with fluid
Wax sits in the canal in front of the drum. Fluid loading the tympanic membrane is middle ear effusion, a mass-loading mechanism.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Which property distinguishes the monocyte from the neutrophil in terms of sustained phagocytic capacity?
opts: The monocyte has a multilobed nucleus permitting repeated division
The multilobed nucleus belongs to the neutrophil, not the monocyte, whose nucleus is kidney-shaped; sustained capacity comes from lysosome renewal.
The monocyte can replace its lysosomal contents
Correct. The neutrophil cannot renew its lysosomes and dies after a few pathogens; the monocyte can replace its lysosomal contents and so keeps working.
The monocyte does not require opsonization of its targets
Opsonins enhance recognition and attachment for phagocytes generally; the monocyte's advantage is that it can replace its lysosomal contents.
The monocyte carries T cell receptors for direct antigen binding
T cell receptors are carried by T lymphocytes; the monocyte's advantage is that it can replace its lysosomal contents.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: A patient's inflamed tissue shows a leukocyte infiltrate dominated by cells with bi-lobed nuclei and pink-orange granules. Which process does this pattern most suggest?
opts: A chronic autoimmune process
Chronic inflammation is characterized by macrophages, monocytes and mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells, not by eosinophils.
A humoral antibody response
Antibody production is mediated by B lymphocytes and plasma cells; bi-lobed nuclei with pink-orange granules identify eosinophils instead.
An acute bacterial infection
Bacterial infection recruits neutrophils, which have multilobed nuclei and fine pale lilac granules.
An allergic or parasitic process
Correct. Bi-lobed nuclei with pink-orange granules identify eosinophils, which predominate in allergic reactions and parasitic infections.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: What is the mechanism of Meniere disease?
opts: Defective endolymph resorption causing hydrops, ballooning the scala media until micro-ruptures occur
Correct. Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion: fluid accumulates because it is not resorbed, the membranous labyrinth distends, and micro-ruptures follow. The episodic nature follows from that cycle.
Inflammatory swelling and vascular congestion of the labyrinth after a viral infection
That is labyrinthitis, and the recent upper respiratory infection is what separates the two clinically.
Dislodged otoconia floating in the semicircular canals
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
Demyelination of the vestibular nerve
Meniere disease is not demyelinating. Its lesion is endolymphatic hydrops, from defective endolymph resorption distending the membranous labyrinth.

B.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
B.q: Why does a central chiasmal lesion spare nasal vision in both eyes?
opts: The macula is spared by a dual blood supply
Macular sparing from a dual blood supply belongs to occipital cortex lesions; a chiasmal lesion spares nasal vision because only crossing fibers are cut.
The lesion affects only one eye at a time
A central chiasmal lesion affects both eyes, producing bitemporal hemianopsia, because the crossing nasal fibers from each eye are interrupted.
Only the crossing nasal retinal fibers are interrupted, and those carry the temporal fields; the temporal retinal fibers travel ipsilaterally and are untouched
Correct — only the nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm, and they carry the temporal fields; the temporal retinal fibers stay ipsilateral, so nasal vision survives.
The lesion damages the temporal retinal fibers instead, and those carry nasal vision
Temporal retinal fibers stay ipsilateral, so a central lesion misses them; it cuts the crossing nasal fibers, which carry the temporal fields.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Where does each step of vitamin D activation take place, beginning in the skin?
opts: Cholecalciferol is produced in the liver, then hydroxylated in the skin and finally in the kidneys
Production starts in the skin, not the liver: ultraviolet B light forms cholecalciferol, which the liver and then the kidneys hydroxylate.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin and hydroxylated entirely within the kidneys in a single step
Two organs are involved in activation, the liver first and then the kidney.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin under ultraviolet B light, then hydroxylated first in the liver and then in the kidneys to the active form calcitriol
Correct. The skin only starts the process; two further hydroxylation steps in separate organs are needed before the hormone is active.
Calcitriol is produced directly in the skin under ultraviolet B light and requires no further modification in either the liver or the kidneys at all
The skin produces cholecalciferol, which is inactive until hydroxylated twice elsewhere.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Which layer forms the semi-impermeable barrier of the skin?
opts: The stratum basale, a single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes at the base
The stratum basale is the deepest layer, where cells divide; the barrier is formed by the outermost layer, the stratum corneum.
The stratum granulosum, 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells
The stratum granulosum holds keratohyalin granules but is not the barrier; the stratum corneum forms the semi-impermeable barrier.
The papillary dermis, a thin superficial connective tissue layer
The papillary dermis is a connective tissue layer, not epidermis; the barrier is the stratum corneum of keratin and dead keratinocytes.
The stratum corneum, 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes cemented together
Correct. The stratum corneum, the outermost layer, packs 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes into a semi-impermeable barrier.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Which description of petechiae is accurate?
opts: Minor bleeding into the dermis from capillary rupture, infection, thrombocytopenia or vasculitis, 1 to 2 millimeters or less
Correct. Petechiae are non-blanchable pinpoint deposits of blood in the dermis, 1 to 2 millimeters or less, from minor bleeding such as capillary rupture.
Permanent dilatation of the superficial dermal vessels, measuring 1 to 2 millimeters across the surface of the skin
Permanent dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels is telangiectasia; petechiae are pinpoint deposits of blood from bleeding into the dermis.
Increased melanin production in the basal layer, up to 5 millimeters
Increased melanin production in the basal layer produces a hyperpigmented macule; petechiae are red or purple deposits of blood 1 to 2 millimeters or less.
Mast cell histamine release with plasma leakage, up to 5 millimeters
Histamine release from mast cells with plasma leaking into the dermis produces a wheal; petechiae are pinpoint deposits of blood from capillary rupture.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Which statement about neutrophils is correct?
opts: They present antigen to T cells after phagocytosis
Presenting antigen to T cells after phagocytosis is the monocyte's role; neutrophils are first responders whose death forms pus.
They are the predominant inflammatory cell in allergic reactions and in parasitic infection
Eosinophils are the predominant inflammatory cells in allergic reactions; neutrophils are first responders whose death in large numbers forms pus.
They are first responders to microbial infection, and their activity and death in large numbers forms pus
Correct. Neutrophils are first responders to microbial infection, and their activity and death in large numbers forms pus.
They mature in the thymus and carry T cell receptors
Maturing in the thymus and carrying T cell receptors describes the T lymphocyte; neutrophils are first responders that form pus.

B.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
B.q: In which cavity does seeding most commonly occur?
opts: The subarachnoid space
Seeding can reach the subarachnoid space, but it most commonly occurs in the peritoneal cavity.
The peritoneal cavity
Correct — seeding most commonly occurs in the peritoneal cavity; the pericardial and pleural cavities and the subarachnoid space can also be seeded.
The pericardial cavity
The pericardial cavity can be seeded, but seeding most commonly occurs in the peritoneal cavity.
The pleural cavity
The pleural cavity can be seeded, but seeding most commonly occurs in the peritoneal cavity.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 15

B.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: What is a metastasis?
opts: Local invasion of a cancer into the tissue immediately surrounding it
That is local invasion; a metastasis is a portion of the cancer that has migrated from the primary site to other sites.
A benign nodule that develops in the tissue draining a cancer
Metastatic deposits are malignant, being part of the original cancer.
A portion of a cancer that has migrated from the primary site to other sites
Correct — the primary remains where it began; the metastasis is what has left.
A second, unrelated primary cancer arising in another organ
A metastasis is derived from the original cancer, not independent of it.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 11

B.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
B.q: What is the mechanism of the most common, senile form of cataract?
opts: Progressive insoluble aggregation and deposition of lens crystallin proteins
Correct — senile cataract, the most common form, results from progressive insoluble aggregation and deposition of lens crystallin proteins, opacifying the lens.
Osmotic swelling of the lens driven by sorbitol accumulating inside it
Sorbitol-driven osmotic swelling is the diabetic mechanism; the senile form is protein aggregation.
Rupture of the lens capsule after blunt trauma
Capsule rupture from blunt or penetrating trauma is the traumatic mechanism; senile cataract comes from crystallin protein aggregation.
Chronic ultraviolet-driven oxidative damage alone
Ultraviolet light is an environmental cataract cause, not the senile mechanism, which is progressive aggregation of insoluble lens crystallin proteins.

B.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
B.q: Why does asymmetrical vestibular input produce a false sense of motion?
opts: The brain reads the mismatch between the two sides as movement
Correct. Balance is a comparison, so unequal input is indistinguishable from turning.
Cerebral perfusion falls on one side
Falling cerebral perfusion produces dizziness and presyncope, which is the category vertigo is separated from.
The otoliths dissolve
Otoconia do not dissolve. They can become dislodged into the semicircular canals, which is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
The cochlea sends conflicting auditory signals
The cochlea handles hearing and contributes nothing to the sense of position or movement.

B.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
B.q: Which description fits a chalazion?
opts: An acute, tender, focal abscess of a gland sitting at the eyelid margin
An acute, tender focal abscess is a hordeolum, usually from Staphylococcus aureus; a chalazion is chronic, non-tender and sterile.
A cholesterol-filled plaque along the nasal eyelid
A cholesterol-filled lid lesion is xanthelasma, linked to hyperlipidemia; a chalazion is a sterile lipogranuloma of a blocked meibomian gland.
Redundant lid skin with prolapse of orbital fat
Redundant lid skin with orbital fat prolapse is dermatochalasis; a chalazion is a chronic, sterile lipogranuloma of a blocked meibomian gland.
A chronic, non-tender, sterile granulomatous lipogranuloma of a blocked meibomian gland
Correct — sterile and granulomatous is what separates it from an infection.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Why does prolonged antibiotic use predispose to FUNGAL otitis externa?
opts: It thins the canal skin directly
Antibiotics do not thin the canal skin. What they remove is the bacterial competition.
It removes the bacterial competition that normally limits fungal growth
Correct. Prolonged antibiotic use suppresses the bacteria, and Aspergillus niger or Candida albicans then take over as fungal otitis externa.
It raises the canal pH to favor fungi
The association is not explained by pH. It is the loss of competing bacteria that lets fungus grow.
It damages the tympanic membrane
Otitis externa is an infection of the canal. Its fungal form follows prolonged antibiotic use or hyperhumid conditions, not membrane damage.

B.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
B.q: Which description matches the optics of myopia?
opts: The globe is normal but the lens has lost elasticity
Loss of lens elasticity is presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focus; myopia is an elongated globe that focuses in front of the retina.
The axial globe is too long, so the focal point falls in front of the retina
Correct — an elongated globe overshoots, focusing short of the retina.
The axial globe is too short, so the focal point falls behind the retina
A globe too short, focusing behind the retina, is hyperopia; in myopia the axial globe is too long, so the focal point falls in front of the retina.
The globe is normal but the cornea is irregularly curved
Irregular corneal or lens curvature is astigmatism, creating non-spherical focal points; myopia is an axial globe that is too long.

B.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
B.q: What are the four grades of neoplastic differentiation, from most to least resemblance?
opts: Anaplasia, poorly differentiated, moderately differentiated, well differentiated
That is the correct sequence in reverse; the scale runs from well differentiated, with close resemblance, down to anaplasia.
In situ, microinvasive, invasive, metastatic
That is a progression of invasion rather than a grading of differentiation; the grades run well, moderately and poorly differentiated, then anaplasia.
Stage I, stage II, stage III, stage IV
Those are stages, which measure extent of spread rather than resemblance; the grades run well, moderately and poorly differentiated, then anaplasia.
Well differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated, anaplasia
Correct — differentiation runs from close resemblance (well) through intermediate and poor resemblance to anaplasia, the lack of differentiation.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 12

B.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
B.q: What does it mean, structurally, for lymph nodes to be MATTED?
opts: They have lost their individual capsules and move as one mass
Correct. Matted nodes move together as one mass, and persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults require assessment to rule out lymphoma.
They are tender and mobile
Tender and mobile describes a reactive node responding to local infection, which is the reassuring picture.
They are smaller than normal
Matting is about nodes moving together as one mass, and says nothing about whether they are large or small.
They fluctuate in size with infection
Nodes that swell and settle with infection are behaving reactively, which is the opposite of the concerning pattern.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Beyond phagocytosis, what is the monocyte's role in the immune response?
opts: Secreting histamine to open the capillary bed
Among the leukocytes, histamine comes from basophils; the monocyte presents pathogen pieces to T cells.
Producing the fibrous network that traps exudate
The fibrous network that traps exudate comes from the coagulation system; monocytes present pathogen pieces to T cells.
Presenting pieces of pathogens to T cells so the pathogen may be recognized again and killed
Correct. After phagocytosis, monocytes present pieces of pathogens to T cells so that the pathogens may be recognized again and killed.
Restoring the immune system to its normal function once the infection has resolved
Returning the immune system to normal after infection is the regulatory (suppressor) T cell's role, not the monocyte's.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: What is the bone remodeling sequence in otosclerosis?
opts: Demineralization of the ossicles from chronic inflammation
Otosclerosis is not an inflammatory demineralization. It is osteoclastic resorption followed by spongy osteoid replacement around the stapes footplate.
Fibrous scarring of the round window membrane
The lesion is at the oval window and the stapes footplate, and it is bone rather than scar.
Osteoblastic overgrowth of dense cortical bone without resorption
The sequence begins with osteoclastic resorption, and the bone laid down is hypervascular spongy osteoid, not dense cortical overgrowth.
Osteoclastic resorption, then spongy osteoid replacement
Correct. Abnormal osteoclastic bone resorption is followed by hypervascular spongy osteoid replacement around the otic capsule and stapes footplate, which then fixes the footplate.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
B.q: How is the avascular cornea oxygenated?
opts: By the choroidal circulation behind it
The choroid is a vascular layer nourishing the retina at the back of the eye; the avascular cornea takes its oxygen from air and tears.
By direct contact with air and tears
Correct — the cornea is entirely avascular, so it is oxygenated through direct contact with air and tears rather than by any blood supply.
By diffusion from the limbal blood vessels alone
No vessels supply the cornea's oxygen, since it is entirely avascular; it is oxygenated by direct contact with air and tears.
By the aqueous humor circulating through the anterior chamber
Aqueous nourishes the cornea and lens, but oxygen comes from air and tears.

B.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: What is metaplasia?
opts: Change of one cell type to another under chronic irritation or injury
Correct — it involves a change in differentiation. Bladder transitional epithelium becoming squamous is the standard example.
Disordered growth of epithelial cells with variation in size and shape and loss of architectural orientation
That is dysplasia, which is the next step along and is precancerous.
Enlargement of an organ because its individual cells enlarge under increased demand
Enlargement of individual cells is hypertrophy; metaplasia changes one cell type into another under chronic irritation.
Autonomous growth of an abnormal mass of tissue derived from a single genetically altered cell
An autonomous clonal mass is a neoplasm; metaplasia is a change of cell type in response to chronic irritation or injury.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 4

B.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
B.q: Which description of lichenification is accurate?
opts: Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with accumulation of fluid between the two layers, forming a large blister that lifts the surface away
Epidermis separating from dermis with fluid between them forms a bulla; lichenification is hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis from the itch-scratch cycle.
Slowing of keratinocyte division with elastin degradation
Slowed keratinocyte division with elastin degradation is atrophy, which thins the skin; lichenification thickens it through hyperplasia.
Long-term scratching or rubbing of a pruritic area in an itch-scratch cycle, producing hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis with solid, firm, thick plaques without scaling
Correct. The itch-scratch cycle drives hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis into firm, thick plaques without scaling, as in lichen simplex chronicus.
Loss of melanocytes across a circumscribed area
Loss of melanocytes produces a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo; lichenification is epidermal thickening from long-term scratching or rubbing.

B.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
B.q: What do initiators do in chemical carcinogenesis?
opts: They cause permanent damage to deoxyribonucleic acid
Correct — permanence is what distinguishes initiation from promotion.
They cause sustained or enhanced proliferation of already-damaged cells
Sustained or enhanced proliferation of damaged cells is promotion; initiators cause the permanent damage first.
They repair damage already caused by another carcinogen
Initiators cause permanent deoxyribonucleic acid damage rather than repairing it; they start chemical carcinogenesis.
They trigger apoptosis in cells with damaged genomes
Triggering apoptosis protects against damaged cells; initiators instead cause permanent deoxyribonucleic acid damage.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 31

B.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
B.q: Besides cervical cancer, which malignancies is high-risk human papillomavirus associated with?
opts: Retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma
Those are associated with the retinoblastoma protein under heredity.
Anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and oropharyngeal cancer
Correct — high-risk human papillomavirus is associated with all five in addition to cervical cancer, the oropharyngeal one being a squamous cell carcinoma.
Hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric adenocarcinoma
Those belong to the hepatitis viruses and Helicobacter pylori respectively.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and certain B cell lymphomas
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and certain B cell lymphomas follow Epstein Barr virus, which immortalizes B lymphocytes.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 37

B.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
B.q: What is iris bombé?
opts: Forward displacement of the iris against the cornea
Correct — in angle closure, pupil dilation pushes the iris forward against the cornea, and this iris bombé blocks aqueous outflow totally so pressure spikes.
Backward displacement of the iris against the lens
The displacement is forward, not backward; in iris bombé the iris is pushed against the cornea, closing the iridocorneal angle.
Atrophy of the iris stroma after an acute attack
Iris bombé is not atrophy; it is forward displacement of the iris against the cornea, which triggers the acute outflow blockage of angle closure.
Adhesion of the iris to the corneal endothelium
Adhesion is not the meaning; iris bombé is forward displacement of the iris against the cornea, closing the angle when the pupil dilates.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Which description of Beau's lines is accurate?
opts: Impaired keratin synthesis, associated with deficiency anemia
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia is koilonychia; Beau's lines come from a halt of keratin production during illness or stress.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal or transverse grooves, associated with illness, stress, injury to the nail and malnourishment
Correct. Beau's lines are horizontal or transverse grooves caused by a halt of keratin production, associated with illness, stress, nail injury and malnourishment.
Overgrowth of connective tissue within the nail bed, associated with chronic liver disease and with diabetes mellitus in particular
Connective tissue overgrowth in the nail bed is Terry's nails; Beau's lines are grooves from a halt in keratin production.
Increased capillary density, associated with lung disease
Increased capillary density with lung disease describes clubbing; Beau's lines are transverse grooves from a halt of keratin production.

B.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
B.q: On the dysplasia spectrum, what separates severe dysplasia from invasive cancer?
opts: The presence of mitoses, which appear only once invasion has occurred
Mitoses are not the dividing line; what separates in situ from invasive cancer is a breach of the basement membrane.
Involvement of the regional lymph nodes
Regional lymph node involvement is scored by N in staging; what separates severe dysplasia from invasive cancer is a breach of the basement membrane.
The basement membrane
Correct — carcinoma in situ has not invaded through the basement membrane, while invasive cancer has broken through it.
The degree of nuclear enlargement, which is greater in invasive cancer
Nuclear changes increase through dysplasia, but invasive cancer is defined by breaching the basement membrane.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 8

B.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
B.q: Which change in the vitreous underlies rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?
opts: It solidifies, pressing the retina more firmly against the pigment epithelium
Solidification is not the change; in rhegmatogenous detachment liquefied vitreous fluid passes through a full-thickness tear into the subretinal space.
It becomes vascularized, bleeding into the subretinal space
Vascularization is not the change; the vitreous is a transparent gel, and in rhegmatogenous detachment liquefied vitreous passes through a retinal break beneath the retina.
It thickens and opacifies, blocking light before it reaches the retina
Thickening is the wrong direction; liquefied vitreous fluid enters the subretinal space through a full-thickness tear, peeling the retina off the pigment epithelium.
It liquefies, so fluid can track through any retinal break into the subretinal space
Correct — once liquefied, vitreous fluid can pass through a full-thickness retinal tear into the subretinal space and peel the neurosensory retina off the pigment epithelium.

B.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
B.q: A lesion of the optic tract produces which defect?
opts: Bitemporal hemianopsia
Bitemporal hemianopsia comes from a central chiasmal lesion such as pituitary adenoma; an optic tract lesion gives contralateral homonymous hemianopsia.
Monocular blindness
Monocular blindness requires an optic nerve lesion before the chiasm; past it, an optic tract lesion gives contralateral homonymous hemianopsia.
Central scotoma with preserved peripheral vision
A central scotoma is a macular picture, as in macular degeneration; a lesion of the optic tract causes contralateral homonymous hemianopsia.
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Correct — an optic tract lesion, from stroke, tumor or demyelination, causes contralateral homonymous hemianopsia, the loss of the opposite visual field.

B.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
B.q: How are dermatofibroma and lipoma characterized in the tissue?
opts: Both are malignant proliferations of keratinocytes
Both are benign, and neither is keratinocyte-derived: dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue in the dermis and lipoma is encapsulated adipocytes.
Dermatofibroma is keratin-filled and lipoma is fluid-filled
Keratin filling describes an epidermal inclusion cyst from a hair follicle; dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue and lipoma is a capsule of adipocytes.
Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis; lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes
Correct. Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis, and lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes.
Dermatofibroma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes; lipoma is a fibrous tissue overgrowth within the dermis
This swaps the two: dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis, and lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes.

B.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
B.q: Which statement about histamine in the inflammatory response is correct?
opts: The final mediator released during the whole response, causing fibrosis and the formation of dense scar tissue at the site
Fibrosis is a healing outcome rather than a histamine effect, and histamine acts first rather than last.
The first mediator of the initial inflammatory response, causing dilation of arterioles and increased permeability of capillaries and venules
Correct. Histamine is the first mediator of the initial response, dilating arterioles and increasing capillary and venule permeability.
A chemotactic factor drawing neutrophils to the site
Chemotaxis to neutrophils and monocytes comes from complement components; histamine dilates arterioles and raises permeability.
An opsonin that coats foreign material for recognition
The opsonins are immunoglobulin G and complement fragment C3b; histamine is the first mediator, acting on the vessels.

B.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
B.q: Histamine and serotonin share which pair of effects?
opts: Chemotaxis and opsonization
Chemotaxis comes from complement components and possibly bradykinin, and opsonization from immunoglobulin G and C3b, not from histamine.
Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Correct. Histamine dilates arterioles and increases capillary and venule permeability, and serotonin likewise causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
Pain and fibrin deposition
Pain belongs to bradykinin and fibrin deposition to the coagulation system; histamine and serotonin share vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
Antibody production and antigen presentation
Antibody production and antigen presentation belong to B lymphocytes and monocytes; histamine and serotonin act on the vessels.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Which physical law explains why a small septal deviation causes disproportionate obstruction?
opts: Boyle's law
Boyle's law does not explain nasal obstruction. Poiseuille's law does: even small airway narrowing dramatically increases resistance to airflow.
Poiseuille's law
Correct. By Poiseuille's law even small airway narrowing dramatically increases resistance, so a modest deviation can produce unilateral resistance and chronic nasal obstruction.
Fick's law of diffusion
Fick's law is not the one that applies. Poiseuille's law is: even a small narrowing of the airway dramatically increases resistance to airflow.
Laplace's law
Laplace's law does not account for the obstruction. By Poiseuille's law, small airway narrowing sharply raises resistance, producing unilateral resistance.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: Which description of the inflammatory phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: Days 1 to 3: type I collagen is laid down in basket-weave orientation
Collagen replacement happens in remodeling, days 21 to one year, when type I collagen lies in parallel bundles; days 1 to 3 bring the fibrin plug and clearance.
Days 1 to 3: a fibrin hemostatic plug forms, neutrophils and macrophages remove dead tissue, and growth factors and cytokines are secreted to signal the next phase
Correct. The phase both cleans the wound and issues the signal that starts proliferation.
Days 4 to 21: granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells that rebuild the wound bed from below over three weeks
Granulation tissue forming over days 4 to 21 is the proliferative phase; the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 3, forms a fibrin plug and clears dead tissue.
Days 21 to one year: type III collagen is replaced by type I
Replacement of type III collagen by type I is the remodeling phase, days 21 to one year; the inflammatory phase spans days 1 to 3.

C.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
C.q: Which statement describes the source of anterior epistaxis?
opts: The anterior ethmoidal artery, about 10 percent
Posterior bleeds are the 10 percent, and they come from Woodruff's plexus; anterior bleeds come from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum.
Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall, about 90 percent
Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall is the posterior source, about 10 percent of cases, not the anterior 90 percent.
Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum, about 90 percent
Correct. Anterior epistaxis, 90 percent of cases, comes from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum; the posterior 10 percent come from Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall.
The sphenopalatine artery, about 50 percent
The sphenopalatine artery is not the anterior source. Anterior bleeds, 90 percent of cases, come from Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum.

C.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
C.q: What is the symptom set of acute angle-closure glaucoma?
opts: Severe eye pain, headache, halos around lights, cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and nausea and vomiting
Correct — iris bombé blocks aqueous outflow totally, and the rapid pressure spike above 50 mmHg produces pain, headache, halos, a cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and vomiting.
Painless gradual bilateral blurring with glare at night
Painless gradual blurring with night glare is cataract; acute angle closure is a sudden, painful pressure spike with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Flashing lights, a sudden shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
Photopsia, a shower of floaters and a falling curtain describe rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; angle closure brings severe pain, halos and vomiting.
Gradual central distortion with a scotoma
Gradual central distortion with a scotoma is dry macular degeneration; acute angle closure is sudden, with severe pain, halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Ulcerative inflammation is characterized by which change?
opts: Formation of a membrane-like covering over intact and otherwise viable mucosa
That is the pseudomembranous pattern, in which the necrotic layer forms a covering rather than exposing tissue beneath.
Damage to blood vessels occurring with other exudates
Damage to blood vessels alongside other exudates is the hemorrhagic pattern; ulceration is necrosis and sloughing of epithelium.
Coagulative necrosis of an entire limb segment
Coagulative necrosis is dry gangrene, a separate pattern; ulcerative inflammation is necrosis and sloughing of surface epithelium.
Necrosis and sloughing of surface epithelium, exposing underlying connective tissue
Correct. That exposure of the underlying connective tissue is what defines the ulcerative pattern.

C.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
C.q: Where does the gene damage in carcinogenesis come from?
opts: It is always acquired during life and never inherited
Gene damage is not always acquired; damaged regulatory genes may be inherited, as with BRCA-1 and BRCA-2.
It arises only from errors during deoxyribonucleic acid replication
Gene damage may be inherited or come from chemical carcinogens, radiation, and microbes, not only from replication errors.
Inherited, and/or acquired from chemicals, radiation or microbes
Correct — damaged genes may be inherited or develop from chemical carcinogens, ultraviolet and ionizing radiation, and microbes: viruses and one bacterium.
It is always inherited through the germline and never acquired during life
Gene damage is not always inherited; chemical carcinogens, radiation, and microbes also damage regulatory genes during life.

C.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
C.q: What is the tissue basis of a papule?
opts: Focal loss of the epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction beneath it
Focal epidermal loss above the junction is an erosion, a secondary lesion; a papule is an elevated solid lesion from epidermal hyperplasia.
Hyperplasia of the epidermis with hyperkeratosis, plus inflammation and dense collagen fibers in the dermis
Correct. A papule is an elevated solid lesion under 5 millimeters, built from epidermal hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis over dermal inflammation, as in seborrheic keratosis.
Fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or beneath the epidermis
Fluid with inflammatory cells within or beneath the epidermis forms a vesicle; a papule is solid, from hyperplasia with hyperkeratosis.
Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid accumulation
Epidermis separating from dermis with fluid accumulation forms a bulla; a papule is solid, from epidermal hyperplasia and dense dermal collagen.

C.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Digestion of foreign material by activated neutrophils and macrophages involves which four steps?
opts: Vasodilation, exudation, stasis, and repair
Vasodilation, exudation and stasis are vascular events; digestion by neutrophils and macrophages is recognition, attachment, engulfment and degradation.
Adhesion, transmigration, aggregation, and chemotaxis
Adhesion, transmigration, aggregation and chemotaxis bring the cell to the site; digestion is recognition, attachment, engulfment and degradation.
Recognition, attachment, engulfment, and degradation
Correct. Those four, and recognition and attachment are enhanced when opsonins are present.
Opsonization, complement fixation, lysis, and clearance
Opsonization enhances recognition and attachment but is not a step; the four steps are recognition, attachment, engulfment and degradation.

C.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
C.q: Which features mark vertigo as PERIPHERAL rather than central?
opts: Absence of nystagmus entirely
Nystagmus is expected, not absent. Peripheral vertigo shows prominent horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.
Gradual onset, vertical nystagmus, non-suppressible, with neurological deficits
Gradual onset, vertical non-suppressible nystagmus and neurological deficits describe CENTRAL vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum.
Gradual onset with hearing loss and tinnitus
Gradual onset is a central feature. Peripheral vertigo is sudden, with horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.
Sudden onset, horizontal or rotational nystagmus, fatigable, suppressed by visual fixation
Correct. Peripheral vertigo involves the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII, with sudden onset and prominent horizontal or rotational nystagmus that is fatigable and suppressed by visual fixation.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: What effects does serotonin have?
opts: Pain generation and leukocyte chemotaxis
Pain and possibly increased chemotaxis are effects of bradykinin; serotonin causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
Opsonization of biomaterials
Opsonization of biomaterials is done by immunoglobulin G and C3b; serotonin causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Correct. Serotonin causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, the same pair of vascular effects as histamine.
Formation of a fibrous network trapping microorganisms
A fibrous network that traps microorganisms is made by the coagulation system; serotonin's effects are vasodilation and permeability.

C.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
C.q: A benign tumor arises from cartilage. Which category does it fall into?
opts: Epithelial, since cartilage lines a surface
Cartilage is supportive tissue rather than a lining epithelium.
Glandular, so it would be called an adenoma
An adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor with a glandular pattern; cartilage is supportive tissue, so the tumor is mesenchymal.
Neither, since the classification covers only epithelial tumors
Benign tumors are classified as mesenchymal or epithelial, and cartilage belongs to the mesenchymal, supportive group.
Mesenchymal, since cartilage is supportive tissue
Correct — mesenchymal tumors arise from supportive tissue: connective tissue, adipose tissue, cartilage, smooth and striated muscle, and bone.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: How do hypertrophic scars and keloids depart from normal healing?
opts: Type I collagen is replaced by weaker type III in basket-weave orientation
Remodeling normally replaces type III collagen with stronger type I; in keloids the defect is an imbalance of collagen deposition and degradation during remodeling.

Fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase, collagen deposition and degradation become imbalanced during remodeling, and collagen bundles develop haphazardly and exceed the boundaries of the initial wound
Correct. Two phases go wrong, and exceeding the original wound margin is the defining outcome.
Keratinocyte division slows and elastin degrades, thinning the tissue
Slowed keratinocyte division and elastin degradation describe atrophy, which thins the skin; keloids come from a prolonged proliferative phase and excess collagen.

The inflammatory phase never resolves, so granulation tissue never forms at all and the wound remains open indefinitely without ever progressing to the proliferative or remodeling phases that normally follow
Hypertrophic scars and keloids do progress through healing; fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase rather than preventing it.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: Which description of collagen in the remodeling phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: Collagen production continues to increase indefinitely
Production does not rise indefinitely: granulation tissue formation ceases in remodeling while type III collagen is replaced by type I.
Type III collagen is replaced with stronger type I collagen oriented in small parallel bundles, whereas normal dermis has a basket-weave orientation
Correct. In remodeling, from day 21 to one year, type III collagen gives way to stronger type I in small parallel bundles, unlike the basket-weave of normal dermis.
Type I collagen is replaced with weaker type III collagen oriented in a basket-weave pattern throughout the scar tissue that results
This reverses both: weaker type III is replaced by stronger type I, laid in parallel bundles rather than the basket-weave of normal dermis.
Collagen is degraded entirely and replaced by elastin
Elastin does not replace collagen in a scar; remodeling swaps type III collagen for stronger type I collagen in parallel bundles.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: Which lid deformity goes with dacryoadenitis?
opts: An outward-turning lid margin
An outward-turning margin is not the sign; dacryoadenitis gives an S-shaped lid deformity, with pain over the superotemporal orbital rim.
A drooping upper lid from levator weakness
A drooping lid from levator weakness is ptosis; dacryoadenitis, inflammation of the lacrimal gland, gives an S-shaped lid deformity.
An S-shaped lid deformity
Correct — dacryoadenitis is inflammation or infection of the lacrimal gland, causing superotemporal orbital rim pain and an S-shaped lid deformity.
An inward-turning lid margin
An inward-turning margin is not the sign; lacrimal gland inflammation in dacryoadenitis produces an S-shaped lid deformity with superotemporal rim pain.

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
C.q: What makes the eye the only place in the body where live neural tissue can be seen directly?
opts: The cornea contains myelinated tracts that can be seen on slit lamp
Corneal nerves are not what is seen; the directly visible neural tissue is the optic nerve head, viewed through the pupil without cutting tissue.
The sclera is thin enough to transilluminate the whole globe
The sclera is a protective white coat, not a window; the optic nerve head is seen through the pupil and clear media without cutting any tissue.
The optic nerve head is visible through the pupil without cutting any tissue
Correct — the eye is a nervous window: the only place in the body where live neural tissue and a cranial nerve, the optic nerve head, can be seen directly.
The retina can be biopsied more safely than any other neural tissue
Biopsy is not the point; the eye is the only place where live neural tissue, the optic nerve head, can be seen directly without cutting any tissue.

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
C.q: What are the steps of hematogenous spread, in order?
opts: Cells separate and degrade intercellular tissue with enzymes, invade the vessel, then travel
Correct — multiple tumor fragments travel to other organs, so one organ may end up with several metastatic nodules.
Tumor cells adhere more tightly to each other; the mass compresses a vessel; a single fragment travels to one other organ
Cells separate rather than adhere, and multiple fragments travel.
Tumor cells enter lymphatic vessels at the margin and follow the natural route of drainage
Entering lymphatics at the tumor margin and following drainage is lymphatic spread, not spread through blood vessels.
Tumor invades through an organ surface into a body cavity and settles on the serosal membranes
Invading through an organ surface into a cavity is seeding, which most commonly occurs in the peritoneal cavity.

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
C.q: What can a hyperopic patient see well?
opts: Objects far away
Correct — hyperopia is farsightedness, so distance vision is the preserved one.
Objects up close
Near vision is what fails in hyperopia, because the short globe focuses behind the retina; distance vision is the preserved one.
Neither near nor far without correction
Distance vision is preserved in hyperopia; only near focus fails, because the short axial globe places the focal point behind the retina.
Only objects directly in the central field
Hyperopia is a refractive error of a short globe, not a field defect; it spares distance vision while near focus fails.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: Which description of the pathology of nail clubbing is accurate?
opts: A halt of keratin production at the matrix
A halt of keratin production causes Beau's lines; clubbing is driven by increased capillary density and vascular endothelial growth factor release.
Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed produces leukonychia; clubbing shows increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release.
Increased capillary density, with increased release of vascular endothelial growth factor
Correct. The main pathologic finding in clubbing is increased capillary density, with increased release of vascular endothelial growth factor.
Overgrowth of the connective tissue within the nail bed itself over a period of time
Connective tissue overgrowth in the nail bed produces Terry's nails; the main pathologic finding in clubbing is increased capillary density.

C.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
C.q: What does falling differentiation mean for the behavior of a tumor?
opts: Aggressiveness is unrelated to differentiation and depends only on stage
Staging and grading are separate measures, but falling differentiation by itself signals a more aggressive tumor.
It becomes more aggressive only once the basement membrane has been breached
Invasion through the basement membrane is a separate matter; aggressiveness rises as differentiation falls, with or without it.
It becomes more aggressive
Correct — poorly differentiated cells stay in the proliferative pool, so the tumor grows faster; benign tumors are usually well differentiated and slow growing.
It becomes less aggressive, because poorly differentiated cells divide more slowly
Poorly differentiated cells are not slower: abnormal differentiation puts a greater percentage of cells in the proliferative pool.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: How is episcleritis best characterized?
opts: A vision-threatening emergency with severe deep boring pain and scleral melting
Deep boring pain, scleral melting and threatened vision describe scleritis, an emergency of the deep sclera; episcleritis is a self-limiting blush without severe pain.
An infection of the corneal stroma
An infection of the corneal stroma is keratitis; episcleritis is a self-limiting inflammatory blush of the superficial episclera that spares vision.
A granulomatous blockage of a meibomian gland
A granulomatous blocked meibomian gland is a chalazion; episcleritis is a self-limiting inflammatory blush of the superficial episclera.
A self-limiting inflammatory blush, not vision-threatening and without severe pain
Correct — inflammation of the superficial episclera is a self-limiting blush with no severe pain and no threat to vision, unlike the deep, emergency inflammation of scleritis.

C.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
C.q: What can an adenoma sometimes do that reflects its origin?
opts: Produce finger-like projections from the epithelial surface
Finger-like projections from an epithelial surface define a papilloma; an adenoma forms a glandular pattern or derives from a gland.
Secrete the hormone or hormones produced by its gland of origin
Correct — the tumor retains a function of the tissue it came from.
Invade through the basement membrane into surrounding tissue
Invasion of surrounding tissue is a malignant behavior; an adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor, which compresses surrounding tissue instead.
Seed the peritoneal cavity through an organ surface
Seeding is invasion of a tumor through an organ surface into a body cavity; an adenoma is benign, so it compresses rather than invades.

C.io: f — Compare and contrast the different types of malignant tumors according to origin
C.q: What is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal origin called?
opts: An adenoma
An adenoma is a benign epithelial tumor with a glandular pattern; the malignant mesenchymal tumor is a sarcoma.
A papilloma
A papilloma is benign and epithelial, with finger-like projections; the malignant mesenchymal tumor is a sarcoma.
A sarcoma
Correct — mesenchymal means supportive tissue, and the malignant form is the sarcoma.
A carcinoma
Carcinoma is the malignant tumor of epithelial origin; malignant tumors of supportive, mesenchymal tissue are sarcomas.

C.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
C.q: Which tumors are associated with an inherited alteration of the retinoblastoma protein?
opts: Retinoblastoma, a rare childhood tumor of the eye, and osteosarcoma
Correct — the same tumor suppressor, two very different tumors.
Neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, with tumors of the central and peripheral nervous system
Nervous system tumors follow NF-1 and NF-2 (neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2), not retinoblastoma protein alteration.
Malignant melanoma
Malignant melanoma follows inherited p16 (INK4a) alteration, not retinoblastoma protein alteration.
Familial adenomatous polyposis and colon cancer
Familial adenomatous polyposis and colon cancer follow adenomatous polyposis coli, not the retinoblastoma protein.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: Which description of actinic keratosis is accurate?
opts: Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes, carrying a higher risk for basal cell carcinoma of the head and neck region in later life especially
Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes is seborrheic keratosis; actinic keratosis is dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation raising squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Human papillomavirus infection of basal cells, carrying higher risk for melanoma
Human papillomavirus invading basal cells produces verrucae vulgaris; actinic keratosis stems from cumulative ultraviolet damage and raises squamous cell carcinoma risk.
Autoimmune T cell infiltration, carrying higher risk for lymphoma
Autoimmune T cell infiltration fits psoriasis, not actinic keratosis, which is ultraviolet-driven dysplasia carrying a higher risk of squamous cell carcinoma.
Damage from excessive cumulative ultraviolet exposure leading to intraepidermal proliferation of dysplastic keratinocytes, carrying higher risk for squamous cell carcinoma
Correct. Actinic keratosis is the most common precancer, arising on skin damaged by chronic ultraviolet exposure, and it carries a higher risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

C.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Why does stasis of blood flow matter mechanistically in acute inflammation?
opts: It terminates the inflammatory response
The sequence continues through adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation and phagocytosis.
It precedes leukocyte adhesion in the sequence, as slowed flow allows leukocytes to contact the endothelium
Correct. Hemoconcentration and stasis sit immediately before leukocyte adhesion in the sequence of events of acute inflammation.
It marks the point at which acute inflammation gives way to chronic inflammation in the tissue
Stasis is an acute event, directly after increased permeability; chronic inflammation is defined by its longer course (days, weeks, months) and lymphocytes and macrophages.
It reverses the earlier increase in permeability
Nothing reverses at this point: increased vascular permeability is the step before stasis, and leukocyte adhesion is the step after it.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: What is the pattern of onset in presbycusis?
opts: Gradual, symmetrical and bilateral
Correct, and it is sensorineural. Asymmetry would point away from aging toward a focal lesion.
Sudden and unilateral
Sudden unilateral sensorineural loss fits labyrinthitis. Presbycusis is gradual, symmetrical and bilateral in older adults.
Episodic and fluctuating
Loss that comes and goes suggests Meniere disease, where endolymph pressure rises and falls.
Gradual but strictly unilateral
Presbycusis is symmetrical and bilateral, not one-sided; its gradual loss begins with the high-frequency tones.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: Why does an ulcer scar while an erosion generally does not?
opts: An ulcer involves a loss of melanocytes from the basal layer which cannot be reversed once it has occurred in the tissue at any point afterwards
Melanocyte loss causes hypopigmentation such as vitiligo; an ulcer is focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of collagen.
An ulcer destroys collagen in the dermis, so healing must lay down new collagen; an erosion spares the dermal-epidermal junction and the dermis beneath it
Correct. Scarring is a dermal repair process, so a lesion confined above the junction has nothing to scar.
An ulcer is infected and an erosion is sterile
Infection does not define either lesion; the difference is depth, since an ulcer destroys dermal collagen and an erosion stays above the junction.
An ulcer is larger, and size alone determines scarring
Size is not the operative difference; depth is, because an ulcer loses dermis and its collagen while an erosion spares the dermal-epidermal junction.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: What are the three causes of chronic inflammation?
opts: Trauma, thermal injury, and radiation exposure
Trauma and similar physical insults cause acute inflammation; chronicity comes from persistent infection, toxic agents or autoimmunity.
Persistent infection, prolonged exposure to potentially toxic agents, and autoimmunity
Correct. Persistent infection, prolonged exposure to toxic agents and autoimmunity cause chronic inflammation; lupus is an autoimmune example.
Vasodilation, increased permeability, and exudation
Vasodilation, increased permeability and exudation are the vascular mechanisms of acute inflammation, not causes of chronicity.
Opsonization of foreign material, phagocytosis by neutrophils, and enzymatic degradation
Opsonization, phagocytosis and degradation handle foreign material; chronic inflammation is caused by persistent infection, toxic agents or autoimmunity.

C.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Which vascular change is directly responsible for allowing fluid and blood proteins to enter the interstitium?
opts: Vasoconstriction of the draining venules
Vasoconstriction opens the sequence of events, before vasodilation; endothelial contraction is what increases capillary permeability.
Endothelial contraction increasing capillary permeability
Correct. Endothelial contraction is what allows the increased permeability through which exudation occurs.
Hemoconcentration occurring within the capillary bed
Hemoconcentration and stasis follow increased vascular permeability rather than causing it; endothelial contraction raises capillary permeability.
Vasodilation of the supplying arterioles
Vasodilation increases blood flow into the region but does not open the vessel wall; endothelial contraction is what increases capillary permeability.

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
C.q: Besides invasion into adjacent structures, which abnormal interaction is a step in invasion?
opts: Abnormal apoptosis of neighbouring stromal cells
Stromal cell apoptosis is not a step; invasion involves abnormal cell-substratum interaction and invasion into adjacent structures.
Abnormal lymphatic valve function
Lymphatic valves play no part; the step alongside invasion into adjacent structures is abnormal cell-substratum interaction.
Abnormal cell-substratum interaction
Correct — the cell's relationship with its own supporting matrix changes.
Abnormal cell-cycle checkpoint control
Checkpoint loss is a gene alteration, as when the viral protein E7 inhibits the retinoblastoma protein; the step alongside invasion is abnormal cell-substratum interaction.

C.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
C.q: Which description defines vertigo as distinct from dizziness?
opts: A hallucination of motion, with NO syncope
Correct. Asymmetry between the two sides is the mechanism, and the absence of syncope is the separator. Dizziness or lightheadedness is a non-vestibular sensation of impending faint.
A sensation of impending faint from cerebral hypoperfusion
That is dizziness or presyncope, driven by hypoperfusion, orthostatic hypotension or metabolic imbalance.
Any unsteadiness on standing
Unsteadiness alone does not distinguish the two; the hallucination of motion does.
Loss of consciousness preceded by spinning
Vertigo explicitly involves NO syncope. Loss of consciousness points away from a vestibular cause and toward cerebral hypoperfusion.

C.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
C.q: What makes the middle ear vulnerable to the pressure changes behind otitis media?
opts: It is an air-filled space vented only by the Eustachian tube
Correct. A sealed air pocket with one vent is why closing the vent drops the pressure and draws in fluid.
It has no blood supply
Blood supply is not the weakness. The middle ear is air-filled, and when the Eustachian tube fails to open, its mucosa absorbs oxygen and nitrogen, creating negative pressure.
It is lined by keratinized skin
A keratinized lining is not the problem. It is the middle ear mucosa that absorbs oxygen and nitrogen when the Eustachian tube fails to open, so pressure falls.
It is fluid-filled and cannot compress
The middle ear is air-filled; the INNER ear holds the fluid.

C.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
C.q: Which chemical carcinogens are classically emphasized in occupational bladder cancer?
opts: Aromatic amines
Correct — aromatic amines are classically emphasized in occupational bladder cancer, whereas tobacco supplies polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
Those are the tobacco combustion products, which also cause bladder cancer.
Alkylating agents
Alkylating agents are not the classic occupational bladder carcinogen; aromatic amines are.
Asbestos fibers
Asbestos fibers are not the classic occupational bladder carcinogen; aromatic amines are.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: What tissue makes up a scale?
opts: Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin
Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin form a crust, as in impetigo; a scale is desquamating stratum corneum.
Thickened epidermis induced by long-term scratching
Epidermal thickening from long-term scratching is lichenification; a scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum.
Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of the collagen beneath
Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with collagen destruction is an ulcer; a scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum.
A compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum, varying in size and thickness
Correct. A scale is a compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum that varies in size and thickness, and psoriasis is an example.

C.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
C.q: Above what cup-to-disc ratio is optic disc cupping progressive?
opts: Greater than 0.8
A ratio of 0.8 is well past the threshold rather than the threshold itself; cupping counts as increased once the ratio exceeds 0.5.
Greater than 1.0
A ratio above 1.0 is not the threshold; progressive glaucomatous cupping is an increased cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.5.
Greater than 0.5
Correct — raised pressure compresses retinal ganglion cell axons, the cells die by apoptosis, and the cup widens to a cup-to-disc ratio above 0.5.
Greater than 0.2
A ratio of 0.2 sits below the threshold; progressive glaucomatous cupping is defined by a cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.5.

C.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
C.q: What is the mechanism of wet, neovascular macular degeneration?
opts: Extracellular lipofuscin debris accumulating beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
Lipofuscin debris beneath the pigment epithelium forms drusen, the hallmark of dry macular degeneration, not the neovascular wet form.
Fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface exert traction
Fibrovascular membranes pulling on the retinal surface cause tractional retinal detachment; wet degeneration is choroidal neovascularization breaching into the subretinal space.
Ganglion cell axons undergo apoptosis from raised pressure
Ganglion cell apoptosis from raised pressure is glaucoma; wet macular degeneration is driven by hypoxia and inflammation triggering choroidal neovascularization.
Hypoxia and inflammation trigger choroidal neovascularization, and new vessels breach beneath the pigment epithelium into the subretinal space
Correct — hypoxia and inflammation trigger choroidal neovascularization, and the new vessels breach beneath the pigment epithelium into the subretinal space, where they leak blood and serous fluid.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: Which skin cancer is the most common malignancy in humans?
opts: Actinic keratosis, which is by far the most common malignancy occurring in human beings
Actinic keratosis is the most common precancer, not a malignancy; basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in humans.
Basal cell carcinoma, slow growing and rarely metastasizing, typically on the head and neck
Correct. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and most common human malignancy; it grows slowly and rarely metastasizes.
Squamous cell carcinoma, rapidly metastasizing
Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin cancer; basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in humans.
Melanoma, slow growing and rarely metastasizing
Melanoma is not the most common malignancy, and it can invade lymphatics and blood vessels; basal cell carcinoma holds that place.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: What single feature separates a pterygium from a pinguecula?
opts: The pterygium encroaches onto the cornea; the pinguecula does not
Correct — both are fibrovascular proliferations from chronic ultraviolet, wind and dust exposure, but only the pterygium encroaches onto the cornea and can impair vision.
The pterygium is yellow; the pinguecula is triangular
The descriptions are reversed: the pinguecula is the yellowish nodule and the pterygium the triangular wing; the separator is corneal encroachment.
The pterygium is painful; the pinguecula is painless
Pain does not separate them; both arise from chronic ultraviolet, wind and dust exposure, and only the pterygium encroaches onto the cornea.
The pterygium is bilateral; the pinguecula is unilateral
Laterality does not separate them; the distinguishing feature is that a pterygium encroaches onto the cornea while a pinguecula does not.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: Why does a lesion of cranial nerve VIII produce the same audiometric pattern as cochlear damage?
opts: Both add mass to the tympanic membrane
Mass loading damps the middle ear structures, which produces conductive rather than sensorineural loss.
Both stiffen the ossicles
Stiffened ossicles cause conductive loss, as in otosclerosis. The cochlea and cranial nerve VIII both lie beyond the conducting chain, so both give sensorineural loss.
Both obstruct the canal
Obstruction blocks the external canal, which is a conductive mechanism rather than a sensorineural one.
Both sit beyond the conducting chain, so both give sensorineural loss
Correct. The category is defined by where the defect sits, not by which of the two structures failed.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: How does human papillomavirus produce a common wart?
opts: It triggers mast cell degranulation in the dermis
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine produces wheals and urticaria; human papillomavirus invades basal cells and drives epidermal proliferation.
It digests keratin using keratinases and proteases
Secreting keratinases and proteases to digest keratin is how dermatophytes metabolize keratin; human papillomavirus instead drives proliferation of the epidermis.
It invades epidermal basal cells through microabrasions, leading to proliferation of the epidermis
Correct. Human papillomavirus invades epidermal basal cells through microabrasions, and that infection leads to proliferation of the epidermis.
It infects the melanocytes that lie along the dermal-epidermal junction within the epidermis
Melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction give rise to melanoma; human papillomavirus infects epidermal basal cells through microabrasions.

C.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
C.q: How does dry macular degeneration affect vision?
opts: Rapid central vision loss over days
Rapid central loss belongs to the wet form, from leaking new vessels; the dry form causes slow, gradual loss of central detail.
Loss of peripheral vision first, with the central field spared until late
Peripheral loss first with central sparing is the tunnel vision of open-angle glaucoma; dry macular degeneration takes central detail slowly.
Sudden painless monocular blindness
Sudden painless monocular blindness is not the pattern; dry macular degeneration causes slow, gradual loss of central detail with distortion.
Slow gradual loss of central detail, with distortion and a scotoma
Correct — slow degeneration of photoreceptors, pigment epithelium and choroid causes gradual loss of central detail, with metamorphopsia and scotoma.

C.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
C.q: How do the causes of anterior and posterior epistaxis differ?
opts: Anterior from hypertension and anticoagulation; posterior from digital trauma
The two etiologies are swapped. Digital trauma and dry air are anterior causes; hypertension and anticoagulation drive posterior bleeds.
Both are caused predominantly by anticoagulation
Anticoagulation belongs with the posterior group; anterior bleeds are usually local.
Anterior from coagulopathy; posterior from low humidity
Reversed again: coagulopathy belongs with posterior bleeding and low humidity with anterior mucosal drying.
Anterior from local trauma and dry air; posterior from hypertension and anticoagulation
Correct. Anterior bleeds are local and mechanical; posterior bleeds reflect a systemic vascular or clotting problem, which is also why they are more profuse and carry airway risk.

C.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
C.q: Which statement correctly describes androgen regulation of hair?
opts: Lanugo hair is androgen-regulated; terminal hair is not
Lanugo is the fine hair of newborns, not the androgen-regulated type; terminal hair is the type that androgens regulate.
All three types are equally androgen-dependent
The types differ: terminal hair of the head, beard, axillae and pubic areas is androgen-regulated, while vellus hair grows independently of androgens.
Terminal hair is androgen-regulated; vellus hair grows independently of androgens
Correct. Thick terminal hair on the head, beard, axillae and pubic areas is androgen-regulated; fine vellus hair grows independently of androgens.
Vellus hair is regulated by androgens; terminal hair grows independently of them
This swaps them: vellus hair, the fine short hair of most of the adult body, grows independently of androgens, and terminal hair is androgen-regulated.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: What is the natural course of a subconjunctival hemorrhage?
opts: Benign, resolving over one to two weeks with bruise-like color changes
Correct — blood leaked from ruptured episcleral or conjunctival capillaries lies beneath the conjunctiva and clears in one to two weeks, changing color like a bruise.
Progressive, threatening vision within days
It is neither progressive nor sight-threatening; blood beneath the conjunctiva is benign and resolves over one to two weeks.
Permanent, leaving a fibrovascular scar
No scar is left; the blood beneath the conjunctiva resolves completely in one to two weeks, passing through bruise-like color changes.
Recurrent by definition, so it requires long-term ophthalmology follow-up
Recurrence is not part of its definition; a subconjunctival hemorrhage is benign and resolves in one to two weeks with bruise-like color changes.

C.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
C.q: Which way does the nystagmus of labyrinthitis beat?
opts: Vertical and non-suppressible
Vertical nystagmus is a central feature, and labyrinthitis is peripheral.
Absent, because hearing rather than balance is affected
Labyrinthitis impairs both hearing and balance, and it presents with horizontal-rotary nystagmus and gait ataxia.
Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating AWAY from the affected side
Correct. Labyrinthitis gives horizontal-rotary nystagmus with the fast phase beating away from the affected side, with severe postural instability, gait ataxia and nausea.
Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating TOWARD the affected side
The direction is reversed; the fast phase beats away from the lesion.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: Why does presbycusis make voices hard to discriminate in noisy environments?
opts: High frequencies go first, taking the speech consonants
Correct. Presbycusis begins with high-frequency tones, which include speech consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/, making voice discrimination difficult in noisy environments.
Low frequencies go first, taking the vowels
Low-tone loss is the pattern of Meniere disease. Presbycusis starts at the high frequencies, taking consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/.
All frequencies fall equally
Presbycusis is not a flat loss. It begins with the high-frequency tones that carry speech consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/.
Only frequencies above the speech range are affected
The lost high-frequency tones lie within speech: consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/, which is why voice discrimination suffers.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: Which pairing of share of circulating serum proteins and action is correct for complement components?
opts: 25%; responsible for the formation of a clot at the site of the injury or lesion
Clot formation belongs to the coagulation system; complement makes up 10% of serum proteins and is chemotactic to neutrophils.
10%; chemotactic to neutrophils and monocytes, with the cascade able to damage bacteria
Correct. Complement components make up 10% of circulating serum proteins, are chemotactic to neutrophils and monocytes, and can damage bacteria.
50%; primarily responsible for oncotic pressure
Complement components make up 10%, not 50%, of circulating serum proteins, and they act through chemotaxis and bacterial damage.
1%; acting solely as opsonins
C3b is an opsonin, but complement components as a group are also chemotactic, can damage bacteria, and account for 10% of serum proteins.

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: What is canalithiasis?
opts: Dislodged otoconia floating free in the semicircular canals

Correct. Canalithiasis means dislodged otoconia, the crystals, lying in the semicircular canals; the result is episodic vertigo, usually under a minute, with head position changes and no hearing loss.
Accumulation of endolymph in the membranous labyrinth
Endolymph accumulating in the membranous labyrinth is the hydrops of Meniere disease, which gives hours-long attacks with hearing loss.
Inflammatory debris within the cochlea after infection
Inflammation within the cochlea is labyrinthitis, which impairs hearing. Canalithiasis causes NO hearing loss.
Calcification of the stapes footplate
Calcification fixing the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion of the middle ear with no vestibular component.

C.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
C.q: Which description fits the rods of the retina?
opts: About 120 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Correct — about 120 million rods give high sensitivity for dim light and night vision, and they are found in the peripheral retina.
About 6 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Six million is the cone population; rods number around 120 million.
About 120 million, for color vision and sharp acuity
The count is right but the function belongs to cones; rods serve dim light, night vision and the peripheral retina.
About 20 million, for color vision in bright light
Neither figure fits: rods number around 120 million and serve dim light and peripheral vision, not color.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: How do phagocytic cells recognize immunoglobulin G bound to foreign material?
opts: Through histamine receptors on the endothelium
Histamine acts on the vessels and plays no part in opsonin recognition; phagocytes bind the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G through Fc receptors.
Through Fc receptors that recognize the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G
Correct. Macrophages and neutrophils carry Fc receptors that bind the Fc portion of the antibody.
Through the complement receptors that bind to the C3b fragment
Complement receptors recognize C3b, the other opsonin; immunoglobulin G is recognized through Fc receptors binding its Fc portion.
Through T cell receptors on the phagocyte surface
T cell receptors are carried by T lymphocytes, not phagocytes; phagocytes recognize immunoglobulin G through Fc receptors binding its Fc portion.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Which pattern of inflammation is defined by mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane?
opts: Catarrhal
Correct. Catarrhal inflammation is mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane.
Pseudomembranous
Pseudomembranous inflammation is a superficial necrotic layer of fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris forming a membrane-like covering.
Serous
Serous inflammation is largely low-protein plasma occurring early or with mild inflammation.
Hemorrhagic
Hemorrhagic inflammation involves damage to blood vessels and occurs alongside other exudates.

C.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
C.q: What distinguishes a vesicle from a bulla?
opts: A vesicle is solid and a bulla is fluid-filled
Both are fluid-filled lesions; a vesicle collects fluid within or beneath the epidermis, and a bulla forms where the epidermis separates from the dermis.
A vesicle contains purulent material and a bulla contains serous fluid
Purulent material of leukocytes and debris defines a pustule; vesicle fluid contains inflammatory cells, and bulla fluid collects between epidermis and dermis.

A vesicle is up to 5 millimeters with fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or directly beneath the epidermis; a bulla is greater than 5 millimeters and involves separation of epidermis from dermis
Correct. The bulla represents a deeper plane of cleavage, not merely a bigger blister.

A vesicle is greater than 5 millimeters and a bulla is up to 5 millimeters in diameter, and the two share an identical mechanism of fluid accumulation entirely within the epidermis rather than beneath it
The sizes are reversed: a vesicle is up to 5 millimeters and a bulla is larger, and a bulla forms by separation of the epidermis from the dermis.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: Which pairing of patient group and organism carries particular risk in keratitis?
opts: Contact lens wearers, from Staphylococcus aureus
Contact lens wear is the right group but the wrong organism; the keratitis risk in lens wearers is Pseudomonas, not Staphylococcus aureus.
Elderly patients, from Streptococcus pneumoniae
