Neither the group nor the organism fits; the particular keratitis risk is Pseudomonas in contact lens wearers, threatening stromal ulceration.
Immunosuppressed patients, from Candida
Candida in immunosuppressed patients is not the at-risk pairing; contact lens wearers face Pseudomonas keratitis, which can ulcerate and perforate the cornea.
Contact lens wearers, from Pseudomonas
Correct — contact lens wearers carry a Pseudomonas risk, and keratitis is an emergency because it can progress to stromal ulceration, perforation and endophthalmitis.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: Which combination of effects does bradykinin produce?
opts: Increased capillary permeability, pain, and possibly increased leukocyte chemotaxis
Correct. Bradykinin is the plasma-protein mediator that adds pain to the permeability effect.
Vasoconstriction, reduced capillary permeability, and analgesia at the site
These are the reverse of bradykinin's effects, which are increased capillary permeability, pain and possibly increased chemotaxis.
Antibody production and antigen presentation
Antibody production and antigen presentation are lymphocyte and monocyte functions; bradykinin increases capillary permeability and causes pain.
Coagulation and trapping of exudate
Coagulation and trapping of exudate belong to the coagulation system; bradykinin increases capillary permeability and causes pain.

C.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
C.q: Which pairing gives an example of dysplasia with its usual cause?
opts: Barrett's esophagus, usually caused by chronic acid reflux
Chronic irritation changing one cell type into another is metaplasia, not dysplasia; high-risk human papillomavirus drives cervical dysplasia toward carcinoma.
Endometrial hyperplasia, usually caused by excess estrogen
Hyperplasia is not dysplasia; dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth with loss of architectural orientation and darker, larger nuclei.
Skeletal muscle hypertrophy, usually caused by resistance training
Skeletal muscle hypertrophy is enlargement of individual cells, not the disordered epithelial growth with variation in cell size and shape that defines dysplasia.
Cervical dysplasia, usually caused by human papillomavirus
Correct — high-risk human papillomavirus infects cervical epithelial cells, and the resulting uncontrolled proliferation raises the risk of progression from dysplasia to carcinoma.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 37

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Which description matches the serous pattern of inflammation?
opts: Mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane surface
Mucus hypersecretion over a mucous membrane is the catarrhal pattern; serous inflammation is largely plasma with low protein.
Largely plasma with low protein content, occurring early or with mild inflammation
Correct. Serous inflammation is largely plasma, low in protein, and occurs early or when inflammation is mild.
Large amounts of fibrinogen forming a thick meshwork
That is the fibrinous pattern, removable only by fibrolytic enzymes; serous inflammation is largely plasma with low protein.
Remnants of white blood cells, protein and tissue debris
Remnants of white blood cells, protein and debris describe suppurative inflammation; serous is largely low-protein plasma.

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: Where do the pressure waves that begin hearing actually travel first?
opts: The cochlear duct itself
The duct holds the endolymph that is displaced, but the wave begins in the scala vestibuli.
The scala vestibuli
Correct. Stapes movement at the oval window starts them there, and they displace endolymph in the cochlear duct.
The semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect rotation and play no part in transmitting sound to the organ of Corti.
The scala tympani
The scala tympani carries the wave later in its course, after it has passed the cochlear duct.

C.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
C.q: Which two malignancies is Helicobacter pylori associated with?
opts: Hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma follows chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C infection; Helicobacter pylori is linked to gastric cancers.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and B cell lymphomas follow Epstein Barr virus, which immortalizes B lymphocytes.
Cervical carcinoma and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
Cervical cancer and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma follow high-risk human papillomavirus, not Helicobacter pylori.
Gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma
Correct — chronic Helicobacter pylori gastritis is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphoma.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 35

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: Why does the vertigo of Meniere disease come in attacks rather than continuously?
opts: Inflammation resolves and recurs
Inflammation across the canals and cochlea is labyrinthitis, whose vertigo lasts days and improves over weeks.
Pressure builds until micro-ruptures occur, then re-equilibrates
Correct. Defective resorption lets endolymph accumulate and balloon the scala media until micro-ruptures occur; that build-up and release makes it episodic.
The virus replicates in waves
Meniere disease is a disorder of endolymph resorption, not an infection, so there is no organism replicating.
Otoconia settle between episodes
Otoconia settling between episodes explains benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which lasts seconds rather than hours.

C.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
C.q: Why is the name agranulocyte somewhat misleading?
opts: Because they are actually a subtype of polymorphonuclear leukocyte
Polymorphonuclear leukocyte refers to all granulocytes, the opposite grouping; agranulocytes still contain non-specific azurophilic granules (lysosomes).
Because these cells acquire granules only after activation
Agranulocytes do not acquire granules on activation; they already contain non-specific azurophilic granules, which are lysosomes.
Because their granules are visible only in chronic inflammation
Inflammatory phase has nothing to do with it; agranulocytes always contain non-specific azurophilic granules, which are lysosomes.
Because these cells do contain non-specific azurophilic granules — lysosomes
Correct. The name implies an absence of granules, but non-specific azurophilic granules (lysosomes) are present.

C.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
C.q: Which statement correctly describes tumor suppressor genes?
opts: They promote regulated cell growth; the examples are growth factors and their receptors
Promoting regulated growth describes protooncogenes, such as growth factors and their receptors; tumor suppressor genes inhibit growth.
They repair damaged deoxyribonucleic acid; the examples are BRCA-1 and BRCA-2
BRCA-1 and BRCA-2 are repair genes for damaged deoxyribonucleic acid; tumor suppressor genes inhibit cell growth.
They trigger apoptosis in damaged cells; no specific examples are named
Genes promoting self destruction of damaged cells form a separate category; tumor suppressor genes inhibit cell growth.
They inhibit cell growth; the examples are NF-1, NF-2, retinoblastoma and adenomatous polyposis coli
Correct — losing them removes a brake rather than adding an accelerator.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 29

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
D.q: Why do cancers spreading through the portal vein and the inferior vena cava reach the liver and the lungs?
opts: Because tumor cells preferentially enter arterial rather than venous blood
Hematogenous tumor spread is typically through veins, especially the portal vein and inferior vena cava, not arteries.
Because lymphatic drainage from most organs terminates in the liver and lungs
Lymphatic spread follows the natural route of lymphatic drainage from the tumor margin; the liver and lung pattern is venous.
Because those are the organs each vein drains into
Correct — hematogenous spread is typically venous, so fragments in the portal vein reach the liver and those in the inferior vena cava reach the lungs.
Because liver and lung tissue are uniquely receptive to any tumor cell
Specific receptors on tumor and endothelial cells do shape metastasis, but the liver and lung pattern follows the venous flow of the portal vein and inferior vena cava.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 14

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Why can a neutrophil kill only a limited number of pathogens before dying?
opts: It converts into a macrophage after a single encounter
Neutrophils do not convert; it is the monocyte that becomes a tissue macrophage, while the neutrophil dies because it cannot renew its lysosomes.
It cannot renew its lysosomes, so it dies after phagocytosing a few pathogens
Correct. Neutrophils are not able to renew their lysosomes, so they die after having phagocytosed a few pathogens.
It lacks the enzymes needed to digest the bacterial cell wall it engulfs
The neutrophil is very active in phagocytizing bacteria, so its digestive enzymes are present; its limit is that it cannot renew its lysosomes.
It must first be opsonized before it can engulf anything
Opsonins coat the target material, not the phagocyte, and they enhance recognition and attachment rather than being a precondition.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
D.q: What is inflammation?
opts: The death of tissue through coagulative or liquefactive pathways
Coagulative and liquefactive necrosis distinguish dry from wet gangrene, a single pattern of inflammation, rather than defining inflammation itself.
The reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury
Correct. Inflammation is defined as the reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury, so living tissue with a blood supply is part of the definition.
The proliferation of fibroblasts following any cellular insult
Fibroblastic scar tissue is one way the process heals the site; inflammation itself is the reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury.
The activation of the adaptive immune system by a foreign antigen
Inflammation can follow purely physical damage with no immune activation, as in trauma; it is defined as the reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury.

D.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
D.q: What gives the spinous layer its alternative name of prickle cell layer?
opts: Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales
Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales form the stratum corneum; the prickle cell appearance comes from desmosomes.
Keratinocytes connected by intercellular connections called desmosomes, which form a spiny appearance
Correct. The 8 to 10 keratinocyte layers of the stratum spinosum are joined by desmosomes, which give the spiny look behind the name prickle cell layer.
Keratohyalin granules that give the cells a rough and irregular outline when viewed on microscopy
Keratohyalin granules mark the stratum granulosum above; the spiny look comes from desmosomes connecting the keratinocytes of the spinous layer.
Melanin granules transferred from melanocytes
Melanin transfer does not create the spiny appearance; desmosomes connecting 8 to 10 layers of keratinocytes form the prickle cell layer.

D.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
D.q: Macular degeneration is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in which group?
opts: Adults over seventy-five in the United States
Correct — macular degeneration is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in United States adults over seventy-five, while diabetic retinopathy leads in younger adults.
Adults aged twenty to seventy-four in the United States
That working-age band is dominated by diabetic retinopathy; macular degeneration leads in adults over seventy-five.
Children and adolescents
Children are not the group; macular degeneration is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in United States adults over seventy-five.
Adults of any age worldwide
The claim is specific to an age band and a country: macular degeneration leads new-onset blindness in United States adults over seventy-five.

D.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
D.q: What is the functional consequence of presbyopia?
opts: Loss of peripheral vision
Presbyopia does not affect the visual field; it is a loss of accommodation, so near objects cannot be brought into focus.
Loss of color discrimination
Color vision, a cone function, is unaffected; presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity and accommodation, impairing near focus.
Inability to focus on near objects, so reading glasses or bifocals are needed
Correct — the sclerotic lens and ciliary muscle can no longer accommodate, so near objects cannot be focused and readers or bifocals are needed.
Inability to focus on distant objects, so distance vision blurs first
Distance vision is not the one lost; presbyopia removes near focus, as the lens and ciliary muscle lose accommodation.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Which description of squamous cell carcinoma is accurate?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and radial growth
Autosomal dominant inherited risk and a radial growth phase belong to melanoma; squamous cell carcinoma involves tp53 mutation and keratin pearls.
Mutation in the tp53 tumor suppressor gene, with keratin pearls and epithelial pearls as pathognomonic features
Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma involves mutation of the tp53 tumor suppressor gene in keratinocytes, and keratin and epithelial pearls are pathognomonic of it.
Overactivation of the Hedgehog pathway, with pearly papules and telangiectasias
Hedgehog pathway overactivation and pearly papules with telangiectasias describe basal cell carcinoma; squamous cell carcinoma involves tp53 mutation.
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, with a stuck-on waxy and scaly appearance on the skin
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 mutation and a stuck-on waxy look describe benign seborrheic keratosis; squamous cell carcinoma shows keratin pearls.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Which description of Henoch-Schonlein purpura is accurate?
opts: The skin alone, with no systemic involvement whatsoever, at any age at all
Henoch-Schonlein purpura is not limited to the skin; this immunoglobulin A vasculitis involves the skin, joints, kidneys and intestines.
Skin, joints, kidneys and intestines, commonly in children aged 3 to 10 years
Correct — an immunoglobulin A vasculitis, which is why it is not confined to the skin.
Skin and lungs only, commonly in older adults
The lungs are not among the organs involved, and it is common in children aged 3 to 10 rather than older adults; skin, joints, kidneys and intestines are affected.
Skin and liver, commonly in neonates
The liver is not among the organs involved and neonates are not the usual group; it involves skin, joints, kidneys and intestines in children aged 3 to 10.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which pairing of response and mediator describes the basophil's chief role?
opts: Antibody production, through immunoglobulin G
Antibody production is the role of B lymphocytes and plasma cells; basophils are chiefly responsible for allergic and antigen response through histamine.
Cell-mediated immunity, through T cell receptors
Cell-mediated immunity through T cell receptors describes T lymphocytes; basophils act through histamine in allergic responses.
Allergic and antigen response, through histamine
Correct. Basophils drive allergic and antigen response via histamine, which causes inflammation.
Parasitic defense, through major basic protein
Parasitic infection is the eosinophil's domain; basophils are chiefly responsible for allergic and antigen responses through histamine.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: Which history most separates labyrinthitis from Meniere disease?
opts: A recent upper respiratory infection
Correct. Labyrinthitis is caused by viral infection, typically a recent viral upper respiratory infection, whereas Meniere disease arises from defective endolymph resorption causing hydrops.
The presence of sensorineural hearing loss
Both cause it. The duration of vertigo and the preceding infection are what differ.
Unilateral rather than bilateral symptoms
Laterality does not separate them: labyrinthitis gives unilateral tinnitus and hearing loss, and Meniere disease gives fullness in the affected ear.
The presence of tinnitus
Both labyrinthitis and Meniere disease produce tinnitus, so its presence tells you nothing about which one you are looking at.

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: What happens to proliferation once a cell has committed to differentiation?
opts: It stops entirely, and the differentiated cells become immortal
Immortality belongs to the stem cell; differentiated cells have a limited life-span.
It stays at the same relatively low rate as the stem cell
Proliferation after commitment can be dramatic; it is the stem cell itself that keeps a relatively low rate of proliferation.
It becomes autonomous and no longer requires physiologic stimuli
Growth without physiologic stimuli defines a neoplasm; a normal cell committed to differentiation can proliferate dramatically but has a limited life-span.
It can be dramatic, but those cells have a limited life-span
Correct — the stem cell itself proliferates slowly; the committed progeny do the expansion, and then die.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 21

D.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
D.q: By what mechanism does diabetes mellitus cause cataract?
opts: Excess glucose glycates the lens capsule until it ruptures
Capsule rupture is the traumatic mechanism; diabetes clouds the lens through sorbitol, which causes osmotic swelling of the lens.
Hyperglycemia causes crystallin proteins to aggregate directly
Aggregation is the senile mechanism; diabetes acts through sorbitol.
Retinal ischemia releases vascular endothelial growth factor into the lens
Growth factor released by retinal ischemia drives proliferative diabetic retinopathy; in the lens, diabetes acts through sorbitol and osmotic swelling.
Excess glucose is converted to sorbitol, causing osmotic swelling of the lens
Correct — in diabetes, excessive glucose is converted to sorbitol, and the resulting osmotic swelling of the lens produces cataract.

D.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
D.q: How differentiated are malignant tumors?
opts: Always anaplastic
Anaplasia, the lack of differentiation, is only the extreme; malignant tumors show various degrees of differentiation.
Always well differentiated
Usually well differentiated describes benign tumors; malignant tumors show various degrees of differentiation.
Various degrees of differentiation
Correct — malignancy does not mean uniformly poor differentiation. Benign tumors are usually well differentiated.
Always poorly differentiated
Malignant tumors show various degrees of differentiation, so they are not always poorly differentiated.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 13

D.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
D.q: Which function of the eye does presbyopia impair?
opts: Light detection by the rods and cones
Rods and cones in the photoreceptor layer are not what presbyopia affects; it is loss of lens elasticity and ciliary muscle accommodation from sclerosis.
Drainage of aqueous humor through the trabecular meshwork
Aqueous drainage through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm regulates intraocular pressure; presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity and accommodation.
Secretion of the lipid layer of the tear film
The tear film's lipid layer comes from the meibomian glands in the tarsal plates; presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity and ciliary muscle accommodation.
Accommodation for near objects
Correct — presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity and ciliary muscle accommodation due to sclerosis, so the eye can no longer focus on near objects.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: Which definitions of acute and chronic rhinosinusitis are accurate?
opts: Acute under 2 weeks; chronic beyond 6 weeks, often with septal deviation
Neither threshold matches: acute rhinosinusitis lasts under 4 weeks, and chronic lasts over 12 weeks despite therapy, often with nasal polyps.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks despite therapy, often with nasal polyps
Correct. The two thresholds are the definition. Acute disease is usually viral — rhinovirus or influenza — with secondary bacterial infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae.
Acute under 12 weeks; chronic beyond 6 months, often with turbinate hypertrophy
The thresholds are wrong: acute rhinosinusitis is under 4 weeks and chronic is beyond 12 weeks despite therapy.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks, usually with no mucosal change
The durations are right but chronic disease often comes WITH polyps rather than without change.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
D.q: Which movement does the term exudation describe?
opts: Fibrin into the vascular lumen to form a thrombus
A fibrous network is made by the coagulation system at the site of injury to trap exudate; exudation is fluid and blood proteins entering the interstitial spaces.
Leukocytes from the interstitium back into the capillary lumen
Leukocytes leave the vessel for the tissue, not the reverse; exudation carries fluid and blood proteins out into the interstitial spaces.
Erythrocytes into the alveolar space
Exudation is not specific to the alveoli; it is fluid and blood proteins moving into the interstitial spaces once capillary permeability rises.
Fluid and blood proteins into the interstitial spaces
Correct. Exudation follows the increased capillary permeability produced by endothelial contraction.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: Which organisms most commonly cause bacterial otitis media?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Correct. The classic middle ear trio. Viral causes are respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, influenza and adenovirus.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus
Those are the otitis EXTERNA organisms, accounting for 80 to 90 percent of that condition.
Aspergillus niger and Candida albicans
Those are the fungal otitis externa organisms, often after prolonged antibiotics or humid conditions.
Group A Streptococcus alone
That is the usual bacterial cause of tonsillitis, not of otitis media.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: How do cisplatin and carboplatin cause permanent bilateral sensorineural loss?
opts: They cross-link DNA in stria vascularis cells, compromising endolymph ion homeostasis
Correct. The stria vascularis maintains the ionic composition of endolymph, and without that gradient transduction fails. Damage there is permanent and bilateral.
They fix the stapes footplate in the oval window
That is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion with no drug involvement.
They generate reactive oxygen species that destroy outer hair cells at the cochlear base
Reactive oxygen species destroying outer hair cells from the cochlear base is the aminoglycoside mechanism, and it takes the high frequencies first.
They inhibit prestin in outer hair cells
That is salicylate, and the effect is tinnitus rather than permanent loss.

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: A patient has thick, leathery plaques on the neck and forearms with no scaling, after months of scratching. Which secondary lesion is this, mechanistically?
opts: Ulcer, arising from focal loss of both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it
An ulcer is loss of epidermis and dermis, but these plaques are thickened, not eroded; long-term scratching produces lichenification.
Atrophy, from slowed keratinocyte division
Atrophy thins the skin through slowed division and collagen synthesis; thick leathery plaques after scratching reflect lichenification.
Lichenification, from hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis driven by the itch-scratch cycle
Correct. The absence of scaling is what separates it from psoriasis, whose plaques do scale.
Scale, from desquamating stratum corneum
Scale is desquamating stratum corneum, and these plaques have none; lichenification forms thick plaques without scaling.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which cells are the agranulocytes (mononuclear leucocytes)?
opts: Basophils, mast cells and macrophages
Basophils are granulocytes and mast cells are neither group; the agranulocytes are lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages.
Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells), monocytes and macrophages
Correct. These three are grouped as the agranulocytes or mononuclear leucocytes.
Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils
Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils are the three granulocytes, the opposite grouping from the mononuclear leukocytes.
Erythrocytes, platelets and circulating plasma cells
Erythrocytes and platelets are not leukocytes at all; the agranulocytes are lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages.

D.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
D.q: What is known about the pathogenesis of macular degeneration overall?
opts: It is a consequence of raised intraocular pressure
Raised intraocular pressure drives glaucoma by compressing ganglion cell axons; the pathogenesis of macular degeneration is unknown.
It is unknown
Correct — the pathogenesis of both dry and wet macular degeneration is unknown, even though drusen and choroidal neovascularization describe what happens in each.
It is entirely genetic
No genetic cause is established; the pathogenesis of macular degeneration is unknown for both forms, described only by drusen or neovascularization.
It is entirely driven by ultraviolet exposure
Ultraviolet light is a cataract risk, not an established cause of macular degeneration, whose pathogenesis remains unknown for both forms.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: Why does a deviated septum cause epistaxis and loss of smell?
opts: Compression of the ethmoid arteries and the olfactory nerve
Compression is not the mechanism. Turbulent air dries the mucosa into crusting and fragile vessel breakdown, and air fails to reach the cribriform plate.
Turbulent airflow dries the mucosa; air misses the cribriform plate
Correct. Two separate consequences of the same disturbed airflow: local drying with fragile vessel breakdown on one hand, and failure to deliver odorant to the superior nasal vault on the other.
Chronic infection eroding the septal vessels and olfactory epithelium
Secondary bacterial rhinosinusitis can follow ostial blockage, but the epistaxis and anosmia are explained by airflow.
Autoimmune destruction of the septal cartilage
Autoimmune destruction of septal cartilage is a different disease process; the consequences here all follow from disturbed airflow.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: What happens to the wider nasal cavity opposite a septal deviation?
opts: It atrophies from disuse
The opposite happens. The wide side carries MORE airflow, so its turbinate enlarges to condition the extra volume rather than wasting away.
It develops polyps from the increased flow
Polyps arise from type 2 inflammation, not from airflow volume.
Nothing changes; only the narrow side is affected
The wide side does change: its inferior turbinate undergoes compensatory hypertrophy to humidify the increased air volume.
Compensatory inferior turbinate hypertrophy
Correct. The contralateral wide cavity undergoes compensatory inferior turbinate enlargement to humidify the increased volume of air passing through it.

D.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
D.q: Middle ear effusion and cholesteatoma impair conduction by which mechanism?
opts: Mass loading
Correct. Both add fluid or tissue weight that damps movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles. The chain is intact and mobile in principle, but it is carrying extra mass.
Stiffness effect
Stiffness is fixation rather than added weight; otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
Discontinuity means the chain is physically broken, which neither of these does.
Obstruction
Obstruction blocks the canal before the drum — wax, foreign bodies, exostoses.

D.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
D.q: How does the mechanism of a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo differ from that of a hyperpigmented macule?
opts: Loss of melanocytes, against increased melanin production in the basal layer of the epidermis
Correct. Vitiligo reflects loss of melanocytes, while hyperpigmented macules such as ephelides, café au lait spots and Mongolian spots reflect increased basal melanin.
Increased melanin production within the epidermis, as against loss of melanocytes entirely
This reverses them: hypopigmentation as in vitiligo is loss of melanocytes, and hyperpigmentation is increased melanin in the basal layer.
Capillary rupture with blood deposition in the dermis
Capillary rupture depositing blood in the dermis produces petechiae and purpura; vitiligo reflects loss of melanocytes.
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels is telangiectasia; a hypopigmented macule reflects loss of melanocytes.

D.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
D.q: Which human papillomavirus subtypes most commonly cause cervical cancer?
opts: Types 1 and 2
Types 1 and 2 are not the cervical cancer subtypes; of many genetic subtypes, types 16 and 18 most commonly cause it.
Types 31 and 33
Types 31 and 33 are not the leading cervical cancer subtypes; types 16 and 18 cause the majority of cervical cancers.
Types 16 and 18
Correct — of many genetic subtypes, these two cause the majority.
Types 6 and 11
Types 6 and 11 are not the cervical cancer subtypes; high-risk types 16 and 18 cause the majority of cervical cancers.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 32

D.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
D.q: Which combination of cause and relationship to other exudates characterizes hemorrhagic inflammation?
opts: Epithelial sloughing, and replacing other exudates
Sloughing of surface epithelium defines the ulcerative pattern; hemorrhagic inflammation comes from damage to blood vessels.
Damage to blood vessels, and occurring together with other exudates
Correct. Hemorrhagic inflammation is damage to blood vessels occurring with other exudates.
Mucus hypersecretion, and occurring in isolation
Mucus hypersecretion defines the catarrhal pattern; hemorrhagic inflammation comes from blood vessel damage and occurs with other exudates.
Fibrinogen deposition, and preceding every other exudate pattern
Fibrinogen deposition defines the fibrinous pattern; hemorrhagic inflammation comes from blood vessel damage alongside other exudates.

D.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
D.q: Which structure separates the external ear from the middle ear?
opts: The oval window, which passes energy to the cochlea
The oval window is the boundary between MIDDLE and INNER ear, driven by the stapes.
The round window, which relieves pressure
The round window is not the external boundary. The tympanic membrane separates external from middle ear, vibrating to pass sound energy to the ossicles.
The Eustachian tube, which equalizes pressure
The Eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure; it vents the middle ear rather than separating it from the external ear.
The tympanic membrane, which vibrates and passes energy to the ossicles
Correct. It is the boundary and the first moving part of the conducting chain, which is why perforating it causes conductive loss.

D.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
D.q: In the sequence of events of acute inflammation, which event immediately follows increased vascular permeability?
opts: Hemoconcentration and stasis
Correct. Hemoconcentration and stasis come directly after increased vascular permeability and directly before leukocyte adhesion.
Chemotaxis
Chemotaxis comes later, after leukocyte adhesion and transmigration; hemoconcentration and stasis directly follow increased vascular permeability.
Phagocytosis
Phagocytosis is the final step, after aggregation; the event right after increased permeability is hemoconcentration and stasis.
Vasoconstriction of the arterioles
Vasoconstriction opens the whole sequence, before vasodilation; hemoconcentration and stasis are what follow increased permeability.

D.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
D.q: Why are genes promoting self destruction of cells with damaged deoxyribonucleic acid necessary?
opts: To limit the total number of cells an organ can contain
Limiting organ size is not the purpose; apoptosis genes stop damage from becoming permanent in dividing cells.
To supply nutrients to neighbouring cells as they proliferate
Apoptosis genes have no nutrient role; their job is to make damaged cells self destruct before the damage becomes permanent.
To slow the rate at which stem cells commit to differentiation
Commitment to differentiation belongs to stem cell kinetics; apoptosis genes make damaged cells self destruct so the damage is not continued in dividing cells.
To stop the damage becoming permanent in dividing cells
Correct — apoptosis prevents a mutation being carried on into the daughter cells.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 30

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: What are the growth phases of melanoma, in order?
opts: Sensitization then elicitation
Sensitization then elicitation are the phases of allergic contact dermatitis; melanoma grows radially, then vertically into the dermis.
Radial growth within the epidermis, then vertical growth penetrating the dermis, then increasing tumor thickness, then metastatic invasion of lymphatics and blood vessels
Correct. Melanoma cells first multiply within the epidermis, then penetrate the dermis, grow deeper and thicker, and finally invade lymphatics and blood vessels.
Vertical growth down into the dermis first, then radial spread within the epidermis afterwards once the tumor has thickened sufficiently to invade
This reverses the first two: melanoma first multiplies radially within the epidermis, then grows vertically to penetrate the dermis.
Inflammatory, proliferative, then remodeling
Inflammatory, proliferative and remodeling are the phases of wound healing; melanoma progresses radial, vertical, thickening, then metastatic.

D.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
D.q: Which statement correctly describes the primary component of the dermis?
opts: Melanin, produced by melanocytes, providing ultraviolet protection
Melanin is an epidermal pigment from melanocytes; collagen made by fibroblasts is the primary component of the dermis.
Collagen, produced by fibroblasts, providing tensile strength
Correct. Collagen is the primary component of the dermis; fibroblasts produce it, and it provides the skin's tensile strength.
Keratin, produced by keratinocytes, providing an impermeable barrier
Keratin is produced by keratinocytes in the epidermis; the primary dermal component is collagen, made by fibroblasts for tensile strength.
Elastin, produced by mast cells, providing tensile strength
Elastin provides elastic recoil, not tensile strength, and mast cells do not make it; collagen from fibroblasts provides tensile strength.

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
D.q: Which two structures make up the fibrous outer tunic of the eye?
opts: The sclera and the cornea
Correct — the protective white coat and the clear refracting window.
The choroid and the ciliary body
The choroid and ciliary body belong to the uvea, the vascular middle tunic; the fibrous outer tunic is the sclera and the cornea.
The retina and the retinal pigment epithelium
The retina forms the neurosensory inner tunic; the fibrous outer tunic is the sclera, a protective white coat, and the clear cornea.
The iris and the lens
The iris belongs to the uvea, the vascular middle tunic, and the lens forms no tunic; the fibrous outer tunic is the sclera and cornea.

D.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
D.q: Cerumen impaction, foreign bodies and canal exostoses all cause conductive loss by which of the four core mechanisms?
opts: Obstruction
Correct. A physical blockage stops sound penetrating down the canal. It is the first of four mechanisms, and the only one that acts before the sound reaches the drum.
Mass loading
That is fluid or tissue weight damping movement of the drum or ossicles — middle ear effusion, cholesteatoma.
Stiffness effect
That is impaired mobility of the ossicles or drum, of which otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
That is physical disruption of the ossicular chain, from temporal bone fracture or ossicular necrosis.

D.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
D.q: What is the classical corneal finding in herpes simplex epithelial keratitis?
opts: A geographic ulcer with a hypopyon
A geographic ulcer with a hypopyon is not the classical sign; herpes simplex epithelial keratitis shows a dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein stain.
A ring infiltrate in a contact lens wearer
Contact lens wear is the Pseudomonas keratitis risk, not the herpes sign; herpes simplex epithelial keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs.
A wedge of fibrovascular tissue growing across and over the corneal limbus
A fibrovascular wing encroaching onto the cornea is a pterygium; herpes simplex keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein.
A dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein staining
Correct — the classical herpes simplex epithelial keratitis lesion is a branching dendritic corneal ulcer whose tips end in terminal bulbs on fluorescein stain.

D.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
D.q: A nodule is greater than 5 millimeters. What tissue does it arise from?
opts: Fluid accumulating between epidermis and dermis
Fluid collecting between a separated epidermis and dermis describes a bulla; a nodule is solid, built of dense dermal collagen bundles and subcutaneous tissue.
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries with no inflammatory infiltration at all
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries without inflammatory infiltrate define telangiectasia; a nodule is a solid lesion of dense dermal collagen bundles.
Dermal-based tissue with dense collagen bundles, extending into subcutaneous tissue
Correct. A nodule is an elevated, solid lesion over 5 millimeters: a dermal-based lesion of dense collagen bundles extending into subcutaneous tissue.
Superficial epidermis only, with no dermal involvement
A nodule is not confined to the epidermis; it is a dermal-based lesion of dense collagen bundles that extends into subcutaneous tissue.

D.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
D.q: Which findings does orbital cellulitis show that periorbital cellulitis lacks?
opts: Erythema and edema of the lid alone, held forward by the orbital septum
Lid erythema and edema held forward by the septum is periorbital cellulitis, which spares eye movement and vision; orbital cellulitis breaches the septum.
Crusting of the lid margin with altered tear film
Lid-margin crusting with altered tear film is blepharitis, from meibomian gland obstruction; orbital cellulitis causes proptosis and reduced eye movement.
A yellowish nodule that does not cross the cornea
A yellowish nodule that stays off the cornea is a pinguecula; orbital cellulitis instead causes proptosis, reduced eye movement and optic nerve risk.
Proptosis, decreased extraocular movement and a risk of optic nerve compression
Correct — bacteria breach the orbital septum into the soft tissue behind the globe, and the purulence there causes proptosis, reduced extraocular movement and optic nerve compression risk.

D.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
D.q: What is the mechanism of primary open-angle glaucoma?
opts: The iridocorneal angle stays open but microscopic resistance in the trabecular meshwork impairs outflow, raising pressure gradually
Correct — the angle is open; the obstruction is microscopic and downstream.
The iridocorneal angle narrows anatomically and blocks aqueous outflow suddenly
Anatomical narrowing that suddenly blocks outflow is angle-closure glaucoma; in open-angle disease the angle stays open and the resistance is microscopic.
Aqueous production by the ciliary body increases sharply
Aqueous production is normal; the fault lies in outflow resistance at the trabecular meshwork, which is why the pressure rises so gradually.
The canal of Schlemm is congenitally absent
The canal of Schlemm is present; the resistance is microscopic, within the trabecular meshwork draining into it.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: What is the mechanism of urticaria?
opts: Capillary rupture with extravasation of blood
Capillary rupture with extravasated blood produces petechiae and purpura; urticaria is histamine-driven wheal formation from mast cells.
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, producing wheals
Correct. In urticaria, mast cells release histamine, which causes vasodilation and plasma leakage into the dermis, forming wheals.
T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity 48 to 72 hours after exposure
T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity is allergic contact dermatitis; urticaria is mast cell degranulation releasing histamine to form wheals.
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage is actinic keratosis; urticaria results from mast cells releasing histamine.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Which description of the origin of melanoma is accurate?
opts: At the dermal-epidermal junction, with ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damaging melanocyte DNA and leading to uninhibited growth
Correct. Melanoma arises from melanocytes, found at the dermal-epidermal junction, when ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damage their DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid).
Within the stratum corneum, transformed by keratinase digestion
Keratinase digestion in the stratum corneum is dermatophyte behavior; melanocytes sit at the dermal-epidermal junction and are damaged by ultraviolet light.
In the reticular layer of the dermis, transformed by dysregulation of the fibroblasts that reside within it over a long period of time
Fibroblast dysregulation drives keloids, not melanoma; melanoma arises from melanocytes at the dermal-epidermal junction after ultraviolet and oxidative damage.
In the basal layer, transformed by Hedgehog pathway activation
Hedgehog pathway activation drives basal cell carcinoma; melanoma arises when ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damage melanocyte DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid).

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: What is the tissue distinction between an erosion and an ulcer?
opts: An erosion is focal loss of epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction; an ulcer is focal loss of epidermis AND dermis, with destruction of collagen and infiltration of inflammatory cells
Correct. The junction is the boundary that separates them, and crossing it is what brings collagen destruction into play.
An erosion involves both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it; an ulcer is limited to the epidermis alone and spares the dermal-epidermal junction entirely, so it never destroys collagen at all
This reverses the two: an erosion stops above the dermal-epidermal junction, while an ulcer loses epidermis and dermis with collagen destruction.
An erosion is fluid-filled and an ulcer is solid
Neither lesion is fluid-filled; an erosion is superficial epidermal loss and an ulcer is loss of epidermis and dermis.
An erosion is a primary lesion and an ulcer is a secondary lesion
Both erosion and ulcer are secondary lesions; they differ in depth, with an ulcer extending through the dermis and destroying collagen.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: Why does labyrinthitis impair hearing AND balance together?
opts: Dislodged otoconia striking structures in the endolymph
That is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which spares hearing entirely.
Fixation of the stapes footplate
Fixation of the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a conductive middle ear lesion with no vestibular component.
Inflammation across both the semicircular canals and the cochlea
Correct. Inflammatory swelling, vascular congestion and endolymphatic disruption affect the semicircular canals and the cochlea at once, impairing balance and the organ of Corti together.
Defective endolymph resorption ballooning the scala media
That is the hydrops of Meniere disease, and it does not begin with inflammation.

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
D.q: What determines where a cancer metastasizes?
opts: Venous blood flow, tumor and endothelial receptors, and genetic fitness
Correct — metastatic spread is NOT random but determined by these three.
Chance alone, since circulating tumor cells lodge wherever the vessel first narrows
Metastatic spread is not random; the pattern of venous blood flow, tumor and endothelial cell receptors, and genetic fitness decide where it lands.
The size of the primary lesion and the duration of the disease
Primary lesion size feeds staging; where a cancer spreads is set by venous blood flow, specific receptors, and genetically determined fitness.
The histological grade of the tumor and its rate of mitosis
Grade and mitotic rate describe the tumor itself; its destination is set by venous blood flow, specific receptors, and genetic fitness.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 27

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: Why does a tumor mass grow faster than normal tissue?
opts: A lower proliferative fraction together with a lower rate of cell loss
A lower proliferative fraction would slow growth; a tumor mass outgrows normal tissue through a higher proliferative fraction and a lower rate of cell loss.
An unchanged proliferative fraction with a shorter individual cell cycle
The proliferative fraction does change: it rises, because abnormal differentiation keeps more cells in the proliferative pool.
A higher proliferative fraction together with a lower rate of cell loss
Correct — both halves matter; it is not only that cells divide faster.
A higher proliferative fraction together with a higher rate of cell loss
A higher loss rate would offset the gain; loss is in fact lower.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
D.q: Which four histological features move a tumor from the benign end towards the malignant end?
opts: Encapsulation, uniform nuclei, absent mitoses, and normal differentiation
Those sit at the benign end, where a tumor often has a fibrous capsule and is usually well differentiated; the malignant end brings pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei and mitoses.
Invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous spread, and seeding
Those are invasion and the routes of tumor spread, not histological features; the histological features are pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses and abnormal differentiation.
Initiation, promotion, progression, and metastasis
Initiation and promotion are steps of chemical carcinogenesis, not histological features; the malignant end shows pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses and abnormal differentiation.
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses, and abnormal differentiation
Correct — pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses and abnormal differentiation increase from the benign end toward the malignant end.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 23

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
D.q: What causes astigmatism?
opts: An axial globe that is too short
An axial globe that is too short causes hyperopia, focusing behind the retina; astigmatism comes from irregular corneal or lens curvature.
Loss of lens elasticity with age, so the lens can no longer change shape
Age-related loss of lens elasticity is presbyopia; astigmatism is irregular corneal or lens curvature creating non-spherical focal points.
Irregular corneal or lens curvature creating non-spherical focal points
Correct — irregular curvature of the cornea or lens creates non-spherical focal points instead of the single focal point needed for a sharp image.
An axial globe that is too long
An axial globe that is too long causes myopia, focusing in front of the retina; astigmatism comes from irregular corneal or lens curvature.

D.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
D.q: Which two mediators are plasma proteins?
opts: Immunoglobulin G and C3b
Immunoglobulin G and C3b are grouped as opsonins; the plasma protein mediators are bradykinin, complement components and coagulation.
Fibrinogen and fibrolytic enzymes
Fibrinogen belongs to the fibrinous pattern and fibrolytic enzymes remove it; the plasma protein mediators are bradykinin and complement.
Bradykinin and complement components
Correct. Bradykinin and complement components are both plasma proteins, as is the coagulation system.
Histamine and serotonin
Histamine and serotonin are separate mediators causing vasodilation and permeability; the plasma proteins are bradykinin, complement and the coagulation system.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which two cell types both act against virus-infected and tumor cells?
opts: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
B lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate antibody production; virus-infected and tumor cells are the targets of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells
Correct. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells are the two subsets that act against virus-infected and tumor cells.
Monocytes and macrophages
Monocytes and macrophages phagocytose and present pathogen pieces to T cells; virus-infected and tumor cells fall to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
T helper cells and regulatory suppressor T cells
T helper cells activate and regulate T and B cells, and regulatory T cells return immune function to normal after infection; neither targets infected cells.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: Which description fits vocal cord nodules?
opts: Unilateral pedunculated fluid-filled growths on the middle third, from a single severe strain
That describes vocal cord POLYPS, and the unilateral-versus-bilateral split is the main distinction.
Bilateral wart-like exophytic lesions from viral infection
Viral wart-like lesions are not nodules. Nodules are bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma, at the junction of the anterior third.
Unilateral firm masses with cord fixation, from malignancy
Nodules are neither malignant nor fixed. They are benign bilateral symmetrical calluses from chronic phonotrauma, the cords slamming together.
Bilateral symmetrical calluses at the anterior third junction, from chronic phonotrauma
Correct. Chronic phonotrauma, the cords slamming together, causes basement membrane hyalinization, a callus. Nodules are bilateral and symmetrical at the anterior third junction.

D.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
D.q: Which forms of radiation cause cancer?
opts: Ultraviolet B, and ionizing radiation
Correct — both ultraviolet B and ionizing radiation cause cancer; unrepaired ultraviolet B mutations explain the skin cancers of xeroderma pigmentosum.
Ultraviolet A only, together with infrared radiation
The radiation forms that cause cancer are ultraviolet B and ionizing radiation; ultraviolet A and infrared are not among them.
Microwave and radiofrequency radiation
The radiation forms that cause cancer are ultraviolet B and ionizing radiation, not microwave or radiofrequency radiation.
Ionizing radiation only, with no ultraviolet contribution
Ultraviolet B causes cancer alongside ionizing radiation, as the skin cancers in sun-exposed areas of xeroderma pigmentosum show.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 38

D.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
D.q: Which time course fits the vertigo of labyrinthitis?
opts: Episodic, with attacks lasting several hours
Episodic attacks lasting hours are the vertigo of Meniere disease. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden, lasts days and improves over weeks.
Episodic, with attacks lasting under a minute
Attacks under a minute, provoked by head position, are benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which spares hearing.
Continuous, permanent and non-improving
It is not permanent. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden, lasts days, and improves over the following weeks.
Sudden, lasting days, improving over weeks
Correct. Labyrinthitis vertigo is sudden and lasts days, improving over weeks, unlike the hours-long attacks of Meniere disease or the sub-minute attacks of positional vertigo.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which leukocyte is the first responder to microbial infection?
opts: The eosinophil
Eosinophils primarily deal with parasitic infections and allergic reactions; the neutrophil is the first responder to microbial infection.
The B lymphocyte
B lymphocytes act through antibody production in the humoral response; the neutrophil is the first responder to microbial infection.
The neutrophil
Correct. The neutrophil is the first responder to microbial infection, defending against bacterial and fungal infection.
The macrophage
Macrophages come from monocytes that have left the bloodstream; the first responder to microbial infection is the neutrophil.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which three cell types are granulocytes?
opts: Lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages
Lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages are the agranulocytes, or mononuclear leukocytes, the opposite grouping.
Neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils
Correct. These are the three granulocytes; polymorphonuclear leukocyte refers to all granulocytes.
Neutrophils, monocytes and B lymphocytes
Monocytes and B lymphocytes are agranulocytes; the three granulocytes are neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils.
Basophils, eosinophils and natural killer cells
Natural killer cells appear among the T lymphocyte subsets, not the granulocytes; the third granulocyte is the neutrophil.

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: Which description of the proliferative phase of wound healing is accurate?
opts: A fibrin hemostatic plug, over days 1 to 3
A fibrin hemostatic plug forms in the inflammatory phase, days 1 to 3; the proliferative phase, days 4 to 21, forms granulation tissue.
Type I collagen laid down in parallel bundles, over days 21 to one year of remodeling
Type I collagen in parallel bundles belongs to remodeling, day 21 to one year; the proliferative phase forms granulation tissue.
Keratohyalin granules within the granular layer
Keratohyalin granules belong to the normal stratum granulosum; the proliferative phase of wound healing forms granulation tissue over days 4 to 21.
Granulation tissue, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, over days 4 to 21
Correct. Over days 4 to 21, granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, before remodeling begins.

D.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
D.q: What are the symptoms of rhegmatogenous detachment?
opts: Gradual painless bilateral blurring with glare at night
Gradual painless bilateral blurring with night glare is cataract; rhegmatogenous detachment brings photopsia, a shower of floaters and a curtain.
Severe pain with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
Severe pain, halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil describe acute angle-closure glaucoma; rhegmatogenous detachment brings photopsia, floaters and a curtain.
Slow loss of central detail with progressive distortion of straight lines
Slow loss of central detail with distortion is dry macular degeneration; rhegmatogenous detachment brings flashing lights, floaters and a curtain.
Flashing lights, a shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
Correct — the symptoms of a full-thickness retinal break with detachment are flashing lights (photopsia), a shower of floaters and a curtain falling across the field.

D.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
D.q: Why does skeletal muscle hypertrophy rather than divide?
opts: Protein intake causes fluid retention within the muscle, so the organ appears larger
Fluid retention is not hypertrophy; hypertrophy is enlargement of a tissue due to enlargement of its individual cells.
Resistance training converts slow fibers to fast fibers, changing the tissue type
A change of cell type would be metaplasia; hypertrophy keeps the same cells and enlarges each one.
Striated muscle cells do not divide, so each fiber gets larger instead
Correct — skeletal muscle is a permanent tissue, so it grows by enlarging each existing fiber, which is hypertrophy rather than hyperplasia.
Resistance training recruits satellite cells, so the number of muscle fibers increases
More fibers would be hyperplasia; skeletal muscle is a permanent tissue whose cells enlarge rather than divide.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 3

D.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
D.q: What happens when a protooncogene mutates?
opts: It becomes a repair gene, which then introduces errors into the genome
Genes promoting repair of damaged deoxyribonucleic acid are a separate category; a mutated protooncogene becomes an oncogene instead.
It becomes silent, so the cell loses its ability to grow at all
Mutation does not silence growth; it converts the protooncogene to an oncogene that drives uncontrolled growth.
It becomes an oncogene, which encodes oncoproteins that promote continued uncontrolled growth
Correct — mutation converts a protooncogene to an oncogene, whose oncoproteins promote continued growth in an uncontrolled manner.
It becomes a tumor suppressor gene, which then inhibits cell growth excessively
Tumor suppressor genes are a separate category that inhibits cell growth; a mutated protooncogene becomes an oncogene that drives uncontrolled growth.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 29

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: Which two abnormalities separate a tumor cell from a normal cell?
opts: Abnormal apoptosis, and abnormal deoxyribonucleic acid repair
Apoptosis and repair genes matter in carcinogenesis, but the normal-versus-tumor contrast is growth regulation and cell-cell interaction.
Abnormal vascular supply, and abnormal stromal composition
Stroma, the connective tissue and blood vessels, is a component of every neoplasm; tumor cells differ from normal cells in growth regulation and cell-cell interactions.
Abnormal differentiation, and abnormal cell size
Differentiation and cell size are not the pair; tumor cells show abnormal regulation of cell growth and abnormal cell-cell interactions.
Abnormal regulation of cell growth, and abnormal cell-cell interactions
Correct — compared with normal cells, tumor cells show abnormal regulation of cell growth and abnormal cell-cell interactions.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
D.q: What causes an ipsilateral optic nerve lesion?
opts: Posterior cerebral artery occlusion in the occipital lobe
Posterior cerebral artery occlusion damages the occipital cortex, sparing the macula; optic nerve lesions follow trauma, optic neuritis or ischemia.
Temporal lobe surgery
Temporal lobe surgery damages the temporal optic radiation, giving pie in the sky; optic nerve lesions follow trauma, optic neuritis or ischemic neuropathy.
Trauma, optic neuritis and ischemic optic neuropathy
Correct — a lesion of the optic nerve before the chiasm follows trauma, optic neuritis or ischemic optic neuropathy, and causes total vision loss in that eye.
Pituitary adenoma compression
Pituitary adenoma compresses the center of the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopsia; optic nerve lesions follow trauma, neuritis or ischemia.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which pairing of maturation site and surface structure is correct for T lymphocytes?
opts: The thymus; T cell receptors
Correct. T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, which gives them their name, and carry T cell receptors on their surface.
The bone marrow; Fc receptors
Fc receptors sit on phagocytic cells that recognize immunoglobulin G; T lymphocytes mature in the thymus and carry T cell receptors.
The spleen; complement receptors
Complement receptors sit on immune cells that recognize C3b; T lymphocytes mature in the thymus and carry T cell receptors.
The lymph nodes; major histocompatibility complexes
T lymphocytes mature in the thymus, not the lymph nodes, and their defining surface structure is the T cell receptor.

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: Which statement describes cochlear damage from long-term chronic noise exposure?
opts: Above 120 decibels, causing tympanic membrane rupture
Tympanic membrane rupture is not the chronic lesion. Long-term exposure above 85 decibels causes irreversible stereocilia degeneration and hair cell apoptosis.
Above 60 decibels, causing endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion of Meniere disease, caused by defective resorption rather than by sound exposure at any level.
Above 85 decibels, by stereocilia degeneration and apoptosis
Correct. Long-term chronic exposure to sound above 85 decibels induces irreversible stereocilia degeneration and apoptosis of the acoustic hair cells.
Above 85 decibels, causing reversible stereocilia fatigue
The threshold is right but the change is not reversible — apoptosis is cell death.

E.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
E.q: Which medication class is a cataract risk?
opts: Chronic corticosteroids
Correct — chronic corticosteroid use is the medication cause of cataract, alongside aging, diabetes, ocular trauma, Down syndrome and ultraviolet light.
Chronic beta-blockers
Beta-blockers are not a cataract risk; the medication class that causes cataract, the opacification of the crystalline lens, is chronic corticosteroids.
Chronic antihistamines
Antihistamines are not a cataract risk; the medication that opacifies the lens is chronic corticosteroid use, with trauma, diabetes and aging as other causes.
Chronic statins
Statins are not a cataract risk; chronic corticosteroid use is, with aging, diabetes, ocular trauma, Down syndrome and ultraviolet light as other causes.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: What are the two connective tissue layers of the dermis?
opts: Papillary, the thin superficial layer, and reticular, the dense deeper layer
Correct. The dermis consists of two connective tissue layers: the thin superficial papillary layer and the dense deeper reticular layer.
Basale and spinosum
The stratum basale and stratum spinosum are epidermal layers; the dermis has a thin superficial papillary layer and a dense deeper reticular layer.
Corneum and lucidum
The stratum corneum and stratum lucidum are outer epidermal layers; the dermis consists of the papillary and reticular connective tissue layers.
The papillary and the subcutaneous, being the superficial and the deepest layers
The subcutaneous layer, or hypodermis, is the third layer of skin rather than dermis; the deeper dermal layer is the dense reticular layer.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which description of leukonychia is accurate?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed
Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed produces Terry's nails, opaque except for a dark band at the tip; leukonychia is incomplete keratinization.
Increased capillary density with release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the nail bed tissue itself
Increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release is the finding in clubbing; leukonychia comes from incomplete keratinization.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually harmless nail bed damage but also seen with heavy metal poisoning
Correct. Leukonychia, or Mee's lines, shows white streaks or spots from temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually from harmless nail bed damage.
A halt of keratin production, associated with illness and malnourishment
A halt of keratin production causes Beau's lines, which are transverse grooves; leukonychia shows white streaks or spots from incomplete keratinization.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which structural epidermal changes occur in psoriasis?
opts: Epidermal hyperplasia, loss of the stratum granulosum, and failure of epidermal cells to secrete lipids producing xeroderma
Correct. Active T cells drive keratinocyte proliferation into epidermal hyperplasia, the stratum granulosum is lost, and epidermal cells stop secreting lipids.
Thinning of the epidermis with slowed keratinocyte division
Thinning with slowed keratinocyte division is atrophy; psoriatic skin cells multiply up to ten times faster, producing epidermal hyperplasia.
Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with fluid accumulating between the two layers of the skin itself
Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid between them forms a bulla; psoriasis causes epidermal hyperplasia and loss of the stratum granulosum.
Loss of melanocytes from the basal layer
Loss of melanocytes produces the hypopigmentation of vitiligo; psoriasis thickens the epidermis through hyperplasia and loses the stratum granulosum.

E.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
E.q: Where must light be focused for an image to form?
opts: On the optic disc, where the nerve exits
The optic disc is the blind spot, with no rods or cones, so no image forms there; light must be focused onto the retina.
On the lens itself, which then transmits the signal
The lens refracts light rather than detecting it; image formation needs the light focused onto the retina, whose photoreceptors convert it to signals.
On the retina, after refraction through the cornea and lens
Correct — image formation requires light refracted through the cornea and lens to be focused onto the retina, where rods and cones convert photons to signals.
On the choroid, after refraction through the cornea alone
The choroid lies behind the retina and nourishes it rather than receiving the image; light must be focused onto the retina itself.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Why does anticoagulation favor POSTERIOR rather than anterior epistaxis?
opts: The posterior mucosa is thinner
Mucosal thickness is not what separates the two. The difference is local insult against systemic vascular and clotting factors.
The anterior septum has no blood supply
Kiesselbach's plexus supplies the anterior septum richly, which is exactly why anterior bleeds are the common ones.
Anticoagulants are concentrated posteriorly
No regional concentration is involved. Anticoagulant therapy sits with hypertension, atherosclerosis and coagulopathy as the systemic causes of posterior bleeds.
Posterior bleeding is driven by systemic vascular and clotting factors
Correct. Anterior causes are local insults to the mucosa; posterior causes act on the vessels and on clotting.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Which ion movement depolarizes the cochlear hair cell?
opts: Influx from the perilymph across the basilar membrane
The depolarizing influx comes from the endolymph, through tip-link channels opened by stereocilia deflection, not from the perilymph across the basilar membrane.
Release from intracellular stores after glutamate binding
Glutamate is what the hair cell RELEASES onto cranial nerve VIII after it depolarizes. It is the output of the cell, not a signal arriving at it.
Efflux into the perilymph through voltage-gated channels
Voltage-gated channels open only AFTER depolarization, triggering glutamate release. The depolarizing event is influx from the endolymph through the tip-link channels.
Influx from the endolymph through the tip-link channels

Correct. Deflected stereocilia open the tip-link channels, permitting rapid influx from the endolymph into the hair cell. Depolarization then opens voltage-gated channels and glutamate is released onto cranial nerve VIII.

E.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
E.q: What distinguishes dry from wet gangrene?
opts: Dry is acute; wet is chronic
Chronicity is a separate axis from pattern; dry versus wet gangrene turns on coagulative versus liquefactive necrosis from infection.
Dry involves fibrinous exudate; wet involves serous exudate
Exudate type does not separate the two; dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis and wet is liquefactive necrosis from infection.
Dry is coagulative necrosis; wet is liquefactive necrosis arising from infection
Correct. Gangrenous inflammation is a severe form of necrosis with or without superimposed bacterial infection, dry being coagulative and wet liquefactive from infection.
Dry gangrene occurs on mucosal surfaces; wet gangrene occurs on serosal surfaces
The surface involved does not separate them; dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis and wet gangrene is liquefactive necrosis from infection.

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: Which feature defines granulocytes under light microscopy?
opts: A kidney-shaped nucleus that permits the cell to transmigrate between two adjacent endothelial cells nearby
A kidney-shaped nucleus belongs to the monocyte, an agranulocyte; granulocytes are defined by differently staining cytoplasmic granules.
Azurophilic granules that function purely as antigen-presenting structures
Non-specific azurophilic granules (lysosomes) are found in agranulocytes; granulocyte granules are enzymes that digest phagocytized particles.
Surface receptors that bind the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G
Fc receptors let phagocytic cells recognize immunoglobulin G during opsonization; granulocytes are defined by their staining cytoplasmic granules.
Differently staining cytoplasmic granules that are membrane-bound enzymes acting in the digestion of phagocytized particles
Correct. The granules are membrane-bound enzymes whose primary action is digesting what has been phagocytized.

E.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
E.q: What do promoters do?
opts: They cause the permanent deoxyribonucleic acid damage that starts the process
Causing permanent deoxyribonucleic acid damage is initiation; promoters drive proliferation of cells already damaged.
They repair the deoxyribonucleic acid damage caused by initiators
Promoters do not repair damage; they cause sustained or enhanced proliferation of cells an initiator has damaged.
They cause tumor cells to detach and enter the circulation
Detachment and entry into the circulation belong to metastasis; promoters drive proliferation of initiated cells.
They drive proliferation of cells already damaged by an initiator
Correct — sustained or enhanced proliferation raises the risk of successive mutations leading to cancer.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 31

E.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
E.q: What does the degree of differentiation of a neoplasm measure?
opts: How rapidly the tumor mass is enlarging over time
Rapid growth is a feature of malignant tumors; differentiation measures resemblance to comparable normal cells in appearance and function.
How many of its cells are in the proliferative pool at any moment
The proliferative pool is a matter of stem cell kinetics; differentiation measures how closely a neoplasm resembles comparable normal cells.
How closely it resembles comparable normal cells in appearance and function
Correct — differentiation is the degree a neoplasm resembles comparable normal cells, which is the basis of histological grading.
How far it has spread from the primary site within the patient
Extent of spread within the patient is what staging indicates; differentiation measures resemblance to comparable normal cells.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 12

E.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
E.q: How does aplasia differ from agenesis?
opts: The primordial tissue never forms, so the organ is completely absent
That describes agenesis, the condition being contrasted, in which the primordial tissue never formed at all.
The organ develops only partially, leaving a functional deficiency
Partial development with a functional deficiency is hypoplasia; in aplasia the primordial tissue fails to mature.
The organ enlarges because its individual cells enlarge
Enlargement of individual cells is hypertrophy; aplasia is failure of existing primordial tissue to develop.
The primordial tissue exists but fails to develop into the mature organ
Correct — in aplasia the primordial tissue exists but fails to develop into the mature organ, whereas in agenesis it never formed at all.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 3

E.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
E.q: What do the lids, cornea and conjunctiva have in common as the outermost ocular structures?
opts: They contain the highest density of nerve endings
Nerve-ending density is not what they share; the outer structures are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environmental change than deeper ones.
They are the last to be affected in systemic disease
Systemic disease shows itself in the deepest structures, the posterior segment, optic nerve and retina; the outer ones are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environment.
They are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environmental change
Correct — as the outer, easily visible structures, the lids, cornea and conjunctiva face the environment directly and are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environmental change.
They are the only structures visible without an ophthalmoscope
Visibility is not the shared feature; as outer, exposed structures the lids, cornea and conjunctiva are more susceptible to infection, trauma and environmental change.

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: A temporal bone fracture causes conductive loss by which mechanism?
opts: Obstruction of the external canal
Obstruction blocks the external canal before the drum. A temporal bone fracture acts deeper, on the ossicular chain itself.
Discontinuity of the ossicular chain
Correct. The chain is physically disrupted so the wave cannot be conducted across it. Ossicular necrosis produces the same end result by erosion rather than trauma.
Stiffness of the ossicular chain
Stiffness is impaired mobility of the ossicles or drum, as in otosclerosis. A temporal bone fracture instead physically disrupts the ossicular chain.
Mass loading of the tympanic membrane
Mass loading requires added fluid or tissue weight damping the chain. A fracture removes continuity rather than adding weight.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Which sequence correctly orders the three linked vascular mechanisms?
opts: Exudation, then vasodilation, then endothelial contraction
Exudation comes last, not first: vasodilation of the arterioles starts the sequence, and endothelial contraction then allows exudation.
Vasodilation of arterioles, then endothelial contraction increasing capillary permeability, then exudation
Correct. Vasodilation raises blood flow, endothelial contraction opens the capillaries, and fluid and blood proteins then move into the interstitial spaces.
Endothelial contraction, then vasodilation of the arterioles, then leukocyte transmigration into the tissue
Transmigration belongs to the later leukocyte events; the three vascular mechanisms run vasodilation, endothelial contraction, then exudation.
Endothelial contraction, then exudation, then vasodilation of arterioles
Exudation is the consequence of increased permeability, so it cannot precede the vasodilation that begins the sequence.

E.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
E.q: What distinguishes atrophy from hypoplasia?
opts: Atrophy is shrinkage of a tissue or organ that had already formed and matured normally
Correct — the timing is what separates them: hypoplasia is a developmental failure.
Atrophy is partial development of an organ that never reached mature size
That is hypoplasia, a failure during development rather than a loss afterwards.
Atrophy is enlargement of an organ because its individual cells enlarge
Enlargement from individual cell enlargement is hypertrophy; atrophy is shrinkage of an organ that had formed and matured normally.
Atrophy is disordered growth of epithelial cells with variation in size and shape
Disordered epithelial growth with variation in size and shape is dysplasia; atrophy is shrinkage of an organ that matured normally.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 3

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: What do regulatory (suppressor) T cells do?
opts: Returning the immune system to normal operation after infection, and preventing autoimmunity
Correct. Regulatory (suppressor) T cells return the immune system to normal operation after infection and prevent autoimmunity.
Producing antibody directed against antigens the host has encountered previously
Producing antibody is a B lymphocyte role; regulatory T cells return immune function to normal after infection and prevent autoimmunity.
Presenting phagocytosed material to naive T cells
