Presenting pieces of pathogens to T cells is a monocyte role; regulatory T cells instead restore normal immune function and prevent autoimmunity.
Killing tumor cells directly through granule release
CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells act against tumor cells; regulatory T cells return immune function to normal and prevent autoimmunity.

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: Which systemic diseases are strongly linked to scleritis?
opts: Sarcoidosis and choroidal melanoma
Sarcoidosis and choroidal melanoma cause exudative retinal detachment; scleritis is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and systemic vasculitis.
Rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic vasculitis

Correct — scleritis, an emergency of the deep sclera with boring pain and a risk of scleral melting, is strongly linked to rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic vasculitis.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis
Lupus, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis are associated with anterior uveitis; scleritis links to rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis.
Diabetes mellitus and hypertension
Diabetes and hypertension are not the scleritis links; scleritis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and vasculitis.

E.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
E.q: Which factors cause bullae?
opts: Androgen stimulation of sebaceous glands
Androgen stimulation is not a cause of blistering; bullae arise from mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemical exposure and autoimmune reactions.
Mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemical exposure and autoimmune reactions
Correct, with bullous impetigo as the bacterial example and bullous pemphigoid as the autoimmune one.
Increased melanin production and cumulative ultraviolet light exposure alone
Increased melanin production causes hyperpigmented macules; bullae arise from mechanical, infectious, toxic, chemical or autoimmune injury.
Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia
Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia cause petechiae and purpura; bullae arise from mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemicals and autoimmunity.

E.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
E.q: Which description fits the semicircular canals?
opts: Linear acceleration and gravitational position, via the otoliths
That is the utricle and saccule — the otolith organs — which handle static and linear balance.
Rotational acceleration, by endolymph bending the cupula
Correct. Three loops in the sagittal, coronal and transverse planes. The fluid lags behind the head, the gelatinous cupula bends, and the hair cell stereocilia inside it are stimulated.
Sound frequency, via the basilar membrane
Sound is transduced by the cochlea, which converts fluid displacement into neural signals through the organ of Corti.
Middle ear pressure, via the Eustachian tube
The Eustachian tube equalizes middle ear pressure. That is a conduction function and has nothing to do with detecting head movement.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: Which statement correctly describes the cell population of the epidermis?
opts: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, with keratinocytes about 90 percent
Correct. The epidermis holds keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, and keratinocytes, which produce keratin, make up about 90 percent of it.
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells, with fibroblasts predominating
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells are cells of the dermis; the epidermis holds keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells.
Melanocytes, Merkel cells, fibroblasts and histiocytes, with melanocytes predominating
Fibroblasts and histiocytes are dermal cells, and melanocytes are a minority; keratinocytes make up about 90 percent of the epidermis.
Keratinocytes and melanocytes only, in roughly equal proportion
The epidermis has four cell types, adding Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, and keratinocytes far outnumber melanocytes at about 90 percent.

E.io: l — Describe the tumor, nodes, metastases (TNM) staging system
E.q: What are the purposes of cancer staging?
opts: To measure how closely the tumor resembles the normal tissue it came from
Resemblance to the normal tissue is histological grading; staging instead describes how far the cancer has spread within the patient.
To identify which gene alterations caused the tumor
Staging describes extent, based on primary lesion size, regional lymph nodes, and blood-borne metastases, not what caused the tumor.
To determine whether the tumor is benign or malignant
Benign versus malignant is settled first; staging then indicates extent of spread, determines prognosis, and guides management.
Extent of spread, prognosis, and guiding management
Correct — all three. Staging answers a different question from histological grading.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 41

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: What is the fate of a monocyte once it leaves the bloodstream?
opts: A dendritic cell that migrates to the thymus
The thymus is where T lymphocytes mature; a monocyte that leaves the bloodstream becomes a tissue macrophage instead.
A tissue macrophage that removes dead cell debris and attacks microorganisms
Correct. Monocytes eventually leave the bloodstream to become tissue macrophages with exactly these roles.
A plasma cell that secretes antibody directly into the interstitium
Monocytes do not become plasma cells; a monocyte leaving the bloodstream becomes a tissue macrophage that clears debris and microorganisms.
A fibroblast that lays down scar tissue
Fibroblastic scar tissue is a healing outcome, not a monocyte fate; monocytes become tissue macrophages after leaving the blood.

E.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
E.q: What are the risk factors for rhegmatogenous detachment?
opts: Chronic corticosteroid use, Down syndrome and ultraviolet light exposure
Corticosteroids, Down syndrome and ultraviolet light are cataract risks; rhegmatogenous risks are vitreous detachment, age, myopia, trauma and lattice degeneration.
Posterior vitreous detachment, age, severe myopia, trauma and lattice degeneration
Correct — posterior vitreous detachment, age, severe myopia, trauma and lattice degeneration set up the full-thickness break through which liquefied vitreous enters.
Diabetes, prior vitrectomy and retinal trauma surgery
Diabetes and prior vitrectomy scarring cause tractional detachment through fibrovascular membranes; rhegmatogenous detachment starts with a retinal break.
Sarcoidosis, malignant hypertension and melanoma
Sarcoidosis, malignant hypertension and melanoma cause exudative detachment without a tear; rhegmatogenous detachment follows a full-thickness break.

E.io: f — Compare and contrast the different types of malignant tumors according to origin
E.q: What is a carcinoma with a glandular growth pattern called?
opts: An adenocarcinoma
Correct — a carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumor, and one with a glandular growth pattern is an adenocarcinoma.
An adenoma
An adenoma is the benign epithelial tumor with a glandular pattern; the malignant glandular carcinoma is an adenocarcinoma.
A squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma is the carcinoma with squamous cell differentiation, not a glandular growth pattern.
A sarcoma
A sarcoma is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal, supportive tissue, not an epithelial carcinoma with glandular growth.
E.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 18

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: What does the lipid layer of the tear film do?
opts: It provides the bulk volume of the tears
Tear volume is not the lipid layer's role; meibomian glands in the tarsal plates produce the lipid layer, whose job is to prevent evaporation.
It anchors the tear film to the corneal epithelium
Anchoring the film is not the lipid layer's role; meibomian lipid prevents evaporation, and without it tear osmolarity rises and damages the corneal epithelium.
It carries immunoglobulin to the ocular surface
Carrying immunoglobulin is not the lipid layer's role; meibomian glands produce it to prevent tear evaporation, which is why their obstruction causes dry eye.
It prevents evaporation
Correct — meibomian glands in the tarsal plates produce the lipid layer, which prevents evaporation; when they are obstructed, as in blepharitis, tears evaporate excessively.

E.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
E.q: Which causes produce CENTRAL vertigo?
opts: Presbycusis and noise trauma
Both are sensorineural hearing loss without a vestibular component.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Meniere disease and labyrinthitis
Those are peripheral causes involving the inner ear, along with vestibular neuritis. Central causes involve the brainstem or cerebellum.
Brainstem stroke, multiple sclerosis and cerebellar tumor
Correct. All involve the brainstem or cerebellum, which is why the nystagmus can be vertical and is not suppressed by fixation, and why other neurological signs appear.
Otosclerosis and cerumen impaction
Otosclerosis and cerumen impaction are conductive hearing problems. Neither involves the vestibular apparatus, so neither causes vertigo at all.

E.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
E.q: Which statement about the causes of otitis externa is accurate?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; fungal disease follows swimming
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are otitis media organisms. Fungal otitis externa follows prolonged antibiotic use or hyperhumid conditions.
Moraxella catarrhalis alone; fungal disease follows trauma
Moraxella catarrhalis sits on the otitis MEDIA list alongside Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, not in the external canal.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus; fungal after antibiotics
Correct. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus cause 80 to 90 percent of cases; fungal disease from Aspergillus niger or Candida albicans often follows prolonged antibiotic use.
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus; fungal disease follows steroid use
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus are viral causes of otitis MEDIA; they are not what colonizes an external canal.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: How is melanoma risk inherited?
opts: As an autosomal recessive trait with complete penetrance
Melanoma risk is not recessive with complete penetrance; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.
As an X-linked trait
Melanoma risk is not X-linked; it is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.
It is entirely environmental with no inherited component
Melanoma risk has an inherited component, autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, alongside ultraviolet light and oxidative stress.
As an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance
Correct, though ultraviolet light and oxidative stress remain the primary driving factor.

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: What is a hypopyon?
opts: Yellow debris beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
Yellow debris beneath the pigment epithelium is drusen, the hallmark of dry macular degeneration; a hypopyon is pus in the anterior chamber.
Pus in the anterior chamber
Correct — a hypopyon is a collection of pus in the anterior chamber, the inflammatory layer seen in the front of a severely inflamed eye.
Blood in the anterior chamber
Blood is not what collects; a hypopyon is pus in the anterior chamber, a sign of severe inflammation in the front of the eye.
Fluid beneath the neurosensory retina
Fluid beneath the neurosensory retina is retinal detachment, in the posterior segment; a hypopyon is pus in the anterior chamber.

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: Which description matches the appearance of a neutrophil?
opts: Kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant cytoplasm that is usually agranulated when it is viewed on light microscopy
A kidney-shaped nucleus with abundant agranulated cytoplasm is the monocyte; the neutrophil has a multilobed nucleus.
Multilobed nucleus that may appear like multiple nuclei, with cytoplasm looking transparent because of fine pale lilac granules
Correct. The neutrophil's multilobed nucleus can look like several nuclei, and fine pale lilac granules make its cytoplasm look transparent.
Bi- or tri-lobed nucleus with a number of coarse granules
A bi- or tri-lobed nucleus with coarse granules is the basophil; the neutrophil has a multilobed nucleus and fine granules.
Bi-lobed nucleus with pink-orange granules
A bi-lobed nucleus with pink-orange granules is the eosinophil; the neutrophil nucleus is multilobed with fine pale lilac granules.

E.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
E.q: Which pair of conditions are examples of autoimmunity causing chronic inflammation?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus
Correct. Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are autoimmune diseases, and autoimmunity is one of the three causes of chronic inflammation.
Atherosclerosis and silicosis
Atherosclerosis and silica are the endogenous and exogenous toxic-agent examples; rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are the autoimmune examples.
Asthma and hay fever
Asthma and hay fever are allergic reactions in which eosinophils predominate; rheumatoid arthritis and lupus are the autoimmune examples.
Trauma and bee sting
Trauma and bee sting contrast physical with immune-activating damage in acute inflammation; the autoimmune examples are rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which description of Terry's nails is accurate?
opts: Increased capillary density together with vascular endothelial growth factor release into the tissue locally over time
Increased capillary density with vascular endothelial growth factor release is clubbing; Terry's nails come from connective tissue overgrowth.
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anemia is koilonychia; Terry's nails reflect overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed produces leukonychia; Terry's nails come from connective tissue overgrowth.
Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, associated with aging, liver disease, congestive heart failure or diabetes
Correct. Terry's nails come from overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, leaving the nail opaque except for a dark band at the tip.

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: Which pair of tuning fork findings indicates conductive hearing loss?
opts: Weber to the affected ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
The Weber is right but Rinne is not — a normal air-over-bone ratio means the conducting apparatus is working.
Weber is equal; Rinne shows bone greater than air bilaterally
An equal Weber implies no lateralizing lesion. In conductive loss Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne there shows bone greater than air.
Weber to the AFFECTED ear; Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air
Correct. With sound wave transmission to the oval window defective, Weber lateralizes to the AFFECTED ear and Rinne is abnormal, with bone conduction greater than air.
Weber to the UNAFFECTED ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
That is the sensorineural pattern: the damaged cochlea cannot hear either route well, so Weber goes to the better ear and Rinne keeps its normal ratio.

E.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
E.q: Suppurative (purulent) inflammation contains which combination of material?
opts: Remnants of white blood cells, protein and tissue debris — that is, pus
Correct. Suppurative (purulent) inflammation contains remnants of white blood cells, protein and tissue debris, which is pus.
Fibrinogen forming a thick meshwork over the serosal surface
Large amounts of fibrinogen forming a thick meshwork define the fibrinous pattern; suppurative inflammation is pus.
Low-protein plasma with minimal cellular content
Largely plasma with low protein is the serous pattern; suppurative inflammation contains white blood cell remnants, protein and debris.
A superficial necrotic layer forming a membrane over affected mucosa
A superficial necrotic layer forming a membrane is the pseudomembranous pattern; suppurative inflammation is pus instead.

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: How does panophthalmitis differ from endophthalmitis?
opts: It involves only the vitreous
Vitreous alone is narrower than endophthalmitis, not broader; panophthalmitis involves every layer of the globe and may reach the orbit.
It is limited to the anterior segment and spares the vitreous
The term means the opposite; panophthalmitis spreads through all layers of the globe, vitreous included, and may extend into the orbital tissue.
It spares the sclera
Sparing the sclera is the opposite of the term; panophthalmitis involves every layer of the globe, sclera included, and may reach the orbit.
It involves all layers of the globe and may extend into orbital tissue
Correct — pan- means all: panophthalmitis involves every layer of the globe and can spread into the orbit, beyond the intraocular infection of endophthalmitis.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: What is sebum primarily composed of?
opts: Collagen and elastin
Collagen and elastin are dermal fibers; sebum is a lipid secretion of triglycerides, wax esters and squalene from sebaceous glands.
Triglycerides, wax esters and squalene
Correct, produced by the sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles to lubricate skin and hair.
Water, sodium and chloride electrolytes
Water, sodium and chloride make up eccrine sweat; sebum from sebaceous glands is mainly triglycerides, wax esters and squalene.
Keratin and keratohyalin
Keratin comes from keratinocytes and keratohyalin fills the granular layer; sebum is mainly triglycerides, wax esters and squalene.

E.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
E.q: How do the borders of benign and malignant tumors differ?
opts: Both have well circumscribed borders, and they are distinguished only by growth rate
Only a benign tumor has a well circumscribed border; a malignant tumor's border is ragged and not easily discernible.
Both have ragged borders, and they are distinguished only by whether they metastasize
Only a malignant tumor has a ragged border; a benign tumor is well circumscribed and often has a fibrous capsule.
Benign is well circumscribed and compresses; malignant is ragged and invades
Correct — the benign tumor pushes surrounding tissue aside, the malignant one infiltrates and goes through it.
Benign has a ragged border and infiltrates surrounding tissue; malignant is well circumscribed and compresses it
That reverses the two: a benign tumor is well circumscribed and compresses surrounding tissue, while a malignant one has a ragged border and infiltrates it.

E.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
E.q: Which inherited tumor suppressor alteration is associated with malignant melanoma?
opts: p16, also called INK4a
Correct — p16 (INK4a) is an inherited tumor suppressor alteration associated with malignant melanoma.
Retinoblastoma protein
Retinoblastoma protein alteration causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma; malignant melanoma follows p16 (INK4a).
Adenomatous polyposis coli
Adenomatous polyposis coli alteration causes familial adenomatosis polyposis; p16 (INK4a) is linked to malignant melanoma.
BRCA-1
That is a deoxyribonucleic acid repair gene, associated with breast cancer.

E.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
E.q: What distinguishes a primary from a secondary skin lesion?
opts: A primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease and retains its original unmodified appearance; a secondary lesion has been modified over time
Correct, and a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble the lesion it came from.
A primary lesion is palpable and a secondary lesion is flat
Palpability separates papules, nodules and plaques from flat macules within the primary group; a secondary lesion is instead one modified over time.
A primary lesion is benign and a secondary lesion is malignant
Neither category implies malignancy; a primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease, while a secondary one has been modified over time.
A primary lesion is the one that appears first in time, and a secondary lesion is any lesion that appears later at a different site elsewhere on the body
Timing and body site do not define it; a secondary lesion is one modified over time, while a primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Which description fits allergic rhinitis?
opts: Immune complex deposition, type 3 hypersensitivity
Immune complex deposition is type 3 hypersensitivity. Allergic rhinitis is type 1, immediate and IgE-mediated on the nasal mucosa.
T cell mediated, type 4 delayed hypersensitivity
Allergic rhinitis is not a delayed T cell reaction. It is an IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa triggered by inhaled allergens.
IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity, with CLEAR rhinorrhea

Correct. Type 1 hypersensitivity driven by IgE (immunoglobulin E) against inhaled allergens. The CLEAR discharge separates it from bacterial sinusitis, which is purulent. Allergic shiners complete the picture.
IgG-mediated type 2 hypersensitivity with purulent rhinorrhea
Purulent discharge points to bacterial rhinosinusitis. Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated type 1 reaction with clear rhinorrhea and nasal itching.

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: Which combination of granule color and nuclear shape identifies the eosinophil?
opts: No visible granules, kidney-shaped nucleus
No visible granules and a kidney-shaped nucleus describe the monocyte, an agranulocyte, not the granule-packed eosinophil.
Pale lilac granules, multilobed nucleus
Pale lilac granules with a multilobed nucleus describe the neutrophil; eosinophils have pink-orange granules and a bi-lobed nucleus.
Coarse dark granules, bi- or tri-lobed nucleus
A bi- or tri-lobed nucleus with coarse granules describes the basophil; the eosinophil nucleus is bi-lobed with pink-orange granules.
Pink-orange granules, bi-lobed nucleus
Correct. The cytoplasm is full of granules that assume a characteristic pink-orange color, with a bi-lobed nucleus.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the site of cellular division?
opts: The stratum corneum, the outermost layer
The stratum corneum is 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes; cell division takes place in the deepest layer, the stratum basale.
The granular layer, known as the stratum granulosum
The stratum granulosum holds 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells with keratohyalin granules; division occurs in the deepest layer, the stratum basale.
The stratum lucidum
The stratum lucidum is 2 to 3 layers of flattened dead keratinocytes, which do not divide; cell division occurs in the stratum basale.
The basal layer, or stratum basale, the deepest layer
Correct. A single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes, which also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Vasodilation of the arterioles supplying an injured region produces which immediate effect?
opts: Increased blood flow to the injured region
Correct. Vasodilation of the supplying arterioles increases blood flow.
Reduced hydrostatic pressure within the capillary bed
A fall in capillary pressure is not the effect; vasodilation of the arterioles supplying the injured region results in increased blood flow.
Contraction of the capillary endothelium
Endothelial contraction is a separate mechanism that follows and allows increased permeability; vasodilation of the arterioles itself increases blood flow.
Movement of blood proteins into the interstitium
Exudation of fluid and protein requires the increased permeability that endothelial contraction provides; vasodilation alone does not achieve it.

E.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
E.q: Which four features define dysplasia?
opts: Invasion through the basement membrane with spread to regional lymph nodes
Invasive growth is a feature of malignancy; dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth that may progress to cancer, which is why it is called precancerous.
Disordered epithelial growth, varied cell size and shape, lost architecture, darker larger nuclei
Correct — dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth with varied cell size and shape, lost architectural orientation and darker, larger nuclei; it may progress to cancer.
Orderly growth, typically mesenchymal; uniform cell size; preserved architecture; nuclei of normal size and staining
Every one of these is the opposite: dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth with varied cell size and shape and darker, larger nuclei.
Complete replacement of one mature epithelium by another mature epithelium, with normal architecture retained
That describes metaplasia, a change of one cell type to another under a chronic irritant; dysplasia is disordered epithelial growth with lost architecture.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: In the five main processes of the inflammatory response, what immediately follows the migration of neutrophils?
opts: Chemotaxis
Correct. The order runs increased blood flow, increased permeability, migration of neutrophils, chemotaxis, then leucocyte recruitment and activation.
Increased permeability
Increased permeability is the second process and precedes neutrophil migration; chemotaxis is the process that immediately follows migration.
Exudation of plasma proteins
Exudation is one of the vascular mechanisms, not one of the five main processes; chemotaxis follows neutrophil migration.
Increased blood flow
Increased blood flow is the first of the five processes, well before neutrophil migration; chemotaxis is the process that immediately follows migration.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which description of seborrheic dermatitis is accurate?
opts: Autoimmune T cell activation, affecting the elbows and knees
Autoimmune T cell activation on elbows and knees describes psoriasis; seborrheic dermatitis involves dysbiosis, altered immunity and barrier dysfunction.
Ultraviolet damage, affecting sun-exposed skin
Ultraviolet damage to sun-exposed skin underlies actinic keratosis; seborrheic dermatitis favors the sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk.
Cutaneous microbiome dysbiosis, altered immune response and epidermal barrier dysfunction, affecting regions rich in sebaceous glands — scalp, face and upper trunk
Correct. The cause is incompletely understood, but dysbiosis, altered immunity and barrier dysfunction contribute, in sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk.
A single fungal pathogen acting alone, affecting mainly the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet rather than the sebaceous areas of the skin
No single pathogen explains it, and the palms and soles are not its territory; it affects sebaceous-rich scalp, face and upper trunk with several contributing factors.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which description of how dermatophytes infect the skin is accurate?
opts: Spores secrete keratinases and proteases to metabolize and digest keratin in skin, hair and nails, typically within the stratum corneum
Correct. Dermatophyte spores secrete keratinases and proteases that digest keratin in skin, hair and nails, and infection typically occurs in the stratum corneum.
They invade epidermal basal cells through microabrasions and drive proliferation of the epidermis above them over time
Invading basal cells through microabrasions is how human papillomavirus causes warts; dermatophytes digest keratin in the stratum corneum.
They release histamine from mast cells producing wheals
Histamine release from mast cells produces urticarial wheals; dermatophyte spores secrete keratinases and proteases to digest keratin.
They proliferate within the dermis, digesting collagen
Dermatophytes do not live in the dermis or digest collagen; they typically occupy the stratum corneum and digest keratin.

E.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
E.q: Which statement about bacterial tonsillitis and its abscess complication is accurate?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae; bilateral exudate
Streptococcus pneumoniae causes otitis media and rhinosinusitis, and tonsillar exudate is a symptom of ordinary tonsillitis, not of abscess.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa; fever above 39 degrees
Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes otitis externa, and fever is a symptom of uncomplicated tonsillitis rather than a sign of abscess.
Haemophilus influenzae; odynophagia
Haemophilus is on the otitis media and sinusitis lists, and odynophagia is present in uncomplicated tonsillitis too.
Group A Streptococcus; asymmetric deviation with trismus
Correct. Tonsillitis is usually Group A Streptococcus, and asymmetric tonsillar deviation with trismus indicates a complicating tonsillar abscess.

E.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
E.q: What does eradicating Helicobacter pylori do to cancer risk?
opts: It reverses established gastric adenocarcinoma
Eradication may induce regression of some early MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphomas, not of established gastric adenocarcinoma.
It reduces gastric cancer risk, and some early MALT lymphomas regress
Correct — eradicating Helicobacter pylori with antibiotics can reduce gastric cancer risk and may induce regression of some early MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphomas.
It has no effect on cancer risk once colonization has occurred
Eradication of Helicobacter pylori with antibiotics can reduce the risk of gastric cancer, so colonization does not fix the risk for good.
It increases the risk, because the inflammatory response is protective
Chronic inflammation raises epithelial cell turnover and the chance of acquiring mutations, so it drives cancer rather than protecting against it.

E.io: l — Describe the tumor, nodes, metastases (TNM) staging system
E.q: What do Nx, N0 and N1 to N2 or higher each mean?
opts: Nx, nodes not yet sampled; N0, one node involved; N1 upwards, two or more nodes
N0 means no regional lymph node metastasis, not one node involved, and Nx means the nodes cannot be assessed.
Nx, nodes removed surgically; N0, nodes present but normal in size; N1 upwards, enlarged nodes
N scores metastatic involvement, not node size or removal: Nx means the nodes cannot be assessed, and N0 means no regional lymph node metastasis.
Cannot be assessed; none; increasing number and range involved
Correct — x always means cannot be assessed, 0 always means none found, and the numbers rise with the number and range of nodes involved.
Nx, no regional nodal metastasis; N0, nodes cannot be assessed; N1 upwards, distant metastasis
The meanings of x and 0 are swapped, and distant metastasis is scored by M, as M1, never by N.

E.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
E.q: What does aqueous humor nourish?
opts: The extraocular muscles
The extraocular muscles lie outside the globe; aqueous flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber, nourishing the avascular lens and cornea.
The avascular lens and cornea
Correct — made by the ciliary body, aqueous flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and nourishes the lens and cornea, both of which lack blood vessels.
The retina and the choroid
The choroid nourishes the retina, which aqueous does not reach; aqueous nourishes the avascular lens and cornea.
The optic nerve head
Aqueous does not reach the optic nerve head; it flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil to nourish the avascular lens and cornea.

E.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
E.q: Which feature of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo separates it most cleanly from the other peripheral causes?
opts: The vertigo lasts several hours
Attacks lasting several hours describe Meniere disease. Positional vertigo attacks are measured in seconds, usually under a minute.
It follows a viral upper respiratory infection
A preceding viral upper respiratory infection points at labyrinthitis, which also takes the hearing with it — unlike positional vertigo.
There is NO hearing loss

Correct. Meniere disease and labyrinthitis both take hearing with them; this does not, because the otoconia are a vestibular problem that never touches the cochlea. Attacks also last under a minute and follow head position.
It produces aural fullness
Aural fullness is the fourth element of the Meniere tetrad. Positional vertigo produces no fullness and no hearing change at all.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Through which two routes can the inflammatory process heal an injury or implant site?
opts: Vasoconstriction of the supplying arterioles, or lymphatic drainage of the exudate
Vasoconstriction is the first event of acute inflammation, not a healing route; healing is by new tissue from native parenchymal cells or by fibroblastic scar tissue.
Generation of new tissue by native parenchymal cells, or formation of fibroblastic scar tissue
Correct. The site heals either by new tissue generated by native parenchymal cells or by formation of fibroblastic scar tissue.
Phagocytosis by neutrophils alone, or opsonization by immunoglobulin G
Phagocytosis and opsonization are steps within the response; healing is by new tissue from native parenchymal cells or by fibroblastic scar tissue.
Hemoconcentration followed by stasis, or leukocyte transmigration
Hemoconcentration, stasis and transmigration are events in acute inflammation; healing is by native parenchymal cells or fibroblastic scar tissue.

E.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
E.q: What are drusen composed of?
opts: Calcium and phosphate crystals
Calcium phosphate crystals are not the composition; drusen are extracellular lipofuscin and apolipoprotein debris beneath the pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane.
Cholesterol esters, as in xanthelasma
Cholesterol-filled lesions are xanthelasma on the lids; drusen are lipofuscin and apolipoprotein debris beneath the retinal pigment epithelium.
Lipofuscin and apolipoproteins
Correct — drusen, the hallmark of dry macular degeneration, are discrete yellow extracellular deposits of lipofuscin and apolipoproteins beneath the pigment epithelium.
Fibrin and platelet aggregates
Fibrin and platelets are not drusen; drusen are yellow extracellular deposits of lipofuscin and apolipoproteins beneath the pigment epithelium.

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in which group?
opts: Adults over fifty worldwide
The claim applies to United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four; over seventy-five, macular degeneration leads.
United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four
Correct — chronic hyperglycemia damages retinal capillaries, and diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four.
United States adults aged over seventy-five years
Adults over seventy-five belong to macular degeneration; diabetic retinopathy leads new-onset blindness in United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four.
Children under sixteen worldwide
Children are not the group; diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in United States adults aged twenty to seventy-four.

E.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
E.q: What is the mechanism of presbyopia?
opts: The axial globe shortens with age
The globe does not shorten in presbyopia; it is a lens and ciliary muscle problem, loss of elasticity and accommodation through sclerosis.
The cornea flattens progressively with age, reducing its refractive contribution
The cornea is not the site; presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity and ciliary muscle accommodation through sclerosis, so near focus fails.
The retinal pigment epithelium thins with age
Pigment epithelium degeneration belongs to dry macular degeneration; presbyopia is sclerosis of the lens and loss of ciliary muscle accommodation.
The lens loses elasticity and the ciliary muscle loses accommodation, through sclerosis
Correct — sclerosis stiffens the lens and the ciliary muscle loses accommodation, so the eye can no longer focus on near objects.

E.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
E.q: Which three processes link chronic hepatitis B infection to hepatocellular carcinoma?
opts: Chronic inflammation, regenerative hyperplasia, genomic instability
Correct — chronic infection causes ongoing liver cell injury, stimulating continuous regenerative proliferation of liver cells that are at risk for genetic mutations.
Initiation, promotion, and progression
Initiation and promotion are steps of chemical carcinogenesis; hepatitis B works through chronic injury and regeneration.
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, and abnormal differentiation
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, and abnormal differentiation are histological features of malignancy, not the hepatitis B triad.
Self-renewal, immortality, and differentiation capacity
Self-renewal, immortality, and differentiation capacity describe stem cells, not how hepatitis B causes liver cancer.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Which single event in otosclerosis produces the hearing loss?
opts: Erosion of the incus by the remodeled bone
Erosion of the incus would be discontinuity. Otosclerosis works by fixation: ankylosis of the stapes footplate in the oval window halts vibration transfer.
Hair cell loss at the cochlear base
Hair cell loss from the cochlear base is aminoglycoside damage and gives sensorineural loss. Otosclerosis is a conductive lesion of the stapes footplate.
Accumulation of endolymph in the scala media
Fluid accumulating in the scala media is endolymphatic hydrops in Meniere disease, a sensorineural and vestibular problem rather than a conductive one.
Ankylosis of the stapes footplate
Correct. Once the footplate is fixed it cannot transfer mechanical vibration into the cochlear fluid, and conduction fails progressively. Fixation is the whole lesion.
